title: Grade 7 daily reading
overview: One hundred eighty authentic public-domain readings for Grade 7, five nights a week for 36 weeks: novel chapters (Anne of Green Gables, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Kari the Elephant), complete detective stories read in six parts, Saki’s satirical stories, memoir and essays by Helen Keller and Zitkala-Sa, and complete poems by Langston Hughes, Claude McKay, Countee Cullen, and W. B. Yeats. Most nights are independent reading followed by a short discussion; shared help with older idiom, dialect, or historical context is welcome. Prose nights assume fluent silent reading of roughly 90 to 150 words a minute (counting hyphenated words separately); short poems deliberately give their reading minutes to several rereadings, including one aloud. The suggested 20 to 25 minutes are editorial estimates, not measured reading levels. Each night names a concrete challenge, and questions move from noticing exact details toward interpretation and judgment. Content notes flag historical prejudice, violence, and grief so families can prepare; the texts themselves are not rewritten.

progression.rationale: Complete Anne chapters establish character growth across a sustained narrative; Kari introduces another first-person storytelling voice; Hughes poems ask for rereading of compressed images. Readers distinguish what a speaker feels from what an action establishes.

Anne’s final chapters close one arc with grief and responsibility. Tom Sawyer’s graveyard, oath, and island chapters and later Kari episodes ask readers to track motives, secrecy, and consequences, and to question narrators’ social and animal generalizations. Short Hughes and McKay poems turn attention to memory and belonging.

A four-night Tom Sawyer run (chapters XX–XXIII) holds a plot across consecutive nights before two six-night detective stories require remembering clues and revising explanations. Keller’s account of language learning separates childhood experience from adult interpretation, and Cullen’s “Incident” demands claims tied to exact words. The stretch closes with Tom Sawyer’s cave climax read straight through: lost in the cave, the escape, Injun Joe’s death, and the treasure.

progression.focus: Perspective, power, and the language of experience
progression.rationale: Zitkala-Sa’s autobiographical essays, a third detective story, and more of Keller’s memoir bring sharply different perspectives on schooling, power, and belonging. Readers distinguish a narrator’s claims from supplied evidence and question historical stereotypes without erasing the author’s wording. McKay’s sonnets of loss and Hughes’s title poem extend poetic demand.

Saki’s complete satires depend on withheld information and reversals; Zitkala-Sa’s three-part Blue-Star Woman story sets irony against documentary injustice; Yeats, Cullen, and McKay add allusion, paradox, and the sonnet’s turn. Readers support more than one defensible interpretation when the text leaves room.

Keller’s reflections on authorship, schooling, and reading, Zitkala-Sa’s reform essay with its quoted government report, and a final six-night detective story demand sustained argument and evidence evaluation. The closing poems by McKay, Yeats, and Cullen ask readers to test explanations against particulars and to qualify their judgments independently.

sources.author: Mark Twain
sources.title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
sources.edition: Hartford: The American Publishing Company, 1876, first American edition (illustrated by True W. Williams). Text established against the 1876 pages: Project Gutenberg 74 was collated word by word, in punctuation, italics and paragraphing with the Wikisource transcription proofread from the scans of that edition (Index:The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.djvu). Where they differed, the 1876 reading was adopted when the independent OCR of the 1881 printing from the same plates (Internet Archive adventurestomsa01twaigoog) confirmed it, PG was kept when that OCR confirmed PG, and every other difference (200 places, including all italics and paragraph breaks) was decided on the 1876 page image. Genuine 1876 misprints are kept (for example “sermom,” “Huek,” “posssble,” “corne”). Normalized: display capitals of chapter openings and engraved initials set in ordinary case, typographic quotation marks, italics shown as _underscores_, prose line wrapping; illustration captions omitted. The oath in chapter X, printed as an engraved facsimile of Tom’s handwriting, is transcribed from the engraving; Twain’s footnotes follow the paragraphs that cite them. The text follows the 1876 print itself; the scan-backed Wikisource transcription linked as the catalogue record differs from that print in about 140 places, so the scan is the text source. In chapter VII the printed “love” (p. 76) has a damaged, ink-filled v and is not a misprint.

rights.basis: Original English text published in the United States in 1876 by the American Publishing Company; its US copyright term has expired. No modern introduction, annotation, or translation is supplied, and the 1876 illustrations are omitted.

days.title: A name with an E (Anne of Green Gables, chapter iii)
days.challenge: Read changes in tone and implied motives beneath literal answers.
days.focus: Track how dialogue changes the meaning of usefulness.
days.context: Matthew Cuthbert has brought Anne from the railway station to Green Gables. He and his sister Marilla expected an orphan boy to help on their farm.
days.contentNote: The adults discuss rejecting an orphan because she is a girl; the scene portrays a child’s distress.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, complete chapter; opens “Marilla came briskly forward as Matthew opened the door. But when her eyes fell on th”; closes “. And up-stairs, in the east gable, a lonely, heart-hungry, friendless child cried herself to sleep.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Anne insist on the E in her name when Marilla says spelling cannot matter in speech?
facilitatorNotes: Anne pictures the written name while hearing it. Her preferred spelling offers dignity and a small choice when adults control whether she belongs.
evidence: A-n-n looks dreadful, but A-n-n-e looks so much more distinguished.

questions.prompt: How does the last sentence enlarge what Anne’s earlier tears have shown?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator describes emotional hunger and isolation, inviting readers to see a need for lasting affection rather than merely a dramatic outburst.
evidence: a lonely, heart-hungry, friendless child cried herself to sleep.

questions.prompt: What changes when Matthew asks whether they might be some good to Anne?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla evaluates what a child could do for the household. Matthew reverses that question to ask what the household could give the child; the decision remains unresolved.
evidence: We might be some good to her,

days.title: The Snow Queen at the window (Anne of Green Gables, chapter iv)
days.challenge: Follow shifts between Anne’s speech and the narrator’s judgments.
days.focus: Distinguish a character’s manner from the narrator’s explanation of it.
days.context: After her first night at Green Gables, Anne still expects to be sent away. Marilla plans to consult the woman who arranged the placement.
days.contentNote: The passage includes anxiety about rejection and a brief instance of whipping a horse.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, complete chapter; opens “It was broad daylight when Anne awoke and sat up in bed, staring confusedly at the wi”; closes “ bounced along and saw that aggravating Matthew leaning over the gate, looking wistfully after them.”.

questions.prompt: Why should readers hesitate before deciding that Marilla’s curtness proves she dislikes Anne?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator explicitly explains that Marilla lacks experience talking with children. Her awkward manner can conceal uncertainty rather than deliberate cruelty.
evidence: her uncomfortable ignorance made her crisp and curt when she did not mean to be.

questions.prompt: How does Anne’s refusal to explore the garden complicate the idea that she is always eager for beauty?
facilitatorNotes: She wants to protect herself from attachment because leaving beloved things would hurt. Imagination comforts her but does not remove the danger of disappointment.
evidence: There is no use in loving things if you have to be torn from them, is there?

questions.prompt: How does Matthew’s announcement about Jerry Buote function as an argument without a direct argument?
facilitatorNotes: Hiring a boy for summer addresses the stated need for farm labor and makes retaining Anne more practical. It reinforces his earlier wish through action.
evidence: I told him I guessed I’d hire him for the summer.

days.title: What Anne tells and Marilla hears (Anne of Green Gables, chapter v)
days.challenge: Separate sympathetic inference from facts the passage actually supplies.
days.focus: Infer hardship through the contrast between a speaker’s account and a listener’s response.
days.context: Marilla drives Anne toward Mrs. Spencer’s house to investigate the mistaken placement. During the journey she asks about Anne’s early life.
days.contentNote: Anne recounts parental deaths, alcoholism, poverty, neglect, and heavy childcare responsibilities.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, complete chapter; opens ““Do you know,” said Anne confidentially, “I’ve made up my mind to enjoy this drive. I”; closes “said Anne mournfully. “I don’t want to get there. Somehow, it will seem like the end of everything.””.

questions.prompt: Why does Anne offer to tell what she imagines before giving her history?
facilitatorNotes: Her imagined life feels more interesting and gives her control over a painful story. Her preference does not prevent her from eventually supplying concrete biographical facts.
evidence: If you’ll only let me tell you what I _imagine_ about myself

questions.prompt: What does Marilla infer that Anne avoids saying directly about her former homes?
facilitatorNotes: Anne tries to credit adults with good intentions, but Marilla recognizes repeated childcare burdens, poverty, and neglect. Her interpretation draws on the account rather than a direct accusation by Anne.
evidence: a life of drudgery and poverty and neglect

questions.prompt: Why does arriving at the destination feel like an ending to Anne while the scenery has offered pleasure?
facilitatorNotes: Beauty has allowed temporary enjoyment and imaginative escape. Arrival may settle her future by ending the possibility of staying at Green Gables.
evidence: Somehow, it will seem like the end of everything.

days.title: The decision at Mrs. Spencer’s (Anne of Green Gables, chapter vi)
days.challenge: Notice the difference between an adult’s stated explanation and the narrator’s account.
days.focus: Trace a decision through external pressures and private reactions.
days.context: Marilla has learned of Anne’s difficult childhood but has not decided whether to keep her. She arrives at Mrs. Spencer’s house to untangle the mistaken request.
days.contentNote: Adults discuss placing an orphan as household labor, and Anne fears renewed mistreatment.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, complete chapter; opens “Get there they did, however, in due season. Mrs. Spencer lived in a big yellow house ”; closes “little girls. Anyhow, we’ve decided on the experiment and goodness only knows what will come of it.””.

questions.prompt: How does Marilla’s response to the message mix-up differ from Mrs. Spencer’s?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs. Spencer blames Nancy’s carelessness; Marilla accepts responsibility for entrusting an important message to an unreliable chain of speakers.
evidence: We should have come to you ourselves

questions.prompt: Why does the convenient offer from Mrs. Blewett fail to feel like a solution to Marilla?
facilitatorNotes: The offer would relieve Marilla of responsibility but expose Anne to harsh treatment. Anne’s distress and Blewett’s expectations make the ethical cost visible.
evidence: I’ll expect you to earn your keep

questions.prompt: Compare the narrator’s sunrise image with Anne’s whispered question. What do both convey?
facilitatorNotes: Hope transforms Anne’s face, but she still fears that the possibility may vanish. Joy and insecurity coexist before the adults make their final decision.
evidence: as if speaking aloud might shatter the glorious possibility

days.title: A prayer in Anne’s own words (Anne of Green Gables, chapter vii)
days.challenge: Interpret religious language as part of the characters’ historical setting.
days.focus: Explain how a comic misunderstanding reveals a serious need.
days.context: Marilla has privately agreed that Anne may stay, but has not yet told her. At bedtime she discovers that Anne’s knowledge of religious words differs from her own expectations.
days.contentNote: The characters express Christian beliefs and use the historical judgmental term “heathen.” Discuss these as the characters’ views.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, complete chapter; opens “When Marilla took Anne up to bed that night she said stiffly:”; closes “ife of it so far, but my time has come at last and I suppose I’ll just have to make the best of it.””.

questions.prompt: What difference appears between Anne’s ability to recite the catechism and her experience of prayer?
facilitatorNotes: She remembers impressive-sounding language but does not share Marilla’s habits or assumptions. Memorization alone has not supplied personal meaning.
evidence: just like a big organ playing

questions.prompt: Why does Marilla abandon the familiar children’s prayer she intended to teach?
facilitatorNotes: She recognizes that a conventional image of secure childhood does not fit a child who has lacked human affection. The narrator links religious understanding with lived care.
evidence: through the medium of human love

questions.prompt: What makes the closing “Yours respectfully” both funny and revealing?
facilitatorNotes: Anne borrows a letter ending because she knows a request should have a conclusion. The mistake shows sincere improvisation, not an intention to mock prayer.
evidence: I felt a prayer should be finished off in some way

days.title: Kari the Elephant: a rescue misunderstood (chapter i)
days.challenge: Track three mistaken interpretations during a rapidly moving rescue and distinguish observation from the narrator’s explanations.
days.focus: How delayed recognition and changing comparisons turn the apparently helpless elephant into the rescuer.
days.context: The nine-year-old narrator remembers caring for Kari, a young elephant. This excerpt opens the novel and completes its first rescue episode.
days.contentNote: Contains a near-drowning and outdated rescue practices; this fictional episode is not first-aid instruction. Its claims about animal behaviour are the narrator’s beliefs, not established scientific guidance.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, opening rescue episode; from “Kari, the elephant, was five months old when he was given to me to take car…” through “…d not punish him that day because he had done his duty by saving the life of the boy.”

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator first think Kari needs rescuing, and which details gradually reverse that judgment?
facilitatorNotes: He sees a trunk struggling above the water and imagines drowning, but Kari summons him, points him toward the boy through action, and finally pulls both humans ashore. Follow the order of discovery rather than saying the narrator knew Kari’s plan from the beginning.
evidence: I thought he was drowning.
his trunk stretched out like a hand waiting for mine
He pulled us both ashore.

questions.prompt: How do the comparisons to a hawk, an arrow and a lasso change the pace and your understanding of Kari?
facilitatorNotes: The hawk makes the normally slow animal suddenly swift; the arrow gives the narrator a brief upward burst; the lasso first suggests danger but becomes rescue. Readers may stress excitement or the limits of the child’s viewpoint, supported by the shifting images.
evidence: suddenly darted down like a hawk
shot upwards like an arrow
I felt a lasso around my neck.

questions.prompt: Why end a heroic rescue with Kari eating his favourite twigs instead of obediently collecting the cows?
facilitatorNotes: The comic ending restores appetite and unpredictability to an animal just presented as a hero. The narrator excuses this lapse because saving the boy outweighs it; discuss whether this is affection, fair judgment or both.
evidence: was eating the best of them, without any concern for the cows, the cowherd or myself.
he had done his duty by saving the life of the boy.

days.title: Kari the Elephant: theft, memory and teaching (chapter i)
days.challenge: Distinguish the sequence of evidence in the banana mystery from the narrator’s moral generalisations about animals.
days.focus: Affection, punishment and the uneasy comparison between educating an elephant and raising a child.
days.context: After Kari rescues a boy, the narrator describes several episodes of training. This completes the opening chapter; it includes the command that will matter in the next jungle adventure.
days.contentNote: Includes whipping an animal and a boy nearly drowned in retaliation. The narrator’s approval of punishment is open to critique, not a recommended way to treat animals or people.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, remaining training episodes; from “Kari was like a baby. He had to be trained to be good and if you did not te…” through “…ou will find that he has made a road right through the jungle straight to your house.”

questions.prompt: How do the banana clues expose unfair blame before they identify the actual thief?
facilitatorNotes: The family blames servants, then the child; the child then wrongly suspects others. A smashed banana and the snake-like trunk finally supply evidence. The episode exposes how readily certainty runs ahead of observation.
evidence: my family blamed the servants
this time the blame was put on me
I realized that Kari was the thief.

questions.prompt: Does the Sudu episode establish that Kari’s retaliation is fair, or only that the narrator considers it fair?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator connects the attack to the earlier whipping and reports later reconciliation, but Sudu’s near-loss of consciousness makes the proportionality troubling. Accept supported disagreement with the narrator; his moral conclusion is not the same as an impartial demonstration.
evidence: he was nearly senseless.
An elephant is willing to be punished for having done wrong
Since that day Sudu has never hurt a living creature.

questions.prompt: Compare “Mali,” “Dhat” and the master call. How does each explanation move from daily convenience toward danger?
facilitatorNotes: Walking and sitting serve routine movement and mounting; the master call creates an escape route in a dark jungle. Learning times also increase, preparing the reader to see training as a sustained relationship rather than instant control.
evidence: Kari learned "Mali" after three lessons
it took him three weeks to learn "Dhat."
Soon you will find that he has made a road right through the jungle straight to your house.

days.title: Kari the Elephant: terror on the night road (chapter ii)
days.challenge: Compare what the children directly witness with what the brother infers about the unseen bear.
days.focus: The movement from lyrical calm to bodily danger, followed by an explanation through wounded pride.
days.context: Kari is now five. The narrator and his brother ride through the jungle at night; they know the master call that asks him to open an escape route.
days.contentNote: Includes a frightened elephant’s bleeding injury and dangerous riding. Statements about bears and elephants belong to this literary narrator’s account rather than practical wildlife instruction.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, complete chapter text excluding its heading; from “When Kari grew to be five years old, he was almost as high as the ceiling. …” through “…rn to the place where he lost his pride. For to be frightened is to lose one's pride.”

questions.prompt: Which details make the beginning feel safe and reverent, and how does the first disturbance overturn that mood?
facilitatorNotes: Silenced bells, star imagery and the children falling asleep create trust and quiet. The roar, lunge and frantic grip abruptly replace that stillness with danger. Read the transition aloud to hear the change in verbs and rhythm.
evidence: silence being the voice of God
the velvet blue of the sky is like a river of stillness
a terrible roar, a ghastly trumpeting of the elephant

questions.prompt: What does the brother know for certain about the bear, and where is he constructing an explanation?
facilitatorNotes: He infers a sleeping bear from season, Kari’s surprise and the injured trunk; the boys did not watch the initial encounter. “Must have” and “no doubt” signal a confident interpretation rather than eyewitness evidence.
evidence: must have come upon him without suspecting his presence
this one, no doubt, was so sleepy
Yes, it was bleeding

questions.prompt: How does Kari’s refusal to return to the road alter the meaning of his rescue?
facilitatorNotes: He remains capable of enormous physical work despite pain, yet the narrator attributes his choice of route to lost pride. Readers may see both vulnerability and ingenuity; challenge the universal claim that no animal returns to a humiliating place.
evidence: He shook his head--that meant "No."
with one push of his back, knocked this tree down.
For to be frightened is to lose one's pride.

days.title: Kari the Elephant: the making of an unlikely pair (chapter iii)
days.challenge: Follow a shift from fear and social ranking to companionship, while questioning the narrator’s human labels for animals.
days.focus: How shared food and mutual observation accomplish what forced introductions do not.
days.context: Before visiting a city, the narrator tries to accustom Kari to unfamiliar dogs and to Kopee, his pet monkey. This passage reaches their first mischievous outing together.
days.contentNote: An elephant kills a dog; people threaten animals with stones. Class-based comparisons such as “inferiors” express the narrator’s analogy, which readers may question.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, preparation for town and the bazaar episode; from “When Kari was about five years old, another adventure befell him. We took h…” through “…you know that mangoes taste very much like strawberries and cream with sugar on them.”

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator’s plan to teach Kari to like unfamiliar dogs initially fail?
facilitatorNotes: Familiar village dogs do not bark, so they provide no practice with the actual problem. In the unfamiliar village, harassment escalates and the training becomes harmful. Distinguish becoming unreactive afterward from having demonstrated a humane teaching method.
evidence: they never paid any attention to him
it all the more difficult to train Kari to like other dogs
Kari had stepped on one of the dogs and killed it

questions.prompt: What changes in the food-sharing scene that makes Kopee willing to approach Kari?
facilitatorNotes: Kari does not attack when the fruit is gone, and Kopee then observes their similar diets from the roof. Trust develops through particular behaviour and recognition of common needs, not merely an order to get along.
evidence: the elephant turned away from him
lived on twigs and fruits and saplings just like himself
he walked on.

questions.prompt: Does the bazaar episode show that the narrator has gained control of his two companions? Explain its irony.
facilitatorNotes: The pair now cooperates socially but not morally: Kopee draws the crowd away while Kari steals fruit. Their friendship fulfils one goal while creating a new problem. It is reasonable to read the episode as deliberate teamwork or opportunistic behaviour; the text does not prove a prior plan.
evidence: the monkey jumped off and climbed up to the top of the pile
Kari, however, put out his trunk and helped himself
The moment he heard the people coming back from the monkey chase, he ran away

days.title: Kari the Elephant: the mysterious night journey (chapter iii)
days.challenge: Reread extended sound and light images and separate admitted uncertainty from confident animal generalisations.
days.focus: The narrator’s movement between wonder, prayer, practical travel and comic social judgment.
days.context: Kari and Kopee have become companions. The boy sets off for the city with both animals; this completes the journey chapter, including its morning prayer.
days.contentNote: The novel makes sweeping claims about Indian religious life and animal behaviour, and refers to predators killing prey. Read these as historical literary representations, not universal statements about a people or scientific facts.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, night journey through arrival beside the caravan; from “At last we set off for the city, Kari, and Kopee now the best of friends. I…” through “… the caravan was ready to move on. Nothing exciting happened the rest of the journey.”

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator leave the dark moving shapes unidentified instead of resolving the mystery?
facilitatorNotes: Possible elephants or clouds remain uncertain, which lets Silence become a personified presence. The passage values the experience of wonder rather than supplying a factual explanation; accept readings that emphasise humility or dreamlike perception.
evidence: We did not know what we saw.
No one knows what it was
Silence walked by

questions.prompt: Choose two images around dawn and explain how sound and light work together in them.
facilitatorNotes: The bird’s note and “gleam of whiteness” join hearing and seeing; the sun as a horse of flame gives light motion. Students should explain their chosen words, not just label a simile. Other well-supported images, including the foam of noise, are valid.
evidence: a bird's note fell through the jungle and there was a gleam of whiteness
the sun came leaping over the forest like a horse of flame

questions.prompt: How does the prayer’s movement from sound to Silence connect with the narrator’s decision to join human company?
facilitatorNotes: The prayer treats silence as a path toward spiritual understanding, while the caravan is chosen for route knowledge and companionship. These can coexist: reverence for the forest does not remove practical needs. A reading that finds tension should show both sides.
evidence: From sound into Silence,
the caravan people knew the shortest way
I also preferred to travel in human company rather than alone.

days.title: Kari the Elephant: ceremony and embarrassment in Benares (chapter iv)
days.challenge: Track changes in the narrator’s confidence as public grandeur gives way to private problems with his animals.
days.focus: Contrasts between solemn description, teasing dialogue and comic loss of control.
days.context: The caravan has reached Benares. The narrator admires its evening streets and joins a dawn gathering, but Kari and Kopee interrupt his sense of dignity.
days.contentNote: Contains a threatened parrot, harsh animal handling and a remembered infant abduction by a monkey. The passage includes broad historical claims about a city and religion and an inaccurate elephant-and-mouse explanation; these belong to the novel’s narrator.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, arrival, dawn ceremony and the stolen purse; from “As the sun went down in the gathering silence of the evening, we entered th…” through “… so that in case he should run away again I could prick his neck and make him behave.”

questions.prompt: How do the descriptions of water make Benares appear both enduring and vulnerable?
facilitatorNotes: The city’s long survival and towers convey age, but the river as an ax and its gnawing whisper threaten foundations. The imagery refuses a simple picture of immovable grandeur; readers can discuss whether the passage admires endurance or imagines decline.
evidence: The river like a liquid ax
the whispering Ganges gnawing at the stone embankments
the age of India

questions.prompt: Compare the narrator’s tone toward the angry parrot owner with his tone when Kari will not tolerate Kopee. What inconsistency emerges?
facilitatorNotes: He dismisses another person’s anger as foolish in a cool evening, yet grows irritated and throws a stone when his own animals embarrass him. This creates a basis for questioning his self-assurance rather than assuming his judgments are always fair.
evidence: Why art thou irate when the evening is so cool
I, too, was very irritated
I threw a stone at the monkey

questions.prompt: Why insert the earlier story of the baby and the baboon into the stolen-purse episode?
facilitatorNotes: The memory offers a strategy: exchange bananas for the held object rather than using force. It also enlarges the comic “bandit” comparison while reminding readers of real fear. The later servant’s false accusation echoes the danger of judging before gathering evidence.
evidence: Monkeys are very much like bandits.
that was not ransom enough for him
one of them was accusing his servant of having stolen his purse

days.title: An insult and an unexpected defender (Anne of Green Gables, chapter ix)
days.challenge: Read irony and shifts in a character’s self-judgment.
days.focus: Distinguish criticism of conduct from empathy for its cause.
days.context: Anne has now lived at Green Gables for two weeks. A neighbor, Mrs. Rachel Lynde, visits to inspect the child whom Matthew and Marilla have adopted.
days.contentNote: The passage includes body-shaming, hostile remarks about orphans, and a suggestion of corporal punishment that Marilla rejects.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, complete chapter; opens “Anne had been a fortnight at Green Gables before Mrs. Lynde arrived to inspect her. M”; closes “nded countenance her lips twitched with amusement and she felt a most reprehensible desire to laugh.”.

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Lynde’s claim to frankness become questionable in this scene?
facilitatorNotes: Her comments attack a child’s appearance without any useful purpose. The narrator’s praise of people who speak their mind is ironic in the setting of the resulting pain.
evidence: pride themselves on speaking their mind without fear or favour

questions.prompt: Why does Marilla’s childhood memory matter to her response to Anne?
facilitatorNotes: Remembering a lasting insult helps Marilla understand why Anne is hurt. She still objects to the outburst, so empathy does not instantly erase her disciplinary judgment.
evidence: Marilla was every day of fifty before the sting had gone out of that memory.

questions.prompt: What conflict makes Anne refuse the required apology?
facilitatorNotes: She regrets upsetting Marilla but remains glad she answered Mrs. Lynde. She thinks an apology would require an untrue claim of remorse.
evidence: I can’t say I’m sorry when I’m not, can I?

days.title: The surprising apology (Anne of Green Gables, chapter x)
days.challenge: Follow the narrator’s explanation of mixed emotions.
days.focus: Evaluate sincerity without assuming that enjoyment makes feeling false.
days.context: After Mrs. Lynde insults her appearance, Anne answers angrily. Marilla confines her to her room until she will apologize; Matthew privately visits her.
days.contentNote: The apology repeats hurtful judgments about Anne’s appearance and social position.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, complete chapter; opens “Marilla said nothing to Matthew about the affair that evening; but when Anne proved s”; closes ““Thanks be to goodness for that,” breathed Marilla in devout relief.”.

questions.prompt: What changes in Anne before Matthew asks her to apologize, and what obstacle remains?
facilitatorNotes: Her anger has faded into shame, but admitting it publicly feels humiliating. Affection for Matthew helps her act on regret that already exists.
evidence: I wasn’t in a temper any more

questions.prompt: Why does Marilla feel her punishment has gone wrong even though Anne apologizes?
facilitatorNotes: Anne enjoys performing a grand, thorough apology. Marilla wanted humiliation to punish her, but the narrator explicitly says the apology is sincere.
evidence: There was no mistaking her sincerity

questions.prompt: How does the walk home show a result beyond settling the quarrel?
facilitatorNotes: Anne identifies Green Gables as a real home and reaches for Marilla’s hand. Marilla experiences unfamiliar parental tenderness, showing a deepening bond.
evidence: It’s lovely to be going home and know it’s home

days.title: Dream Variations
days.challenge: Reread both stanzas aloud, tracking changed verbs, punctuation, and the final color words rather than treating the second stanza as a copy.
days.focus: How variation transforms a wish for free movement into an energetic assertion of belonging.
days.context: This complete poem from The Weary Blues uses two related versions of a dreamed day. Read it twice, then compare corresponding lines.

excerpt.locator: DREAM VARIATIONS; complete individual poem; opening “To fling my arms wide In some place of the sun, To whirl and to dance Till the”; closing “quick day is done. Rest at pale evening.... A tall, slim tree.... Night coming tenderly Black like me.”.

questions.prompt: How does “Dance! whirl! whirl!” change the energy of the second stanza compared with the first stanza’s account of dancing?
facilitatorNotes: The first uses a flowing wish, “To whirl and to dance”; the second breaks into urgent commands and repetition. Readers may hear celebration or insistence, but should explain how punctuation and shortened phrasing produce that tone.
evidence: Dance! whirl! whirl!

questions.prompt: Why might the speaker welcome night as “Dark like me” and then “Black like me,” rather than describe darkness as frightening?
facilitatorNotes: The night arrives gently and tenderly, offering rest and recognition. The speaker makes Blackness a source of kinship with the natural world. Do not require a single equation between each color and a historical event.
evidence:
Night coming tenderly
Black like me.

questions.prompt: What changes when the dream moves from “some place of the sun” to “the face of the sun”?
facilitatorNotes: The vague first location becomes more direct and exposed. Connect that shift with the more forceful movement in the second stanza; an interpretation emphasizing intimacy with nature or bold self-presence can both be supported.
evidence: In the face of the sun,

days.title: Puffed sleeves and unanswered questions (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xi)
days.challenge: Recognize that a comic child’s criticism may expose adult concerns.
days.focus: Compare social belonging, outward correctness, and understanding.
days.context: Marilla has made Anne three plain dresses and prepared her for Sunday school. Anne attends alone because Marilla has a headache.
days.contentNote: The scene includes social exclusion, Christian worship, and a quoted verse referring to battle.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, complete chapter; opens ““Well, how do you like them?” said Marilla.”; closes “en visible and accusing shape and form in the person of this outspoken morsel of neglected humanity.”.

questions.prompt: Why is imagining puffed sleeves harder in class than at home?
facilitatorNotes: Surrounded by classmates wearing real fashionable sleeves, Anne feels the social difference directly. Her wish concerns belonging as well as pretty clothing.
evidence: it was awfully hard there among the others who had really truly puffs

questions.prompt: How does Anne’s complaint about who asks questions challenge the teaching method?
facilitatorNotes: She answers successfully but has questions of her own that the stern classroom discourages. Recitation is not the same as curiosity or understanding.
evidence: I don’t think it was fair for her to do all the asking.

questions.prompt: Why is Marilla unable to condemn all Anne’s remarks about the service?
facilitatorNotes: Some criticisms echo opinions Marilla has kept private. Anne’s frankness makes the adult confront her own unspoken judgments.
evidence: what she herself had really thought deep down in her heart for years

days.title: The promise in the garden (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xii)
days.challenge: Use differences in speech to compare characters without ranking them.
days.focus: Trace the movement from fear of rejection toward reciprocal friendship.
days.context: Anne is reprimanded for decorating her Sunday hat with real flowers. Then Marilla offers to introduce her to a neighboring girl, Diana Barry.
days.contentNote: Anne fears being sent away again; adults also voice historical assumptions about girls’ behavior.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, complete chapter; opens “It was not until the next Friday that Marilla heard the story of the flower-wreathed ”; closes “nted to keep the child and that I’m getting fond of her, but don’t you rub it in, Matthew Cuthbert.””.

questions.prompt: What inconsistency does Anne see in the criticism of her flowered hat?
facilitatorNotes: Flowers on dresses and artificial flowers on hats are accepted, while her real flowers are condemned. Her question exposes an unstated social convention.
evidence: What was the difference?

questions.prompt: How do Anne and Diana approach their new friendship differently?
facilitatorNotes: Anne treats it as a solemn lifelong bond with an oath; Diana responds with practical pleasure at having a nearby playmate. Both welcome friendship despite different styles.
evidence: It will be jolly to have somebody to play with.

questions.prompt: What does Anne’s plan for the chocolates reveal about what friendship means to her?
facilitatorNotes: She values being able to give Diana something. Sharing increases her pleasure because the relationship is reciprocal, not simply a source of gifts.
evidence: The other half will taste twice as sweet to me if I give some to her.

days.title: The Negro Speaks of Rivers
days.challenge: Distinguish a collective poetic speaker from one person’s literal lifetime, and follow the long river sentences across their clauses.
days.focus: Ancestral memory expressed through repeated river imagery and the depth of a soul.
days.context: The speaker links several rivers and distant periods through a single “I.” Treat this as a literary voice rather than a claim that one person witnessed every event.
days.contentNote: The title retains the period racial term “Negro.” The poem refers to slavery-era history without graphic depiction.

excerpt.locator: THE NEGRO SPEAKS OF RIVERS; complete individual poem; opening “I’ve known rivers:”; closing “My soul has grown deep like the rivers.”.

questions.prompt: How does “older than the flow of human blood” prepare us to understand the speaker’s extraordinary memories?
facilitatorNotes: It establishes a timescale larger than an individual life. The memories can represent a people’s inherited experience or humanity’s long relationship with rivers; the text does not require a literal immortal narrator.
evidence: older than the flow of human blood in human veins.

questions.prompt: What work does the change from the Mississippi’s “muddy” appearance to “golden” sunset do in the poem?
facilitatorNotes: It turns an ordinary or devalued surface into radiance while retaining the same river. Readers may connect it to dignity, hope, or changed perception, but should keep those claims tied to the visual transformation.
evidence: I’ve seen its muddy bosom turn all golden in the sunset.

questions.prompt: Read the repeated sentence about the soul before and after the river memories. How has its meaning expanded?
facilitatorNotes: Initially it announces depth; after the memories, depth includes long experience, building, nurturing, and endurance. Repetition frames and gathers the intervening images rather than merely repeating information.
evidence: My soul has grown deep like the rivers.

days.title: The pleasure before the picnic (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xiii)
days.challenge: Follow a long speech whose digressions reveal values.
days.focus: Compare conflicting arguments about hope and disappointment.
days.context: Anne and Diana have made a woodland playhouse. News of a Sunday-school picnic brings Anne excitement and a worry about contributing food.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIII, complete chapter; opens ““It’s time Anne was in to do her sewing,” said Marilla, glancing at the clock and the”; closes “e hold the brooch for one minute, Marilla? Do you think amethysts can be the souls of good violets?””.

questions.prompt: Why does Marilla’s promise of a food basket mean more than permission to attend?
facilitatorNotes: Anne fears the embarrassment of arriving without a contribution. The basket lets her participate on similar terms to the other children.
evidence: I’d feel terribly humiliated if I had to go without a basket.

questions.prompt: How do Marilla and Anne assess the risk of looking forward to something?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla worries that high hopes magnify disappointment. Anne argues that anticipation provides pleasure even if the event never happens; readers can weigh both claims.
evidence: nothing can prevent you from having the fun of looking forward to them

questions.prompt: How does the brooch connect the two characters despite their different styles?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla cherishes its family history and beauty; Anne responds imaginatively to the color. Both value something beyond usefulness, though they express it differently.
evidence: her mother who in turn had bequeathed it to Marilla

days.title: Friends across a classroom (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xvii)
days.challenge: Read allusions and formal language without losing the emotional situation.
days.focus: Use actions and indirect messages to qualify a character’s dramatic claims.
days.context: Anne accidentally served Diana wine while believing it was raspberry cordial. Diana’s mother has forbidden their friendship. Anne has also stayed away from school after a conflict with Gilbert Blythe.
days.contentNote: The context involves accidental alcohol consumption; Anne speaks melodramatically of dying of grief.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVII, complete chapter; opens “The next afternoon Anne, bending over her patchwork at the kitchen window, happened t”; closes “about her. But really, Marilla, one can’t stay sad very long in such an interesting world, can one?””.

questions.prompt: What discovery gives Anne comfort during the painful farewell?
facilitatorNotes: Diana explicitly says she loves Anne. Anne had assumed being liked was the most she could expect, so this assurance matters even while separation continues.
evidence: I didn’t think anybody could love me.

questions.prompt: Why is Diana’s silence in class misleading if considered without her later note?
facilitatorNotes: The silence follows her mother’s command, not a change of affection. The note and handmade bookmark supply evidence that her loyalty continues.
evidence: Mother says I’m not to play with you or talk to you even in school.

questions.prompt: How does the narration distinguish Gilbert’s academic rivalry from Anne’s?
facilitatorNotes: Gilbert competes in a friendly spirit and congratulates her. Anne’s unresolved grudge makes his generosity frustrate her wish to make defeat sting.
evidence: It would have been ever so much sweeter to her if he had felt the sting of his defeat.

days.title: Mother to Son
days.challenge: Follow one extended metaphor while hearing the mother’s dialect as a purposeful literary voice.
days.focus: The relationship between a speaker’s lived example and her advice to a child.
days.context: The mother speaks directly to her son. Read the staircase both as a pictured place and as her way of describing a life.
days.contentNote: The original dialect and the transcription’s spelling “a-cimbin’” are retained; they should not be treated as errors in a student’s intelligence or voice.

excerpt.locator: MOTHER TO SON; complete individual poem; opening “Well, son, I’ll tell you: Life for me ain’t been no crystal stair. It’s had tacks in it,”; closing “now— For I’se still goin’, honey, I’se still climbin’, And life for me ain’t been no crystal stair.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem name tacks, splinters, torn boards, and bare places instead of simply saying that life was difficult?
facilitatorNotes: The concrete hazards make hardship bodily and uneven: some hurt the feet, others interrupt safe support. Different readers may emphasize poverty, danger, or uncertainty if they connect the inference to these details.
evidence:
It’s had tacks in it,
And splinters,
And boards torn up,

questions.prompt: How do the landings, corners, and darkness complicate the idea that climbing is a simple straight path?
facilitatorNotes: Landings suggest stages or pauses; corners hide what comes next; darkness means moving without assurance. These features make persistence flexible and uncertain rather than an effortless upward march.
evidence:
And reachin’ landin’s,
And turnin’ corners,
And sometimes goin’ in the dark

questions.prompt: Does the mother base her authority mainly on a promise that things will soon be easy, or on something else?
facilitatorNotes: She gives no promise of a crystal stair ahead. Her authority is her ongoing effort and affection: she is still climbing and addresses him as honey. Discuss encouragement without turning it into blame for people who need help.
evidence:
For I’se still goin’, honey,
I’se still climbin’,

days.title: The wood Anne made haunted (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xx)
days.challenge: Track how imagery turns ordinary sensations into imagined threats.
days.focus: Separate an experience of fear from evidence supporting a belief.
days.context: A year after Anne’s arrival, Green Gables feels like home. Anne and Diana have invented frightening stories about a nearby grove.
days.contentNote: Imagined ghost stories mention murder, death, and frightening bodily images; an adult compels Anne to face her fear.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XX, complete chapter; opens “Spring had come once more to Green Gables—the beautiful, capricious, reluctant Canadi”; closes “h, Mar—Marilla,” chattered Anne, “I’ll b-b-be cont-t-tented with c-c-commonplace places after this.””.

questions.prompt: How can the gable room remain physically similar yet have a different character?
facilitatorNotes: Anne’s belongings and vivid inner life give emotional warmth to the once-bare room. The narrator uses imagined fabric to represent that transformation.
evidence: tapestried the bare room with splendid filmy tissues of rainbow and moonshine

questions.prompt: What weakness appears in Anne’s story about a warning that someone would die within nine days?
facilitatorNotes: The person lived another two years, contradicting the specific prediction. Anne treats a much later death as confirmation instead of testing the original claim.
evidence: He didn’t, but he died two years after

questions.prompt: Choose one sensation on Anne’s walk and explain how the narration supplies an ordinary source for it.
facilitatorNotes: Birch bark becomes a frightening white shape; rubbing boughs produce a wail; bats suggest supernatural wings. The fear is real although these details do not establish ghosts.
evidence: The long-drawn wail of two old boughs rubbing against each other

days.title: An invitation addressed to Miss Anne (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxii)
days.challenge: Compare an adult’s model of good behavior with a child’s account of effort.
days.focus: Explain how recognition and belonging change an ordinary event’s importance.
days.context: Mrs. Allan, the new minister’s wife, invites members of her Sunday-school class to tea. Anne receives her own written invitation.
days.contentNote: The characters discuss Christian ideas of goodness and historical objections to women teachers.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXII, complete chapter; opens ““And what are your eyes popping out of your head about now?” asked Marilla, when Anne”; closes “ see how I’m going to live through the two weeks before school begins, I’m so impatient to see her.””.

questions.prompt: Why does the address on the invitation become a treasure to Anne?
facilitatorNotes: Being addressed formally as Miss Anne Shirley gives her a feeling of importance and recognition. The emotional value exceeds the practical message.
evidence: That is the first time I was ever called ‘Miss.’

questions.prompt: How does Marilla’s advice about Mrs. Allan redirect Anne’s worries about etiquette?
facilitatorNotes: Instead of monitoring every possible mistake, Anne can consider her host’s comfort. The advice shifts attention from self-conscious performance to consideration.
evidence: think of Mrs. Allan and what would be nicest and most agreeable for her

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs. Allan’s admission about geometry encourage Anne?
facilitatorNotes: Someone Anne regards as admirable shares an academic difficulty. That challenges Anne’s tendency to see goodness or competence as an all-or-nothing natural gift.
evidence: Mrs. Allan told me she was a dunce at geometry, too.

days.title: Epilogue (“I, too, sing America”)
days.challenge: Notice the change from singing America to being America and connect it to the poem’s shift from present exclusion to future confidence.
days.focus: The table and kitchen as concrete images of exclusion, dignity, and national belonging.
days.context: This poem is titled “Epilogue” in the 1926 collection and is widely recognizable by its opening “I, too, sing America.” The supplied text follows that edition.
days.contentNote: The poem depicts racial exclusion at a meal and challenges it.

excerpt.locator: EPILOGUE; complete individual poem; opening “I, too, sing America.”; closing “I, too, am America.”.

questions.prompt: What does sending the speaker to the kitchen when company comes reveal about the people issuing the order?
facilitatorNotes: They want to hide or subordinate him while presenting themselves to visitors. The domestic action suggests a wider exclusion, but readers should first explain exactly who controls visibility and seating.
evidence:
They send me to eat in the kitchen
When company comes,

questions.prompt: Why do laughing, eating well, and growing strong matter before the prediction about tomorrow?
facilitatorNotes: They show the speaker retaining life and self-worth under exclusion, and prepare the strength of the future claim. The laughter can sound defiant or confident; it need not mean the treatment is harmless.
evidence:
But I laugh,
And eat well,
And grow strong.

questions.prompt: How is the final “I, too, am America” different from the opening “I, too, sing America”?
facilitatorNotes: Singing contributes a voice, while being America claims membership as a fact. The final line makes the speaker part of the nation itself, not merely someone asking permission to perform for it.
evidence: I, too, am America.

days.title: The cost of a dare (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxiii)
days.challenge: Track irony without minimizing an injury.
days.focus: Evaluate competing meanings of courage and responsibility.
days.context: At Diana’s party, competitive dares become increasingly risky. Anne is especially unwilling to let Josie Pye appear superior.
days.contentNote: A child accepts a dangerous roof-walking dare, falls, and breaks her ankle; the scene includes fear that she may have died.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIII, complete chapter; opens “Anne had to live through more than two weeks, as it happened. Almost a month having e”; closes “e,” said Marilla, “and that is that your fall off the Barry roof hasn’t injured your tongue at all.””.

questions.prompt: How do Diana and Anne disagree about what the dare requires?
facilitatorNotes: Diana says a dangerous dare is unfair and should be refused. Anne imagines her honor requires accepting it, confusing social pride with obligation.
evidence: My honour is at stake

questions.prompt: What does Marilla discover when she sees Anne being carried home?
facilitatorNotes: Fear exposes the depth of affection she has not fully acknowledged. Her later sharpness occurs alongside relief, so it does not erase this discovery.
evidence: Anne was dearer to her than anything on earth.

questions.prompt: How does Anne’s experience revise one of her romantic wishes?
facilitatorNotes: She had wanted to faint because it seemed dramatic. Actual injury makes fainting painful and unpleasant, separating imagined glamour from lived consequences.
evidence: It’s not a bit nice to faint, after all.

days.title: What counts as learning? (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxiv)
days.challenge: Consider whether pleasure and worthwhile effort can coexist.
days.focus: Compare assumptions about useful schoolwork.
days.context: Anne returns to school after recovering from a broken ankle. Her new teacher, Miss Stacy, introduces field studies, exercises, recitations, and a concert.
days.contentNote: The dialogue includes body-shaming and historical attitudes toward schooling and gender.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIV, complete chapter; opens “It was October again when Anne was ready to go back to school—a glorious October, all”; closes “appreciation” sometimes does quite as much good as all the conscientious “bringing up” in the world.”.

questions.prompt: What evidence suggests Miss Stacy helps Anne in more than the subjects she already enjoys?
facilitatorNotes: Anne loves compositions but also reports beginning to understand geometry because explanations are clear. Support includes a difficult area, not only praise for a strength.
evidence: Miss Stacy makes it so clear.

questions.prompt: How do Marilla and Anne evaluate the concert’s mixture of fun and purpose?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla suspects fun is replacing serious study and patriotic claims are an excuse. Anne sees no necessary conflict between enjoyment and raising money for a flag.
evidence: when you can combine patriotism and fun, isn’t it all right?

questions.prompt: What judgment does the last sentence offer about Matthew’s role?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator values appreciation alongside conscientious discipline. Matthew’s encouragement can help Anne even though he does not manage her daily training.
evidence: a little “appreciation” sometimes does quite as much good

days.title: As I Grew Older
days.challenge: Track how line length, repeated words, and shifts from past narration to commands represent a changing sense of agency.
days.focus: An obstructed dream made visible through sun, wall, shadow, and hands.
days.context: The poem moves from remembering a bright dream to confronting an obstruction. Notice when the speaker stops describing and begins calling for action.
days.contentNote: The speaker explicitly links Black identity with exclusion and struggle; the wall is metaphorical.

excerpt.locator: AS I GREW OLDER; complete individual poem; opening “It was a long time ago. I have almost forgotten my dream. But it was there then, In”; closing “night, To break this shadow Into a thousand lights of sun, Into a thousand whirling dreams Of sun!”.

questions.prompt: What does the repeated “slowly” make us experience as the wall rises?
facilitatorNotes: It slows the reading and makes obstruction seem cumulative rather than sudden. Pair that pacing with the wall gradually dimming and hiding the dream; a reader can also hear the speaker’s helpless watching.
evidence:
Rose slowly,
Slowly,
Between me and my dream.

questions.prompt: How do the isolated lines “Shadow” and “I am black” connect the physical image with the speaker’s circumstances?
facilitatorNotes: The brief statements interrupt the description and connect imposed darkness with racial identity. Avoid suggesting the speaker’s identity itself is the fault; the surrounding wall is what blocks access to the dream.
evidence:
Shadow.
I am black.

questions.prompt: Why are the hands called “dark” at the moment the poem seeks a thousand lights?
facilitatorNotes: The same identity associated with the shadow becomes a source of action. The hands break rather than passively endure the wall; multiple lights and dreams enlarge the earlier single dream. Alternative readings should explain this movement from obstruction to agency.
evidence:
My hands!
My dark hands!
Break through the wall!

days.title: The story club’s critics (Anne of Green Gables, from chapter xxvi)
days.challenge: Read a story inside a story and distinguish its conventions from its author’s judgments.
days.focus: Explain the gap between intended effect and audience response.
days.context: After the excitement of the school concert has faded, the winter passes quietly. On Anne’s thirteenth birthday she and Diana walk home from school talking about growing up, and Anne soon begins writing stories with her friends.
days.contentNote: Anne summarizes an invented story involving murder, drowning, and confinement for mental illness; the discussion uses stigmatizing historical language.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXVI, from “Just think, Diana, I’m thirteen years old to-day” to the end of the chapter; opens ““Just think, Diana, I’m thirteen years old to-day,” remarked Anne in an awed voi”; closes “hour longer than you should with all your chattering. Learn to work first and talk afterwards.””.

questions.prompt: How does Anne’s treatment of the proposal scene show what she values in fiction?
facilitatorNotes: She rejects a plain real-life proposal as insufficiently romantic and rewrites an ornate speech repeatedly. She prioritizes drama and elevated language over everyday plausibility.
evidence: I rewrote it five times

questions.prompt: Why do the adults’ responses puzzle the story club?
facilitatorNotes: The writers intend tragedy, but exaggerated plots and abundant deaths strike some adults as comic. Approval can concern an effect different from the one the author planned.
evidence: the stories were all very pathetic and almost everybody died

questions.prompt: How does Anne’s view of past mischief differ from Mrs. Lynde’s?
facilitatorNotes: Anne sees admitting past mistakes as honest and encouraging evidence that people can improve. Mrs. Lynde treats a minister’s childhood theft as permanently discrediting.
evidence: what an encouraging thing it would be for small boys nowadays

days.title: Learning to be her own critic (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxxi)
days.challenge: Hold progress and continuing anxiety in view at the same time.
days.focus: Trace growth through changes in language, study, and relationships.
days.context: Anne is preparing for the entrance examination to Queen’s Academy. After a restorative summer she returns to Miss Stacy’s class with new energy.
days.contentNote: The chapter includes historical views on women’s roles and health, and strong examination anxiety.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXI, complete chapter; opens “Anne had her “good” summer and enjoyed it whole-heartedly. She and Diana fairly lived”; closes “in passing the Entrance Anne felt convinced that she would never recover sufficiently to enjoy them.”.

questions.prompt: What argument does Anne make against excluding women from ministry?
facilitatorNotes: She points to work women already do and the abilities she sees in Mrs. Lynde. These examples challenge the assumption that custom alone proves women cannot serve.
evidence: the women have to turn to and do the work

questions.prompt: How has Anne’s idea of effective writing changed?
facilitatorNotes: She is learning to favor strong simple words, plausible local subjects, and self-criticism over ornate language and melodramatic plots. She describes this as learned practice.
evidence: trained myself to be my own severest critic

questions.prompt: Why do Marilla and Anne see possible examination failure differently?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla sees another year of school and another attempt. Anne imagines disgrace and lasting loss of pleasure, showing that greater maturity has not ended her catastrophic fears.
evidence: go to school next year and try again

days.title: Aunt Sue’s Stories
days.challenge: Distinguish the frame scene from the lives evoked inside the stories, and assess how the poem establishes a storyteller’s authority.
days.focus: Oral memory, care, and a child’s developing recognition of lived history.
days.context: A child listens on a porch while Aunt Sue tells stories of enslaved people. The poem attends to both the remembered lives and the act of listening.
days.contentNote: The poem refers to enslavement, labor, and sorrow without graphic violence.

excerpt.locator: AUNT SUE’S STORIES; complete individual poem; opening “Aunt Sue has a head full of stories. Aunt Sue has a whole heart full of stories. Summer”; closing “And the dark-faced child is quiet Of a summer night Listening to Aunt Sue’s stories.”.

questions.prompt: What does the move from a “head full” to a “whole heart full” add to the introduction of Aunt Sue?
facilitatorNotes: Head suggests remembered knowledge; heart adds emotional attachment and care. The two capacities work together, so a response that dismisses the stories as merely sentimental misses the child’s later recognition of their source.
evidence:
Aunt Sue has a head full of stories.
Aunt Sue has a whole heart full of stories.

questions.prompt: How do sun, dewy night, and singing make the enslaved people more than one static image?
facilitatorNotes: The poem gives work, movement, and expressive life across different times of day. Repeated “black slaves” names the shared condition, while changing actions let listeners perceive human experience within it.
evidence:
Working in the hot sun,
And black slaves
Walking in the dewy night,

questions.prompt: Why is the child’s knowledge that the stories did not come from a book important, and what should we avoid claiming from it?
facilitatorNotes: It establishes Aunt Sue’s experience as the poem’s source of authority and explains the attentive silence. It does not prove that all books are unreliable or that every oral account is automatically complete.
evidence:
Never got her stories out of any book at all,
But that they came
Right out of her own life.

days.title: The joy of the effort (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxxv)
days.challenge: Qualify a general life lesson using differences in characters’ circumstances.
days.focus: Compare changing definitions of success and the conditions behind them.
days.context: Anne has entered Queen’s Academy, where she studies away from home and competes for academic honors. End-of-year examinations approach.
days.contentNote: Students discuss financial pressure and worry surrounding examinations.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXV, complete chapter; opens “Anne’s homesickness wore off, greatly helped in the wearing by her week-end visits ho”; closes “rking rosily in the oncoming years—each year a rose of promise to be woven into an immortal chaplet.”.

questions.prompt: What has changed in Anne’s rivalry with Gilbert even though she still wants to win?
facilitatorNotes: She now values an earned victory over a worthy competitor rather than causing him pain. Losing no longer seems to make life unbearable.
evidence: the bitterness had gone out of it

questions.prompt: Why should readers be cautious about treating everyone’s examination anxiety as identical?
facilitatorNotes: Jane worries about money already spent and obtaining a license, while Josie says her father can fund another year. Their practical circumstances affect the stakes.
evidence: My father can afford to send me.

questions.prompt: How do the chestnut buds and remembered violets help explain Anne’s claim about trying and failing?
facilitatorNotes: Nature and home remind her of value beyond rankings. She has worked hard, but she can imagine a worthwhile life even without the prize.
evidence: Next to trying and winning, the best thing is trying and failing.

days.title: The Avery and an evening walk (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxxvi)
days.challenge: Notice how a chapter of triumph quietly plants warnings of loss.
days.focus: The cost of ambition and the meaning of being wanted.
days.context: Anne has spent a year at Queen’s Academy in town, studying for a teacher’s license and competing for the Avery scholarship in English. Her old rival, Gilbert Blythe, is competing for the gold medal.
days.contentNote: The chapter discusses heart illness and a possibly failing bank, and closes by foreshadowing sorrow. Mrs. Lynde’s opposition to women’s higher education is reported.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXVI, complete chapter; opens “On the morning when the final results of all the examinations were to be posted ”; closes “life is ever quite the same again when once that cold, sanctifying touch has been laid upon it.”.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator mean by saying that ambitions “exact their dues”? Use Jane and Anne as examples.
facilitatorNotes: Jane, without “soaring ambitions,” walks happily; Anne is pale with anxiety. The narrator values ambition but counts its price in work and worry. Readers may debate whether Jane’s contentment is presented as lesser or simply different.
evidence: they are not to be cheaply won, but exact their dues of work and self-denial, anxiety and discouragement.

questions.prompt: Why does Matthew say he would rather have Anne “than a dozen boys”? What earlier mistake does this answer?
facilitatorNotes: The Cuthberts first expected a boy to help on the farm, and Anne still wishes she could spare Matthew’s labor. Matthew rejects usefulness as the measure of her worth and claims her as “my girl.”
evidence: I’d rather have you than a dozen boys, Anne

questions.prompt: Which details about Matthew’s heart and the Abbey Bank prepare readers for trouble while Anne’s day stays golden?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla’s report of heart “spells,” the bank rumors, and Matthew’s tired walk are placed among celebrations. The last sentence openly foreshadows grief. Readers may argue whether announcing sorrow weakens suspense or makes the evening more tender.
evidence: It was the last night before sorrow touched her life

days.title: The reaper and the rose-bush (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xxxvii)
days.challenge: Compare different expressions of grief and evaluate a consolation without forcing agreement.
days.focus: How sudden loss changes speech, silence, and relationships.
days.context: Anne has come home after winning the Avery scholarship. Matthew has had heart trouble, and the Cuthberts’ savings are in the Abbey Bank, which is rumored to be unsound.
days.contentNote: This chapter depicts a sudden death, a body laid out at home, a funeral, and intense grief, including Christian beliefs about death.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXVII, complete chapter; opens ““Matthew—Matthew—what is the matter? Matthew, are you sick?””; closes “ me and John. I’d forgotten myself. But it all came back to me when I saw Gilbert last Sunday.””.

questions.prompt: How does Anne’s grief on the first night differ from Marilla’s, and why does Diana understand only one of them?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla’s grief breaks out in a storm; Anne’s is a tearless ache that needs solitude. Diana can recognize visible weeping more easily than silence. Anne later explains that Diana is “outside” this sorrow, which is not a criticism of her kindness.
evidence: I want to be quite silent and quiet and try to realize it.

questions.prompt: What does Marilla finally say aloud, and why can she say it now?
facilitatorNotes: She declares that she loves Anne as her own child. Grief loosens a reserve that earlier chapters showed as curtness. Readers might notice that her admission comes with an apology for having been “strict and harsh.”
evidence: It’s never been easy for me to say things out of my heart, but at times like this it’s easier.

questions.prompt: Anne feels something like shame when she enjoys the world again. How does Mrs. Allan answer, and is her answer convincing?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs. Allan says the feeling is common and that Matthew liked Anne’s laughter. Some readers find this comforting; others may find it too neat for fresh grief. The chapter’s ending, Marilla’s regret about John Blythe, adds a different kind of lasting loss.
evidence: we almost feel as if we were unfaithful to our sorrow when we find our interest in life returning to us.

days.title: Aunt Polly’s investigation (Tom Sawyer, chapter i)
days.challenge: Read dialect and shifting sympathy without adopting the characters’ judgments.
days.focus: Separate apparent cleverness from evidence and narrator irony.
days.context: In a nineteenth-century Missouri village, Tom Sawyer lives with his Aunt Polly. This opening chapter introduces their struggle over rules and mischief.
days.contentNote: The chapter includes racist historical terminology, threats and use of corporal punishment, and a fight between children.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, complete chapter; opens ““Tom!””; closes “on to turn his Saturday holiday into captivity at hard labor became adamantine in its firmness.”.
excerpt.inlineReason: No library work holds this text: it is an edition established chapter by chapter by collating Project Gutenberg 74, the Wikisource transcription and the 1876 page images (see the source edition), and no single downloadable transcription of the whole book matches it, so the night keeps its own text until the remaining chapters are collated the same way.

blocks.text: “Tom!”
No answer.
“TOM!”
No answer.
“What’s gone with that boy, I wonder? You TOM!”
No answer.

The old lady pulled her spectacles down and looked over them about the room; then she put them up and looked out under them. She seldom or never looked _through_ them for so small a thing as a boy; they were her state pair, the pride of her heart, and were built for “style,” not service—she could have seen through a pair of stove lids just as well. She looked perplexed for a moment, and then said, not fiercely, but still loud enough for the furniture to hear:
“Well, I lay if I get hold of you I’ll—”
She did not finish, for by this time she was bending down and punching under the bed with the broom, and so she needed breath to punctuate the punches with. She resurrected nothing but the cat.
“I never did see the beat of that boy!”

She went to the open door and stood in it and looked out among the tomato vines and “jimpson” weeds that constituted the garden. No Tom. So she lifted up her voice at an angle calculated for distance, and shouted:
“Y-o-u-u _Tom!_”
There was a slight noise behind her and she turned just in time to seize a small boy by the slack of his roundabout and arrest his flight.
“There! I might ’a’ thought of that closet. What you been doing in there?”
“Nothing.”
“Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What _is_ that truck?”
“_I_ don’t know, aunt.”
“Well, _I_ know. It’s jam—that’s what it is. Forty times I’ve said if you didn’t let that jam alone I’d skin you. Hand me that switch.”
The switch hovered in the air—the peril was desperate—
“My! Look behind you, aunt!”
The old lady whirled round, and snatched her skirts out of danger. The lad fled, on the instant, scrambled up the high board-fence, and disappeared over it.
His aunt Polly stood surprised a moment, and then broke into a gentle laugh.

“Hang the boy, can’t I never learn anything? Ain’t he played me tricks enough like that for me to be looking out for him by this time? But old fools is the biggest fools there is. Can’t learn an old dog new tricks, as the saying is. But my goodness, he never plays them alike, two days, and how is a body to know what’s coming? He ’pears to know just how long he can torment me before I get my dander up, and he knows if he can make out to put me off for a minute or make me laugh, it’s all down again and I can’t hit him a lick. I ain’t doing my duty by that boy, and that’s the Lord’s truth, goodness knows. Spare the rod and spile the child, as the Good Book says. I’m a laying up sin and suffering for us both, _I_ know. He’s full of the Old Scratch, but laws-a-me! he’s my own dead sister’s boy, poor thing, and I ain’t got the heart to lash him, somehow. Every time I let him off, my conscience does hurt me so, and every time I hit him my old heart most breaks. Well-a-well, man that is born of woman is of few days and full of trouble, as the Scripture says, and I reckon it’s so. He’ll play hookey this evening,* and I’ll just be obleeged to make him work, tomorrow, to punish him. It’s mighty hard to make him work Saturdays, when all the boys is having holiday, but he hates work more than he hates anything else, and I’ve _got_ to do some of my duty by him, or I’ll be the ruination of the child.”
* South-western for “afternoon.”

Tom did play hookey, and he had a very good time. He got back home barely in season to help Jim, the small colored boy, saw next-day’s wood and split the kindlings before supper—at least he was there in time to tell his adventures to Jim while Jim did three-fourths of the work. Tom’s younger brother (or rather, half-brother) Sid, was already through with his part of the work (picking up chips) for he was a quiet boy, and had no adventurous, troublesome ways.

While Tom was eating his supper, and stealing sugar as opportunity offered, Aunt Polly asked him questions that were full of guile, and very deep—for she wanted to trap him into damaging revealments. Like many other simple-hearted souls, it was her pet vanity to believe she was endowed with a talent for dark and mysterious diplomacy, and she loved to contemplate her most transparent devices as marvels of low cunning. Said she:
“Tom, it was middling warm in school, warn’t it?”
“Yes’m.”
“Powerful warm, warn’t it?”
“Yes’m.”
“Didn’t you want to go in a-swimming, Tom?”
A bit of a scare shot through Tom—a touch of uncomfortable suspicion. He searched Aunt Polly’s face, but it told him nothing. So he said:
“No’m—well, not very much.”
The old lady reached out her hand and felt Tom’s shirt, and said:

“But you ain’t too warm now, though.” And it flattered her to reflect that she had discovered that the shirt was dry without anybody knowing that that was what she had in her mind. But in spite of her, Tom knew where the wind lay, now. So he forestalled what might be the next move:
“Some of us pumped on our heads—mine’s damp yet. See?”
Aunt Polly was vexed to think she had overlooked that bit of circumstantial evidence, and missed a trick. Then she had a new inspiration:
“Tom, you didn’t have to undo your shirt collar where I sewed it, to pump on your head, did you? Unbutton your jacket!”
The trouble vanished out of Tom’s face. He opened his jacket. His shirt collar was securely sewed.

“Bother! Well, go ’long with you. I’d made sure you’d played hookey and been a-swimming. But I forgive ye, Tom. I reckon you’re a kind of a singed cat, as the saying is—better’n you look. _This_ time.”
She was half sorry her sagacity had miscarried, and half glad that Tom had stumbled into obedient conduct for once.
But Sidney said:
“Well, now, if I didn’t think you sewed his collar with white thread, but it’s black.”
“Why, I did sew it with white! Tom!”
But Tom did not wait for the rest. As he went out at the door he said:
“Siddy, I’ll lick you for that.”
In a safe place Tom examined two large needles which were thrust into the lappels of his jacket, and had thread bound about them—one needle carried white thread and the other black. He said:

“She’d never noticed if it hadn’t been for Sid. Confound it! sometimes she sews it with white, and sometimes she sews it with black. I wish to geeminy she’d stick to one or t’other—_I_ can’t keep the run of ’em. But I bet you I’ll lam Sid for that. I’ll learn him!”
He was not the Model Boy of the village. He knew the model boy very well though—and loathed him.

Within two minutes, or even less, he had forgotten all his troubles. Not because his troubles were one whit less heavy and bitter to him than a man’s are to a man, but because a new and powerful interest bore them down and drove them out of his mind for the time—just as men’s misfortunes are forgotten in the excitement of new enterprises. This new interest was a valued novelty in whistling, which he had just acquired from a negro, and he was suffering to practice it undisturbed. It consisted in a peculiar bird-like turn, a sort of liquid warble, produced by touching the tongue to the roof of the mouth at short intervals in the midst of the music—the reader probably remembers how to do it, if he has ever been a boy. Diligence and attention soon gave him the knack of it, and he strode down the street with his mouth full of harmony and his soul full of gratitude. He felt much as an astronomer feels who has discovered a new planet—no doubt, as far as strong, deep, unalloyed pleasure is concerned, the advantage was with the boy, not the astronomer.

The summer evenings were long. It was not dark, yet. Presently Tom checked his whistle. A stranger was before him—a boy a shade larger than himself. A new comer of any age or either sex was an impressive curiosity in the poor little shabby village of St. Petersburgh. This boy was well-dressed, too—well-dressed on a week-day. This was simply astounding. His cap was a dainty thing, his close-buttoned blue cloth roundabout was new and natty, and so were his pantaloons. He had shoes on—and it was only Friday. He even wore a necktie, a bright bit of ribbon. He had a citified air about him that ate into Tom’s vitals. The more Tom stared at the splendid marvel, the higher he turned up his nose at his finery and the shabbier and shabbier his own outfit seemed to him to grow. Neither boy spoke. If one moved, the other moved—but only sidewise, in a circle; they kept face to face and eye to eye all the time. Finally Tom said:
“I can lick you!”
“I’d like to see you try it.”
“Well, I can do it.”
“No you can’t, either.”
“Yes I can.”
“No you can’t.”
“I can.”
“You can’t.”
“Can!”
“Can’t!”
An uncomfortable pause. Then Tom said:
“What’s your name?”
“’Tisn’t any of your business, maybe.”
“Well I ’low I’ll _make_ it my business.”
“Well why don’t you?”
“If you say much I will.”
“Much—much—_much_. There now.”
“Oh, you think you’re mighty smart, _don’t_ you? I could lick you with one hand tied behind me, if I wanted to.”
“Well why don’t you _do_ it? You _say_ you can do it.”
“Well I _will_, if you fool with me.”
“Oh yes—I’ve seen whole families in the same fix.”
“Smarty! You think you’re _some_, now, _don’t_ you? Oh what a hat!”
“You can lump that hat if you don’t like it. I dare you to knock it off—and anybody that’ll take a dare will suck eggs.”
“You’re a liar!”
“You’re another.”
“You’re a fighting liar and dasn’t take it up.”
“Aw—take a walk!”
“Say—if you give me much more of your sass I’ll take and bounce a rock off’n your head.”
“Oh, of _course_ you will.”
“Well I _will_.”
“Well why don’t you _do_ it then? What do you keep _saying_ you will for? Why don’t you _do_ it? It’s because you’re afraid.”
“I _ain’t_ afraid.”
“You are.”
“I ain’t.”
“You are.”
Another pause, and more eyeing and sidling around each other. Presently they were shoulder to shoulder. Tom said:
“Get away from here!”
“Go away yourself!”
“I won’t.”
“_I_ won’t either.”

So they stood, each with a foot placed at an angle as a brace, and both shoving with might and main, and glowering at each other with hate. But neither could get an advantage. After struggling till both were hot and flushed, each relaxed his strain with watchful caution, and Tom said:
