blocks.text: There was something about Aunt Polly’s manner, when she kissed Tom, that swept away his low spirits and made him light-hearted and happy again. He started to school and had the luck of coming upon Becky Thatcher at the head of Meadow Lane. His mood always determined his manner. Without a moment’s hesitation he ran to her and said:
“I acted mighty mean to-day, Becky, and I’m so sorry. I won’t ever, ever do that way again, as long as ever I live—please make up, won’t you?”
The girl stopped and looked him scornfully in the face:
“I’ll thank you to keep yourself _to_ yourself, Mr. Thomas Sawyer. I’ll never speak to you again.”

She tossed her head and passed on. Tom was so stunned that he had not even presence of mind enough to say “Who cares, Miss Smarty?” until the right time to say it had gone by. So he said nothing. But he was in a fine rage, nevertheless. He moped into the school-yard wishing she were a boy, and imagining how he would trounce her if she were. He presently encountered her and delivered a stinging remark as he passed. She hurled one in return, and the angry breach was complete. It seemed to Becky, in her hot resentment, that she could hardly wait for school to “take in,” she was so impatient to see Tom flogged for the injured spelling-book. If she had had any lingering notion of exposing Alfred Temple, Tom’s offensive fling had driven it entirely away.

Poor girl, she did not know how fast she was nearing trouble herself. The master, Mr. Dobbins, had reached middle age with an unsatisfied ambition. The darling of his desires was, to be a doctor, but poverty had decreed that he should be nothing higher than a village schoolmaster. Every day he took a mysterious book out of his desk and absorbed himself in it at times when no classes were reciting. He kept that book under lock and key. There was not an urchin in school but was perishing to have a glimpse of it, but the chance never came. Every boy and girl had a theory about the nature of that book; but no two theories were alike, and there was no way of getting at the facts in the case. Now, as Becky was passing by the desk, which stood near the door, she noticed that the key was in the lock! It was a precious moment. She glanced around; found herself alone, and the next instant she had the book in her hands. The title-page—Professor somebody’s “_Anatomy_”—carried no information to her mind; so she began to turn the leaves. She came at once upon a handsomely engraved and colored frontispiece—a human figure, stark naked. At that moment a shadow fell on the page and Tom Sawyer stepped in at the door, and caught a glimpse of the picture. Becky snatched at the book to close it, and had the hard luck to tear the pictured page half down the middle. She thrust the volume into the desk, turned the key, and burst out crying with shame and vexation.
“Tom Sawyer, you are just as mean as you can be, to sneak up on a person and look at what they’re looking at.”
“How could _I_ know you was looking at anything?”
“You ought to be ashamed of yourself Tom Sawyer; you know you’re going to tell on me, and O, what shall I do, what shall I do! I’ll be whipped, and I never was whipped in school.”
Then she stamped her little foot and said:
“_Be_ so mean if you want to! _I_ know something that’s going to happen. You just wait and you’ll see! Hateful, hateful, hateful!”—and she flung out of the house with a new explosion of crying.
Tom stood still, rather flustered by this onslaught. Presently he said to himself:

“What a curious kind of a fool a girl is. Never been licked in school! Shucks. What’s a licking! That’s just like a girl—they’re so thin-skinned and chicken hearted. Well, of course _I_ ain’t going to tell old Dobbins on this little fool, because there’s other ways of getting even on her, that ain’t so mean; but what of it? Old Dobbins will ask who it was tore his book. Nobody’ll answer. Then he’ll do just the way he always does—ask first one and then t’other, and when he comes to the right girl he’ll know it, without any telling. Girl’s faces always tell on them. They ain’t got any back-bone. She’ll get licked. Well, it’s a kind of a tight place for Becky Thatcher, because there ain’t any way out of it.” Tom conned the thing a moment longer and then added: “All right, though; she’d like to see me in just such a fix—let her sweat it out!”

Tom joined the mob of skylarking scholars outside. In a few moments the master arrived and school “took in.” Tom did not feel a strong interest in his studies. Every time he stole a glance at the girls’ side of the room Becky’s face troubled him. Considering all things, he did not want to pity her, and yet it was all he could do to help it. He could get up no exultation that was really worthy the name. Presently the spelling-book discovery was made, and Tom’s mind was entirely full of his own matters for a while after that. Becky roused up from her lethargy of distress and showed good interest in the proceedings. She did not expect that Tom could get out of his trouble by denying that he spilt the ink on the book himself; and she was right. The denial only seemed to make the thing worse for Tom. Becky supposed she would be glad of that, and she tried to believe she was glad of it, but she found she was not certain. When the worst came to the worst, she had an impulse to get up and tell on Alfred Temple, but she made an effort and forced herself to keep still—because, said she to herself, “he’ll tell about me tearing the picture sure. I wouldn’t say a word, not to save his life!”

Tom took his whipping and went back to his seat not at all broken-hearted, for he thought it was possible that he had unknowingly upset the ink on the spelling-book himself, in some skylarking bout—he had denied it for form’s sake and because it was custom, and had stuck to the denial from principle.

A whole hour drifted by, the master sat nodding in his throne, the air was drowsy with the hum of study. By and by, Mr. Dobbins straightened himself up, yawned, then unlocked his desk, and reached for his book, but seemed undecided whether to take it out or leave it. Most of the pupils glanced up languidly, but there were two among them that watched his movements with intent eyes. Mr. Dobbins fingered his book absently for a while, then took it out and settled himself in his chair to read! Tom shot a glance at Becky. He had seen a hunted and helpless rabbit look as she did, with a gun leveled at its head. Instantly he forgot his quarrel with her. Quick—something must be done! done in a flash, too! But the very imminence of the emergency paralyzed his invention. Good!—he had an inspiration! He would run and snatch the book, spring through the door and fly. But his resolution shook for one little instant, and the chance was lost—the master opened the volume. If Tom only had the wasted opportun ity back again! Too late. There was no help for Becky now, he said. The next moment the master faced the school. Every eye sunk under his gaze. There was that in it which smote even the innocent with fear. There was silence while one might count ten, the master was gathering his wrath. Then he spoke:
“Who tore this book?”
There was not a sound. One could have heard a pin drop. The stillness continued; the master searched face after face for signs of guilt.
“Benjamin Rogers, did you tear this book?”
A denial. Another pause.
“Joseph Harper, did you?”
Another denial. Tom’s uneasiness grew more and more intense under the slow torture of these proceedings. The master scanned the ranks of boys—considered a while, then turned to the girls:
“Amy Lawrence?”
A shake of the head.
“Gracie Miller?”
The same sign.
“Susan Harper, did you do this?”
Another negative. The next girl was Becky Thatcher. Tom was trembling from head to foot with excitement and a sense of the hopelessness of the situation.
“Rebecca Thatcher,” [Tom glanced at her face—it was white with terror,]—“did you tear—no, look me in the face”—[her hands rose in appeal]—“did you tear this book?”
A thought shot like lightning through Tom’s brain. He sprang to his feet and shouted—“_I_ done it!”

The school stared in perplexity at this incredible folly. Tom stood a moment, to gather his dismembered faculties; and when he stepped forward to go to his punishment the surprise, the gratitude, the adoration that shone upon him out of poor Becky’s eyes seemed pay enough for a hundred floggings. Inspired by the splendor of his own act, he took without an outcry the most merciless flaying that even Mr. Dobbins had ever administered; and also received with indifference the added cruelty of a command to remain two hours after school should be dismissed—for he knew who would wait for him outside till his captivity was done, and not count the tedious time as loss, either.

Tom went to bed that night planning vengeance against Alfred Temple; for with shame and repentance Becky had told him all, not forgetting her own treachery; but even the longing for vengeance had to give way, soon, to pleasanter musings, and he fell asleep at last, with Becky’s latest words lingering dreamily in his ear—
“Tom, how _could_ you be so noble!”

days.title: Examination evening (Tom Sawyer, chapter xxi)
days.challenge: Recognize satire aimed at habits of writing and test the narrator’s sweeping generalizations.
days.focus: How quoted compositions and narrative commentary expose insincere “fine language” and a tyrannical schoolmaster.
days.context: Summer vacation is near. Tom has recently taken a whipping to protect Becky Thatcher after she tore the schoolmaster’s book. Mr. Dobbins now prepares the school for a public “Examination” evening of recitations and compositions.
days.contentNote: The schoolmaster beats younger pupils and is drunk at the public event; a frightened cat is lowered on a string. The satire of girls’ compositions also reflects period assumptions about young women.

excerpt.inlineReason: No library work holds this text: it is an edition established chapter by chapter by collating Project Gutenberg 74, the Wikisource transcription and the 1876 page images (see the source edition), and no single downloadable transcription of the whole book matches it, so the night keeps its own text until the remaining chapters are collated the same way.

blocks.text: Vacation was approaching. The schoolmaster, always severe, grew severer and more exacting than ever, for he wanted the school to make a good showing on “Examination” day. His rod and his ferule were seldom idle now—at least among the smaller pupils. Only the biggest boys, and young ladies of eighteen and twenty escaped lashing. Mr. Dobbins’s lashings were very vigorous ones, too; for although he carried, under his wig, a perfectly bald and shiny head, he had only reached middle age and there was no sign of feebleness in his muscle. As the great day approached, all the tyranny that was in him came to the surface; he seemed to take a vindictive pleasure in punishing the least shortcomings. The consequence was, that the smaller boys spent their days in terror and suffering and their nights in plotting revenge. They threw away no opportunity to do the master a mischief. But he kept ahead all the time. The retribution that followed every vengeful success was so sweeping and majestic that the boys always retired from the field badly worsted. At last they conspired together and hit upon a plan that promised a dazzling victory. They swore-in the sign-painter’s boy, told him the scheme, and asked his help. He had his own reasons for being delighted, for the master boarded in his father’s family and had given the boy ample cause to hate him. The master’s wife would go on a visit to the country in a few days, and there would be nothing to interfere with the plan; the master always prepared himself for great occasions by getting pretty well fuddled, and the sign-painter’s boy said that when the dominie had reached the proper condition on Examination Evening he would “manage the thing” while he napped in his chair; then he would have him awakened at the right time and hurried away to school.

In the fullness of time the interesting occasion arrived. At eight in the evening the schoolhouse was brilliantly lighted, and adorned with wreaths and festoons of foliage and flowers. The master sat throned in his great chair upon a raised platform, with his blackboard behind him. He was looking tolerably mellow. Three rows of benches on each side and six rows in front of him were occupied by the dignitaries of the town and by the parents of the pupils. To his left, back of the rows of citizens, was a spacious temporary platform upon which were seated the scholars who were to take part in the exercises of the evening; rows of small boys, washed and dressed to an intolerable state of discomfort; rows of gawky big boys; snow-banks of girls and young ladies clad in lawn and muslin and conspiciously conscious of their bare arms, their grandmothers’ ancient trinkets, their bits of pink and blue ribbon and the flowers in their hair. All the rest of the house was filled with non-participating scholars.

The exercises began. A very little boy stood up and sheepishly recited, “You’d scarce expect one of my age to speak in public on the stage, etc”—accompanying himself with the painfully exact and spasmodic gestures which a machine might have used—supposing the machine to be a trifle out of order. But he got through safely, though cruelly scared, and got a fine round of applause when he made his manufactured bow and retired.
A little shame-faced girl lisped “Mary had a little lamb, etc.,” performed a compassion-inspiring curtsy, got her meed of applause, and sat down flushed and happy.

Tom Sawyer stepped forward with conceited confidence and soared into the unquenchable and indestructible “Give me liberty or give me death” speech, with fine fury and frantic gesticulation, and broke down in the middle of it. A ghastly stage-fright siezed him, his legs quaked under him and he was like to choke. True, he had the manifest sympathy of the house—but he had the house’s silence, too, which was even worse than its sympathy. The master frowned, and this completed the disaster. Tom struggled awhile and then retired, utterly defeated. There was a weak attempt at applause, but it died early.

“The Boy stood on the Burning Deck” followed; also “The Assyrian Came Down,” and other declamatory gems. Then there were reading exercises, and a spelling fight. The meager Latin class recited with honor. The prime feature of the evening was in order, now—original “compositions” by the young ladies. Each in her turn stepped forward to the edge of the platform, cleared her throat, held up her manuscript (tied with dainty ribbon), and proceeded to read, with labored attention to “expression” and punctuation. The themes were the same that had been illuminated upon similar occasions by their mothers before them, their grandmothers, and doubtless all their ancestors in the female line clear back to the Crusades. “Friendship” was one; “Memories of Other Days;” “Religion in History;” “Dream Land;” “The Advantages of Culture;” “Forms of Political Government Compared and Contrasted;” “Melancholy;” “Filial Love;” “Heart Longings,” etc., etc.

A prevalent feature in these compositions was a nursed and petted melancholy; another was a wasteful and opulent gush of “fine language;” another was a tendency to lug in by the ears particularly prized words and phrases until they were worn entirely out; and a peculiarity that conspicuously marked and marred them was the inveterate and intolerable sermon that wagged its crippled tail at the end of each and every one of them. No matter what the subject might be, a brain-racking effort was made to squirm it into some aspect or other that the moral and religious mind could contemplate with edification. The glaring insincerity of these sermons was not sufficient to compass the banishment of the fashion from the schools, and it is not sufficient to-day; it never will be sufficient while the world stands, perhaps. There is no school in all our land where the young ladies do not feel obliged to close their compositions with a sermom; and you will find that the sermon of the most frivolous and least religious girl in the school is always the longest and the most relentlessly pious. But enough of this. Homely truth is unpalatable.
Let us return to the “Examination.” The first composition that was read was one entitled “Is this, then, Life?” Perhaps the reader can endure an extract from it:

“In the common walks of life, with what delightful emotions does the youthful mind look forward to some anticipated scene of festivity! Imagination is busy sketching rose-tinted pictures of joy. In fancy, the voluptuous votary of fashion sees herself amid the festive throng, ‘the observed of all observers.’ Her graceful form, arrayed in snowy robes, is whirling through the mazes of the joyous dance; her eye is brightest, her step is lightest in the gay assembly.

“In such delicious fancies time quickly glides by, and the welcome hour arrives for her entrance into the elysian world, of which she has had such bright dreams. How fairy-like does every thing appear to her enchanted vision! each new scene is more charming than the last. But after a while she finds that beneath this goodly exterior, all is vanity: the flattery which once charmed her soul, now grates harshly upon her ear; the ball-room has lost its charms; and with wasted health and imbittered heart, she turns away with the conviction that earthly pleasures cannot satisfy the longings of the soul!”

And so forth and so on. There was a buzz of gratification from time to time during the reading, accompanied by whispered ejaculations of “How sweet!” “How eloquent!” “So true!” etc., and after the thing had closed with a peculiarly afflicting sermon the applause was enthusiastic.
Then arose a slim, melancholy girl, whose face had the “interesting” paleness that comes of pills and indigestion, and read a “poem.” Two stanzas of it will do:
A MISSOURI MAIDEN’S FAREWELL TO ALABAMA.

Alabama, good-bye! I love thee well!
But yet for awhile do I leave thee now!
Sad, yes, sad thoughts of thee my heart doth swell,
And burning recollections throng my brow!
For I have wandered through thy flowery woods;
Have roamed and read near Tallapoosa’s stream;
Have listened to Tallassee’s warring floods,
And wooed on Coosa’s side Aurora’s beam.

Yet shame I not to bear an o’er-full heart,
Nor blush to turn behind my tearful eyes;
’Tis from no stranger land I now must part,
’Tis to no strangers left I yield these sighs.
Welcome and home were mine within this State,
Whose vales I leave—whose spires fade fast from me:
And cold must be mine eyes, and heart, and tête,
When, dear Alabama! they turn cold on thee!
There were very few there who knew what “_tête_” meant, but the poem was very satisfactory, nevertheless.
Next appeared a dark complexioned, black eyed, black haired young lady, who paused an impressive moment, assumed a tragic expression and began to read in a measured, solemn tone.
A VISION.

Dark and tempestuous was night. Around the throne on high not a single star quivered; but the deep intonations of the heavy thunder constantly vibrated upon the ear; whilst the terrific lightning revelled in angry mood through the cloudy chambers of heaven, seeming to scorn the power exerted over its terror by the illustrious Franklin! Even the boisterous winds unanimously came forth from their mystic homes, and blustered about as if to enhance by their aid the wildness of the scene.
At such a time, so dark, so dreary, for human sympathy my very spirit sighed; but instead thereof,

“My dearest friend, my counsellor, my comforter and guide—
My joy in grief, my second bliss in joy,” came to my side.

She moved like one of those bright beings pictured in the sunny walks of fancy’s Eden by the romantic and young, a queen of beauty unadorned save by her own transcendent loveliness. So soft was her step, it failed to make even a sound, and but for the magical thrill imparted by her genial touch, as other unobtrusive beauties, she would have glided away unperceived—unsought. A strange sadness rested upon her features, like icy tears upon the robe of December, as she pointed to the contending elements without, and bade me contemplate the two beings presented.

This nightmare occupied some ten pages of manuscript and wound up with a sermon so destructive of all hope to non-Presbyterians that it took the first prize. This composition was considered to be the very finest effort of the evening. The mayor of the village, in delivering the prize to the author of it, made a warm speech in which he said that it was by far the most “eloquent” thing he had ever listened to, and that Daniel Webster himself might well be proud of it.
It may be remarked, in passing, that the number of compositions in which the word “beauteous” was over-fondled, and human experience referred to as “life’s page,” was up to the usual average.

Now the master, mellow almost to the verge of geniality, put his chair aside, turned his back to the audience, and began to draw a map of America on the blackboard, to exercise the geography class upon. But he made a sad business of it with his unsteady hand, and a smothered titter rippled over the house. He knew what the matter was and set himself to right it. He sponged out lines and re-made them; but he only distorted them more than ever, and the tittering was more pronounced. He threw his entire attention upon his work, now, as if determined not to be put down by the mirth. He felt that all eyes were fastened upon him; he imagined he was succeeding, and yet the tittering continued; it even manifestly increased. And well it might. There was a garret above, pierced with a scuttle over his head; and down through this scuttle came a cat, suspended around the haunches by a string; she had a rag tied about her head and jaws to keep her from mewing; as she slowly descended she curved upward and clawed at the string, she swung downward and clawed at the intangible air. The tittering rose higher and higher—the cat was within six inches of the absorbed teacher’s head—down, down, a little lower, and she grabbed his wig with her desperate claws, clung to it and was snatched up into the garret in an instant with her trophy still in her possession! And how the light did blaze abroad from the master’s bald pate—for the sign-painter’s boy had _gilded_ it!
That broke up the meeting. The boys were avenged. Vacation had come.

NOTE.—The pretended “compositions” quoted in this chapter are taken without alteration from a volume entitled “Prose and Poetry, by a Western Lady”—but they are exactly and precisely after the school-girl pattern and hence are much happier than any mere imitations could be.

Some may also question whether the narrator’s claim that every school shares the fault is itself an exaggeration.

days.title: Freedom, temptation, and a relapse (Tom Sawyer, chapter xxii)
days.challenge: Follow a narrator’s figurative use of a medical term.
days.focus: Explain repeated ironic reversals.
days.context: During vacation Tom joins a temperance group, seeks entertainment, and then becomes ill while a religious revival changes the town’s mood.
days.contentNote: The chapter mentions tobacco and alcohol, racist minstrel entertainment, serious childhood illness, death, and fear of divine punishment.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXII, complete chapter; opens “Tom joined the new order of Cadets of Temperance, being attracted by the showy c”; closes “d Huck Finn up an alley eating a stolen melon. Poor lads! they—like Tom—had suffered a relapse.”.
excerpt.inlineReason: No library work holds this text: it is an edition established chapter by chapter by collating Project Gutenberg 74, the Wikisource transcription and the 1876 page images (see the source edition), and no single downloadable transcription of the whole book matches it, so the night keeps its own text until the remaining chapters are collated the same way.

blocks.text: Tom joined the new order of Cadets of Temperance, being attracted by the showy character of their “regalia.” He promised to abstain from smoking, chewing and profanity as long as he remained a member. Now he found out a new thing—namely, that to promise not to do a thing is the surest way in the world to make a body want to go and do that very thing. Tom soon found himself tormented with a desire to drink and swear; the desire grew to be so intense that nothing but the hope of a chance to display himself in his red sash kept him from withdrawing from the order. Fourth of July was coming; but he soon gave that up—gave it up before he had worn his shackles over forty-eight hours—and fixed his hopes upon old Judge Frazer, justice of the peace, who was apparently on his death-bed and would have a big public funeral, since he was so high an official. During three days Tom was deeply concerned about the Judge’s condition and hungry for news of it. Sometimes his hopes ran high—so high that he would venture to get out his regalia and practice before the looking-glass. But the Judge had a most discouraging way of fluctuating. At last he was pronounced upon the mend—and then convalescent. Tom was disgusted; and felt a sense of injury, too. He handed in his resignation at once—and that night the Judge suffered a relapse and died. Tom resolved that he would never trust a man like that again.

The funeral was a fine thing. The Cadets paraded in a style calculated to kill the late member with envy. Tom was a free boy again, however—there was something in that. He could drink and swear, now—but found to his surprise that he did not want to. The simple fact that he could, took the desire away, and the charm of it.
Tom presently wondered to find that his coveted vacation was beginning to hang a little heavily on his hands.
He attempted a diary—but nothing happened during three days, and so he abandoned it.
The first of all the negro minstrel shows came to town, and made a sensation. Tom and Joe Harper got up a band of performers and were happy for two days.

Even the Glorious Fourth was in some sense a failure, for it rained hard, there was no procession in consequence, and the greatest man in the world (as Tom supposed) Mr. Benton, an actual United States Senator, proved an overwhelming disappointment—for he was not twenty-five feet high, nor even anywhere in the neighborhood of it.
A circus came. The boys played circus for three days afterward in tents made of rag carpeting—admission, three pins for boys, two for girls—and then circusing was abandoned.
A phrenologist and a mesmerizer came—and went again and left the village duller and drearier than ever.
There were some boys-and-girls’ parties, but they were so few and so delightful that they only made the aching voids between ache the harder.
Becky Thatcher was gone to her Constantinople home to stay with her parents during vacation—so there was no bright side to life anywhere.
The dreadful secret of the murder was a chronic misery. It was a very cancer for permanency and pain.
Then came the measles.

During two long weeks Tom lay a prisoner, dead to the world and its happenings. He was very ill, he was interested in nothing. When he got upon his feet at last and moved feebly down town, a melancholy change had come over everything and every creature. There had been a “revival,” and everybody had “got religion,” not only the adults, but even the boys and girls. Tom went about, hoping against hope for the sight of one blessed sinful face, but disappointment crossed him everywhere. He found Joe Harper studying a Testament, and turned sadly away from the depressing spectacle. He sought Ben Rogers, and found him visiting the poor with a basket of tracts. He hunted up Jim Hollis, who called his attention to the precious blessing of his late measles as a warning. Every boy he encountered added another ton to his depression; and when, in desperation, he flew for refuge at last to the bosom of Huckleberry Finn and was received with a scriptural quotation, his heart broke and he crept home and to bed realizing that he alone of all the town was lost, forever and forever.

And that night there came on a terrific storm, with driving rain, awful claps of thunder and blinding sheets of lightning. He covered his head with the bedclothes and waited in a horror of suspense for his doom; for he had not the shadow of a doubt that all this hubbub was about him. He believed he had taxed the forbearance of the powers above to the extremity of endurance and that this was the result. It might have seemed to him a waste of pomp and ammunition to kill a bug with a battery of artillery, but there seemed nothing incongruous about the getting up such an expensive thunder storm as this to knock the turf from under an insect like himself.
By and by the tempest spent itself and died without accomplishing its object. The boy’s first impulse was to be grateful, and reform. His second was to wait—for there might not be any more storms.

The next day the doctors were back; Tom had relapsed. The three weeks he spent on his back this time seemed an entire age. When he got abroad at last he was hardly grateful that he had been spared, remembering how lonely was his estate, how companionless and forlorn he was. He drifted listlessly down the street and found Jim Hollis acting as judge in a juvenile court that was trying a cat for murder, in the presence of her victim, a bird. He found Joe Harper and Huck Finn up an alley eating a stolen melon. Poor lads! they—like Tom—had suffered a relapse.

days.title: Tom takes the witness stand (Tom Sawyer, chapter xxiii)
days.challenge: Distinguish circumstantial observations from an eyewitness account.
days.focus: Explain a moral decision through evidence and risk.
days.context: Muff Potter is on trial for a killing Tom and Huck saw Joe commit. Fear has kept the boys silent, though they have privately brought Potter small comforts.
days.contentNote: The passage concerns murder, threatened lynching and execution, alcoholism, and racist anti-Indigenous slurs applied to the villain.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIII, complete chapter; opens “At last the sleepy atmosphere was stirred—and vigorously: the murder trial came ”; closes “ lightning the half-breed sprang for a window, tore his way through all opposers, and was gone!”.
excerpt.inlineReason: No library work holds this text: it is an edition established chapter by chapter by collating Project Gutenberg 74, the Wikisource transcription and the 1876 page images (see the source edition), and no single downloadable transcription of the whole book matches it, so the night keeps its own text until the remaining chapters are collated the same way.

blocks.text: At last the sleepy atmosphere was stirred—and vigorously: the murder trial came on in the court. It became the absorbing topic of village talk immediately. Tom could not get away from it. Every reference to the murder sent a shudder to his heart, for his troubled conscience and fears almost persuaded him that these remarks were put forth in his hearing as “feelers;” he did not see how he could be suspected of knowing anything about the murder, but still he could not be comfortable in the midst of this gossip. It kept him in a cold shiver all the time. He took Huck to a lonely place to have a talk with him. It would be some relief to unseal his tongue for a little while; to divide his burden of distress with another sufferer. Moreover, he wanted to assure himself that Huck had remained discreet.
“Huck, have you ever told anybody about—that?”
“’Bout what?”
“You know what.”
“Oh—’course I haven’t.”
“Never a word?”
“Never a solitary word, so help me. What makes you ask?”
“Well, I wasafeard.”
“Why Tom Sawyer, we wouldn’t be alive two days if that got found out. _You_ know that.”
Tom felt more comfortable. After a pause:
“Huck, they couldn’t anybody get you to tell, could they?”
“Get me to tell? Why if I wanted that half-breed devil to drownd me they could get me to tell. They ain’t no different way.”
“Well, that’s all right, then. I reckon we’re safe as long as we keep mum. But let’s swear again, anyway. It’s more surer.”
“I’m agreed.”
So they swore again with dread solemnities.
“What is the talk around, Huck? I’ve heard a power of it.”
“Talk? Well, it’s just Muff Potter, Muff Potter, Muff Potter all the time. It keeps me in a sweat, constant, so’s I want to hide som’ers.”
“That’s just the same way they go on round me. I reckon he’s a goner. Don’t you feel sorry for him, sometimes?”

“Most always—most always. He ain’t no account; but then he hain’t ever done anything to hurt anybody. Just fishes a little, to get money to get drunk on—and loafs around considerable; but lord we all do that—leastways most of us,—preachers and such like. But he’s kind of good—he give me half a fish, once, when there warn’t enough for two; and lots of times he’s kind of stood by me when I was out of luck.”
“Well, he’s mended kites for me, Huck, and knitted hooks on to my line. I wish we could get him out of there.”
“My! we couldn’t get him out Tom. And besides, ’twouldn’t do any good; they’d ketch him again.”
“Yes—so they would. But I hate to hear ’em abuse him so like the dickens when he never done—that.”
“I do too, Tom. Lord, I hear ’em say he’s the bloodiest looking villain in this country, and they wonder he wasn’t ever hung before.”
“Yes, they talk like that, all the time. I’ve heard ’em say that if he was to get free they’d lynch him.”
“And they’d do it, too.”

The boys had a long talk, but it brought them little comfort. As the twilight drew on, they found themselves hanging about the neighborhood of the little isolated jail, perhaps with an undefined hope that something would happen that might clear away their difficulties. But nothing happened; there seemed to be no angels or fairies interested in this luckless captive.
The boys did as they had often done before—went to the cell grating and gave Potter some tobacco and matches. He was on the ground floor and there were no guards.
His gratitude for their gifts had always smote their consciences before—it cut deeper than ever, this time. They felt cowardly and treacherous to the last degree when Potter said:

“You’ve been mighty good to me, boys—better’n anybody else in this town. And I don’t forget it, I don’t. Often I says to myself, says I, ‘I used to mend all the boys’ kites and things, and show ’em where the good fishin’ places was, and befriend ’em what I could, and now they’ve all forgot old Muff when he’s in trouble; but Tom don’t, and Huck don’t—_they_ don’t forget him,’ says I, ‘and I don’t forget them.’ Well, boys, I done an awful thing—drunk and crazy at the time—that’s the only way I account for it—and now I got to swing for it, and it’s right. Right, and _best_, too I reckon—hope so, anyway. Well, we won’t talk about that. I don’t want to make _you_ feel bad; you’ve befriended me. But what I want to say, is, don’t _you_ ever get drunk—then you won’t ever get here. Stand a little furder west—so—that’s it; it’s a prime comfort to see faces that’s friendly when a body’s in such a muck of trouble, and there don’t none come here but yourn. Good friendly faces—good friendly faces. Git up on one another’s backs and let me touch ’em. That’s it. Shake hands—yourn’ll come through the bars, but mine’s too big. Little hands, and weak—but they’ve helped Muff Potter a power, and they’d help him more if they could.”

Tom went home miserable, and his dreams that night were full of horrors. The next day and the day after, he hung about the court room, drawn by an almost irresistible impulse to go in, but forcing himself to stay out. Huck was having the same experience. They studiously avoided each other. Each wandered away, from time to time, but the same dismal fascination always brought them back presently. Tom kept his ears open when idlers sauntered out of the court room, but invariably heard distressing news—the toils were closing more and more relentlessly around poor Potter. At the end of the second day the village talk was to the effect that Injun Joe’s evidence stood firm and unshaken, and that there was not the slightest question as to what the jury’s verdict would be.

Tom was out late, that night, and came to bed through the window. He was in a tremendous state of excitement. It was hours before he got to sleep. All the village flocked to the Court house the next morning, for this was to be the great day. Both sexes were about equally represented in the packed audience. After a long wait the jury filed in and took their places; shortly afterward, Potter, pale and haggard, timid and hopeless, was brought in, with chains upon him, and seated where all the curious eyes could stare at him; no less conspicuous was Injun Joe, stolid as ever. There was another pause, and then the judge arrived and the sheriff proclaimed the opening of the court. The usual whisperings among the lawyers and gathering together of papers followed. These details and accompanying delays worked up an atmosphere of preparation that was as impressive as it was fascinating.

Now a witness was called who testified that he found Muff Potter washing in the brook, at an early hour of the morning that the murder was discovered, and that he immediately sneaked away. After some further questioning, counsel for the prosecution said—
“Take the witness.”
The prisoner raised his eyes for a moment, but dropped them again when his own counsel said—
“I have no questions to ask him.”
The next witness proved the finding of the knife near the corpse. Counsel for the prosecution said:
“Take the witness.”
“I have no questions to ask him,” Potter’s lawyer replied.
A third witness swore he had often seen the knife in Potter’s possession.
“Take the witness.”
Counsel for Potter declined to question him. The faces of the audience began to betray annoyance. Did this attorney mean to throw away his client’s life without an effort?
Several witnesses deposed concerning Potter’s guilty behavior when brought to the scene of the murder. They were allowed to leave the stand without being cross-questioned.

Every detail of the damaging circumstances that occurred in the graveyard upon that morning which all present remembered so well, was brought out by credible witnesses, but none of them were cross-examined by Potter’s lawyer. The perplexity and dissatisfaction of the house expressed itself in murmurs and provoked a reproof from the bench. Counsel for the prosecution now said:
“By the oaths of citizens whose simple word is above suspicion, we have fastened this awful crime beyond all possibility of question, upon the unhappy prisoner at the bar. We rest our case here.”

A groan escaped from poor Potter, and he put his face in his hands and rocked his body softly to and fro, while a painful silence reigned in the courtroom. Many men were moved, and many women’s compassion testified itself in tears. Counsel for the defence rose and said:

“Your honor, in our remarks at the opening of this trial, we foreshadowed our purpose to prove that our client did this fearful deed while under the influence of a blind and irresponsible delirium produced by drink. We have changed our mind. We shall not offer that plea.” [Then to the clerk]: “Call Thomas Sawyer!”

A puzzled amazement awoke in every face in the house, not even excepting Potter’s. Every eye fastened itself with wondering interest upon Tom as he rose and took his place upon the stand. The boy looked wild enough, for he was badly scared. The oath was administered.
“Thomas Sawyer, where were you on the seventeenth of June, about the hour of midnight?”

Tom glanced at Injun Joe’s iron face and his tongue failed him. The audience listened breathless, but the words refused to come. After a few moments, however, the boy got a little of his strength back, and managed to put enough of it into his voice to make part of the house hear:
“In the graveyard!”
“A little bit louder, please. Don’t be afraid. You were—”
“In the graveyard.”
A contemptuous smile flitted across Injun Joe’s face.
“Were you anywhere near Horse Williams’s grave?”
“Yes, sir.”
“Speak up—just a trifle louder. How near were you?”
“Near as I am to you.”
“Were you hidden, or not?”
“I was hid.”
“Where?”
“Behind the elms that’s on the edge of the grave.”
Injun Joe gave a barely perceptible start.
“Any one with you?”
“Yes, sir. I went there with—”
“Wait—wait a moment. Never mind mentioning your companion’s name. We will produce him at the proper time. Did you carry anything there with you.”
Tom hesitated and looked confused.
“Speak out my boy—don’t be diffident. The truth is always respectable. What did you take there?”
“Only a—a—dead cat.”
There was a ripple of mirth, which the court checked.
“We will produce the skeleton of that cat. Now my boy, tell us everything that occurred—tell it in your own way—don’t skip anything, and don’t be afraid.”

Tom began—hesitatingly at first, but as he warmed to his subject his words flowed more and more easily; in a little while every sound ceased but his own voice; every eye fixed itself upon him; with parted lips and bated breath the audience hung upon his words, taking no note of time, rapt in the ghastly fascinations of the tale. The strain upon pent emotion reached its climax when the boy said—
“—and as the doctor fetched the board around and Muff Potter fell, Injun Joe jumped with the knife and—”
Crash! Quick as lightning the half-breed sprang for a window, tore his way through all opposers, and was gone!

questions.prompt: Why does Potter’s gratitude deepen the boys’ distress instead of simply making them feel helpful?
facilitatorNotes: He believes they have helped as much as they can, while they know their withheld testimony could change his situation. Kindness heightens their awareness of the larger obligation.
evidence: they’d help him more if they could

questions.prompt: Which distinction matters between the prosecution’s witnesses and Tom?
facilitatorNotes: Other witnesses connect Potter with a knife and suspicious behavior after the event. Tom claims direct knowledge of the killing itself, which can overturn the interpretation of those circumstances.
evidence: tell us everything that occurred—tell it in your own way

questions.prompt: What details show that testifying requires courage rather than absence of fear?
facilitatorNotes: Tom initially cannot speak while looking at Joe and then answers with difficulty before gaining fluency. The action is brave precisely because the threat still frightens him.
evidence: his tongue failed him

days.title: Incident
days.challenge: Explain how understatement and a simple ballad form intensify a painful memory.
days.focus: How one moment of hatred can overwrite a child’s whole experience of a place.
days.context: Cullen recalls, in short ballad stanzas, a childhood visit to Baltimore.
days.contentNote: The poem quotes the racial slur that a white child shouted at the eight-year-old speaker. Cullen makes that one word the event of the poem: its cruelty is what erases everything else he saw in Baltimore.

evidence: They are important, you understand, without being interesting.

questions.prompt: Why is Watson’s surprise at Holmes’s patient listening useful to readers?
facilitatorNotes: Watson initially calls Mary’s family history irrelevant, but Holmes’s concentration signals that details he dismisses may matter. The contrast warns readers against adopting Watson’s first assessment.
evidence: he had listened with the greatest concentration of attention

days.title: Income, letters, and a whisper: part 2 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, a case of identity)
days.challenge: Keep financial facts and explanations offered by characters distinct.
days.focus: Identify patterns without treating a suspicion as proof.
days.context: Mary Sutherland asks Holmes to find her missing fiancé, Hosmer Angel. She lives with her mother and a stepfather only a few years older than herself.
days.contentNote: The client describes restrictions on her social life and family use of her income.

excerpt.locator: A Case of Identity, income inquiry through Angel’s appearance and voice; opens ““Your own little income,” he asked, “does it come out of the business?””; closes ““Well, and what happened when Mr. Windibank, your step-father, returned to France?””.

questions.prompt: Who currently benefits from Mary’s inherited income, and why might that matter to an investigation?
facilitatorNotes: Her stepfather collects the interest for her mother while Mary lives at home. A change in where she lives could affect the household’s finances; this is a possible motive, not proof of wrongdoing.
evidence: they have the use of the money just while I am staying with them

questions.prompt: What pattern connects Angel’s visits with Windibank’s travel?
facilitatorNotes: Angel appears when Windibank is away and avoids visiting when he returns. Readers should record the timing as a clue while allowing explanations besides identity or collusion.
evidence: Mr. Hosmer Angel could not come to the house any more

questions.prompt: How do Mary and Holmes respond differently to Angel’s objection to typed letters from her?
facilitatorNotes: Mary regards his preference as evidence of affection. Holmes calls it suggestive, inviting inquiry into why Angel types his own letters while discouraging hers.
evidence: the machine had come between us

days.title: A disappearance at the church: part 3 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, a case of identity)
days.challenge: Distinguish forewarning from independent evidence of an accident.
days.focus: Compare a client’s interpretation with alternative explanations.
days.context: Mary has described a secretive fiancé who writes typed letters, wears tinted glasses, and visits only when her stepfather is away.
days.contentNote: The passage includes emotional manipulation, a broken wedding plan, and dismissive descriptions of a distressed woman.

excerpt.locator: A Case of Identity, marriage plan through Watson’s question about observation; opens ““Mr. Hosmer Angel came to the house again, and proposed that we should marry before f”; closes ““You appeared to read a good deal upon her which was quite invisible to me,” I remarked.”.

questions.prompt: How does the separate cab create a gap in what Mary actually observes?
facilitatorNotes: She and her mother ride ahead while Angel travels separately. The driver sees him enter but neither Mary nor the driver supplies continuous observation of him inside.
evidence: he put us both into it, and stepped himself into a four-wheeler

questions.prompt: Why does Mary interpret Angel’s repeated demand for loyalty as evidence of danger?
facilitatorNotes: She assumes his devotion is sincere and reads the disappearance as fulfillment of his warning. The same warning could also be preparation for a planned absence; her interpretation is not the only one.
evidence: I believe that he foresaw some danger

questions.prompt: What tension appears between Holmes’s advice and Mary’s response?
facilitatorNotes: He urges her to let the vanished man go; she insists on fidelity. Solving the factual puzzle may not automatically change her emotional commitment.
evidence: I shall be true to Hosmer.

days.title: What Watson overlooked: part 4 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, a case of identity)
days.challenge: Compare observation with an explanation of how a trace formed.
days.focus: Connect physical traces with carefully qualified inferences.
days.context: After Mary leaves her letters, Holmes asks Watson to describe her appearance and explains what he noticed during their interview.
days.contentNote: Holmes’s discussion includes gendered assumptions and paternalistic treatment of the client; tobacco appears.

excerpt.locator: A Case of Identity, details of appearance through Watson’s departure; opens ““Not invisible, but unnoticed, Watson. You did not know where to look, and so you mis”; closes “he clews which would lead up to the identity of the disappearing bridegroom of Miss Mary Sutherland.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Holmes compare marks made by typing with marks made by a sewing machine?
facilitatorNotes: A mark alone can have more than one cause. He distinguishes the position and distribution of marks before inferring typing, showing the role of comparison.
evidence: only on the left arm, and on the side of it farthest from the thumb

questions.prompt: How do the boots support an inference of haste more specifically than a general impression of untidiness?
facilitatorNotes: The mismatched boots and irregularly fastened buttons contrast with otherwise neat dress. The combination suggests hurried dressing rather than a settled habit.
evidence: odd boots, half-buttoned

questions.prompt: What makes the signature different from the rest of Angel’s typed letter?
facilitatorNotes: Typing the body could be ordinary convenience, but replacing a handwritten signature removes a personal identifying mark. Holmes calls it conclusive while withholding his exact inference, creating suspense.
evidence: Not only that, but the signature is type-written.

days.title: The machine’s peculiar marks: part 5 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, a case of identity)
days.challenge: Distinguish a defensive claim from an explanation of the facts.
days.focus: Assess converging physical and behavioral evidence.
days.context: Watson returns the next evening. Holmes has written to Windibank and his employer; Windibank arrives for the appointment.
days.contentNote: The scene depicts coercive control and Holmes locking a visitor in the room. The characters’ legal claims are part of the fiction.

excerpt.locator: A Case of Identity, Watson’s return through Windibank’s claim that the act is not actionable; opens “A professional case of great gravity was engaging my own attention at the time, and t”; closes “ with a ghastly face, and a glitter of moisture on his brow. “It—it’s not actionable,” he stammered.”.

questions.prompt: How does Windibank attempt to reduce the importance of Mary’s complaint before hearing the evidence?
facilitatorNotes: He calls it a little family matter, describes her as impulsive, and stresses privacy and expense. These remarks redirect attention from the disappearance to her decision to seek help.
evidence: it is far better not to wash linen of the sort in public

questions.prompt: Why is the comparison of letters stronger than merely noting that both men use a typewriter?
facilitatorNotes: Holmes identifies matching defects in particular letters plus fourteen other characteristics. A shared general method is common; a cluster of distinctive marks is more specific.
evidence: the fourteen other characteristics to which I have alluded are there as well

questions.prompt: What shift occurs when Windibank says the act is not actionable?
facilitatorNotes: He moves from dismissing the investigation and challenging Holmes to invoking legal consequences. The shift suggests fear of exposure, but the physical evidence remains more important than demeanor alone.
evidence: It—it’s not actionable

days.title: An explanation without repair: part 6 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, a case of identity)
days.challenge: Separate explanatory success from justice and respect for a client.
days.focus: Evaluate both a solved deception and an unresolved human problem.
days.context: Matching typewriter defects have connected Windibank’s reply with Angel’s letters. Holmes now explains the deception and the financial motive.
days.contentNote: A stepfather impersonates a suitor to manipulate a young adult’s affections and control her income. The ending includes threats of whipping and a sexist proverb.

excerpt.locator: A Case of Identity, Holmes’s reconstruction through the story’s final saying; opens ““I am very much afraid that it is not. But between ourselves, Windibank, it was as cr”; closes “on from a woman.’ There is as much sense in Hafiz as in Horace, and as much knowledge of the world.””.

questions.prompt: How do the vows and dramatic disappearance serve the same financial purpose?
facilitatorNotes: They bind Mary to a missing fiancé and discourage another marriage, preserving the household’s access to her income. Uncertainty is part of the scheme rather than an accidental result.
evidence: so uncertain as to his fate, that for ten years to come

questions.prompt: What independent check does Holmes obtain beyond the typewriter comparison?
facilitatorNotes: He removes potential disguise features from the description and asks the employer to identify the remaining features. The employer’s reply corroborates Windibank’s identity.
evidence: the description tallied in every respect with that of their employé

questions.prompt: Why can readers question Holmes’s final decision even after accepting his explanation?
facilitatorNotes: He assumes Mary will not believe him and uses a sexist saying to justify withholding the truth. Readers may argue that she deserves the evidence and a chance to judge it herself.
evidence: If I tell her she will not believe me.

days.title: The Story of My Life: remembering the first years (chapter i)
days.challenge: Distinguish remembered sensations, family testimony and the adult narrator’s interpretive images.
days.focus: How a memoir establishes both the richness and the uncertainty of childhood memory.
days.context: Keller opens her autobiography by explaining how she reconstructs infancy and the illness after which she became deafblind.
days.contentNote: Includes illness, blindness and deafness, and references to a plantation and Confederate relatives. The family account does not explain slavery; its comfortable description of plantation life is a limited perspective, not an endorsement.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter I, complete chapter prose; from “IT is with a kind of fear that I begin to write the history of my life. I h…” through “…wholly blot out. If we have once seen, "the day is ours, and what the day has shown."”

questions.prompt: What kinds of knowledge does Keller distinguish in her opening chapter, and why does that distinction matter?
facilitatorNotes: She separates vivid impressions from accounts supplied by relatives and admits that adult imagination shapes childhood scenes. Compare “I am told” with the doubly qualified illness memory; the admission invites careful trust rather than claiming perfect recall.
evidence: fact and fancy look alike
I am told that while I was still in long dresses
if, indeed, they be memories

questions.prompt: How does the garden description establish perception beyond sight?
facilitatorNotes: Touch and smell locate flowers and provide comfort; visual analogies remain part of the adult writer’s vocabulary. Readers should not assume that a rich description proves she saw the remembered scene. The roses connect sensory pleasure with religious imagery.
evidence: guided by the sense of smell
hide my hot face in the cool leaves and grass
they felt so soft, so pure

questions.prompt: How does the rapid sequence of seasons change the force of the illness paragraph and the chapter’s ending?
facilitatorNotes: The abundance of spring, summer and autumn creates a compressed happy beginning; February brings an abrupt loss. The ending preserves the value of early experience and anticipates teaching, so the chapter contains loss without presenting her later life as empty.
evidence: One brief spring
the illness which closed my eyes and ears
which the darkness that followed could not wholly blot out

days.title: The Story of My Life: signs and childhood companions (chapter ii)
days.challenge: Read communication through gesture while identifying power differences within seemingly playful memories.
days.focus: The reach and limits of improvised signs in the family, with Martha Washington and with a dog.
days.context: Before Anne Sullivan arrived, Keller developed signs with people around her. These episodes include Martha Washington, the cook’s daughter, and Belle, the family dog.
days.contentNote: Contains historical racial descriptions, unequal treatment of a Black child, kicking a caregiver and hitting a dog. Keller’s retrospective words “tyranny” and “domineer” invite examination of her behaviour.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter II, opening through the episode with Belle; from “I CANNOT recall what happened during the first months after my illness. I o…” through “…th and lie down again, and I, wearied and disappointed, went off in search of Martha.”

questions.prompt: How do the bread, ice-cream and egg-hunting signs turn actions or shapes into shared meaning?
facilitatorNotes: The bread sign reenacts preparation; the ice-cream sign combines an action with bodily cold; the egg sign combines shape and location. Martha and the mother supply interpretation, so communication is a shared accomplishment.
evidence: imitate the acts of cutting the slices and buttering them
made the sign for working the freezer and shivered
something round in the grass

questions.prompt: What complicates the picture of friendship between Helen and Martha?
facilitatorNotes: They share work, food and mischief, yet Helen describes coercion and assigns herself control over carrying eggs. The reciprocal haircut briefly contests that hierarchy. Accept readings that recognize genuine companionship alongside an unequal relationship.
evidence: It pleased me to domineer over her
I never allowed her to carry the eggs home
turn and turn about is fair play

questions.prompt: Why does the attempt to teach Belle belong beside the scenes of human communication?
facilitatorNotes: Helen wrongly expects the dog to share her goals and interprets its hunting response as disobedience. The comic exit exposes her frustration and limited understanding; it also contrasts Martha’s skilled interpretation with Belle’s indifference.
evidence: I tried hard to teach her my sign language
I did not then know why Belle acted in this way
went off in search of Martha

days.title: The Story of My Life: family, danger and affection (chapter ii)
days.challenge: Track shifts in chronology and distinguish the adult narrator’s moral explanation from the child’s understanding.
days.focus: How isolated incidents build a complicated portrait of family attachment.
days.context: The second half of Chapter II moves among childhood dangers, memories of Keller’s parents and jealousy toward her sister Mildred.
days.contentNote: Includes a child’s burns, confinement as a prank, a father’s death and an infant almost injured when a cradle is overturned. The text’s association of isolation with limited affection describes Keller’s interpretation of her own past, not every deafblind child.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter II, concluding episodes; from “Many incidents of those early years are fixed in my memory, isolated, but c…” through “…us, although she could not understand my finger language, nor I her childish prattle.”

questions.prompt: How do the fire and locked-door incidents show the gap between what Helen can do and what she understands?
facilitatorNotes: She can manipulate clothing and keys but does not anticipate danger or others’ distress. The adult labels the prank naughty and explains its effect on the parents, information the delighted child does not grasp.
evidence: the flames encircled me
laughed with glee as I felt the jar of the pounding
convinced my parents that I must be taught

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter jump from the father’s newspapers and berries to his death years later?
facilitatorNotes: The later event gives emotional weight to the affectionate portrait rather than following a strict childhood timeline. His clumsy finger spelling marks an effort to connect; the first sorrow becomes part of the adult’s judgment of those memories.
evidence: he used to spell clumsily into my hand
This was my first great sorrow

questions.prompt: How does the Nancy episode change by its final sentences, and how far can Keller’s explanation be generalized?
facilitatorNotes: The doll initially receives possessive affection while Mildred seems an intruder; later shared experience produces mutual love despite imperfect communication. Her causal account is personal and retrospective, not a universal claim that disability prevents affection.
evidence: I guarded both doll and cradle with the most jealous care
Mildred and I grew into each other's hearts

days.title: The Story of My Life: finding a teacher (chapter iii)
days.challenge: Compare a child’s pleasant journey with the adults’ uncertainty and trace a chain of practical help.
days.focus: How access to education depends on both relationships and information.
days.context: Keller’s family seeks help when her improvised signs no longer meet her desire to communicate. This chapter ends just before Anne Sullivan’s arrival.
days.contentNote: Uses historical institutional terms and biblical imagery. Darkness and light express this author’s experience and are not a measure of the worth of blind people.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter III, complete chapter prose; from “MEANWHILE the desire to express myself grew. The few signs I used became le…” through “…sacred mountain I heard a voice which said, "Knowledge is love and light and vision."”

questions.prompt: Why does the train journey feel different to Helen and to her father?
facilitatorNotes: She enjoys objects, sympathetic strangers and movement; he worries about treatment and education. The doll-eye solution demonstrates active problem solving at the very moment others doubt that she can be taught.
evidence: so many things to keep my mind and fingers busy
my father with a sad heart and many misgivings
the problem was solved

questions.prompt: Trace the shift from seeking an eye treatment to finding a teacher. What does each person contribute?
facilitatorNotes: Chisholm cannot treat her eyes but affirms educability and refers the family to Bell; Bell identifies Perkins and Anagnos; Anagnos finds a teacher. A failed medical hope becomes an educational route through coordinated practical assistance.
evidence: He said, however, that I could be educated
ask him if he had a teacher competent to begin my education
a teacher had been found

questions.prompt: How does the ending’s religious language enlarge the earlier image of invisible hands holding Helen?
facilitatorNotes: The opening presents blocked expression as confinement; the Exodus and Sinai allusions turn knowledge into liberation and revelation. Explain the image without requiring belief in it, and preserve the distinction between intellectual access and literal restoration of eyesight.
evidence: invisible hands were holding me
Thus I came up out of Egypt and stood before Sinai
Knowledge is love and light and vision.

days.title: An unusual advertisement: part 1 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the red-headed league)
days.challenge: Compare the narrator’s general impression with specific observations.
days.focus: Read apparently comic details as possible evidence.
days.context: Watson arrives while Holmes interviews pawnbroker Jabez Wilson, whose red hair has led him into an extraordinary paid position.
days.contentNote: The narrator makes condescending judgments about appearance and class; tobacco use appears.

excerpt.locator: The Red-headed League, opening through the assistant’s photography habit; opens “I had called upon my friend, Mr. Sherlock Holmes, one day in the autumn of last year,”; closes “is pictures. That is his main fault; but, on the whole, he’s a good worker. There’s no vice in him.””.

questions.prompt: How does Holmes’s reading of Wilson’s appearance differ from Watson’s description?
facilitatorNotes: Watson groups him as an ordinary tradesman; Holmes connects particular marks with activities, such as developed hand muscles and worn cuffs. Specific traces replace a broad social label.
evidence: the left one with the smooth patch near the elbow

questions.prompt: What makes the advertisement attractive and puzzling at the same time?
facilitatorNotes: It offers substantial weekly pay for nominal work with eligibility based on hair color. The reward attracts applicants while the unusual criterion leaves the practical purpose unexplained.
evidence: a salary of £4 a week for purely nominal services

questions.prompt: Why might the assistant’s willingness to accept half wages deserve attention apart from the advertisement?
facilitatorNotes: It is another unusually favorable bargain. Wilson sees a benefit, while Holmes suggests there may be an unexamined reason for accepting less than market pay.
evidence: your assistant is not as remarkable as your advertisement

days.title: The successful applicant: part 2 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the red-headed league)
days.challenge: Track persuasion through flattery, crowd behavior, and practical reassurance.
days.focus: Analyze how an offer makes its conditions seem reasonable.
days.context: Wilson’s assistant Spaulding has shown him an advertisement offering easy work to red-haired men. Wilson explains how they went to apply.
days.contentNote: The scene includes painful hair-pulling and historical assumptions about marriage and heredity.

excerpt.locator: The Red-headed League, Wilson’s household through his acceptance of the copying post; opens ““He is still with you, I presume?””; closes “t home with my assistant, hardly knowing what to say or do, I was so pleased at my own good fortune.”.

questions.prompt: How does Spaulding influence the process beyond merely passing along information?
facilitatorNotes: He explains eligibility in Wilson’s favor, urges the application, gets him through the crowd, and offers to run the shop. Each action removes an obstacle to Wilson’s absence.
evidence: I shall be able to look after that for you.

questions.prompt: What purpose does the manager’s praise of Wilson’s hair serve during the interview?
facilitatorNotes: Flattery makes the arbitrary requirement feel like a rare personal qualification. Apparent competition and special exceptions heighten the value of winning the post.
evidence: we must stretch a point in favor of a man with such a head of hair as yours

questions.prompt: Which condition seems stricter than the apparently simple copying work requires?
facilitatorNotes: Wilson must remain in the building for the entire four hours regardless of illness or business. The rule draws attention to his location rather than the usefulness of the copy.
evidence: No excuse will avail

days.title: The league vanishes: part 3 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the red-headed league)
days.challenge: Evaluate what new checks establish and what they leave open.
days.focus: Distinguish receiving payment from understanding a scheme.
days.context: Wilson has accepted four hours of daily encyclopedia copying. He is forbidden to leave the office during that time and must supply his own writing materials.
days.contentNote: The account uses dismissive class judgments and a brief historical reference to a “gypsy.” Its printed dates are not internally consistent.

excerpt.locator: The Red-headed League, Wilson’s doubts through Holmes’s promise to investigate; opens ““Well, I thought over the matter all day, and by evening I was in low spirits again; ”; closes “ course of a day or two. To-day is Saturday, and I hope that by Monday we may come to a conclusion.””.

questions.prompt: Why does being paid weaken Wilson’s suspicion without disproving fraud?
facilitatorNotes: Regular wages make the arrangement feel genuine, but a scheme can pay one participant in order to gain something larger. Payment establishes that money changed hands, not the stated purpose.
evidence: four golden sovereigns for my week’s work

questions.prompt: How do Wilson’s inquiries undermine the manager’s presented identity?
facilitatorNotes: The landlord knows a different name and occupation, while the forwarding address leads to a business that recognizes neither name. These checks contradict the story he was given.
evidence: no one in it had ever heard of either Mr. William Morris or Mr. Duncan Ross

questions.prompt: Why does Holmes focus on how the assistant was hired after hearing the league has closed?
facilitatorNotes: The assistant introduced the offer and accepted unusually low pay. His hiring and physical description may connect the supposed opportunity to a person still inside Wilson’s business.
evidence: Because he was handy, and would come cheap.

days.title: A walk around the block: part 4 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the red-headed league)
days.challenge: Hold several clues in memory while resisting premature certainty.
days.focus: Track investigative actions before their purpose is explained.
days.context: The league has dissolved after eight weeks. Holmes suspects the assistant and takes Watson to inspect Wilson’s shop and the neighboring streets.
days.contentNote: Holmes anticipates danger and asks Watson to carry a revolver; tobacco is mentioned.

excerpt.locator: The Red-headed League, Watson’s uncertainty through his evening arrival; opens ““Well, Watson,” said Holmes, when our visitor had left us, “what do you make of it al”; closes “ther was a long, thin, sad-faced man, with a very shiny hat and oppressively respectable frock-coat.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the request for directions have a second purpose?
facilitatorNotes: Holmes admits he wanted to inspect the assistant’s trouser knees. The ordinary request lets him obtain a physical observation without revealing the investigation.
evidence: The knees of his trousers.

questions.prompt: What does walking around the corner reveal that looking only at the shop front would miss?
facilitatorNotes: The shabby square backs onto a busy commercial street containing a bank. The two appearances conceal the buildings’ physical proximity.
evidence: they really abutted on the other side upon the faded and stagnant square

questions.prompt: How does Watson’s description of Holmes at the concert complicate the image of constant visible activity?
facilitatorNotes: Quiet absorption in music alternates with intense investigation. Watson’s experience leads him to expect decisive action after apparent leisure, though the exact plan remains withheld.
evidence: the reaction against the poetic and contemplative mood

days.title: Waiting beneath the bank: part 5 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the red-headed league)
days.challenge: Connect a location’s physical details to the developing threat.
days.focus: Analyze suspense created by limited light and delayed movement.
days.context: Watson joins Holmes, police detective Jones, and bank director Merryweather for a late-night operation. Holmes has inspected the shop adjacent to the bank.
days.contentNote: The scene includes an armed police ambush and instructions about shooting if the intruders fire.

excerpt.locator: The Red-headed League, introductions through the intruders’ alarm; opens ““Ha! our party is complete,” said Holmes, buttoning up his pea-jacket, and taking his”; closes “ispered. “Have you the chisel and the bags. Great Scott! Jump, Archie, jump, and I’ll swing for it!””.

questions.prompt: How does the exchange about protection from above and below revise the bank director’s confidence?
facilitatorNotes: Strong doors and gates protect normal entry, but a hollow floor suggests another route. Security depends on examining the actual vulnerability rather than counting barriers.
evidence: Why, dear me, it sounds quite hollow!

questions.prompt: What information explains why this particular cellar is attractive to thieves?
facilitatorNotes: An unusually large reserve of borrowed French gold remains packed there. The opportunity concerns a temporary concentration of value, not just the existence of a bank.
evidence: much larger at present than is usually kept in a single branch office

questions.prompt: How does the hand emerging before the rest of the intruder intensify suspense?
facilitatorNotes: The tiny light and isolated fingers reveal the approach gradually while the watchers must stay still. Limited visibility delays recognition and concentrates attention on small movements.
evidence: a white, almost womanly hand, which felt about in the centre

days.title: The purpose of the copying: part 6 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the red-headed league)
days.challenge: Assess the relationship between personal motives and public benefit.
days.focus: Reconstruct a causal explanation from clues gathered earlier.
days.context: Two intruders have emerged through the bank cellar floor. Holmes and his companions are waiting in darkness, while officers cover the exit through Wilson’s shop.
days.contentNote: An intruder draws a gun and is struck on the wrist; the scene includes class arrogance, alcohol, and gendered assumptions.

excerpt.locator: The Red-headed League, capture through the final quotation; opens “Sherlock Holmes had sprung out and seized the intruder by the collar. The other dived”; closes “ he remarked. “‘L’homme c’est rien—l’oeuvre c’est tout,’ as Gustave Flaubert wrote to Georges Sand.””.

questions.prompt: How does the apparently wasteful copying job become useful within Holmes’s explanation?
facilitatorNotes: The job reliably removes Wilson for hours while the assistant digs. The wages are small compared with the intended theft, and the copied material itself need not be valuable.
evidence: secure his absence every morning in the week

questions.prompt: What connects the assistant’s worn knees with the bank’s location?
facilitatorNotes: Kneeling and burrowing explain the clothing marks, while the adjacent bank supplies a plausible destination for the tunnel. The clues reinforce one another rather than functioning alone.
evidence: They spoke of those hours of burrowing.

questions.prompt: How do Watson and Holmes differ when discussing what the case accomplished?
facilitatorNotes: Watson emphasizes service to others; Holmes emphasizes relief from boredom before allowing some usefulness. Personal fascination and public benefit both appear, without requiring identical motives.
evidence: It saved me from ennui

days.title: The Story of My Life: two trees and two lessons (chapter v)
days.challenge: Trace a sensory sequence through suspense and compare the two climbing episodes.
days.focus: Nature as a source of both kinship and danger, with renewed confidence earned through action.
days.context: After learning that objects have names, Keller explores outdoors with Sullivan. A storm changes her view of nature before a flowering mimosa draws her back to climbing.
days.contentNote: Contains a frightening storm while a child is in a tree. The episode is a memoir, not advice on climbing or storm safety.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter V, complete chapter prose; from “I RECALL many incidents of the summer of 1887 that followed my soul's sudde…” through “…appy hours in my tree of paradise, thinking fair thoughts and dreaming bright dreams.”

questions.prompt: How does Keller know a storm is coming without describing something she sees or hears?
facilitatorNotes: Loss of warmth, an earth smell and movement through the tree provide evidence. The sequence advances from anticipation to bodily danger, making touch and smell carry the suspense.
evidence: all the heat, which meant light to me, had died out
the odour that always precedes a thunderstorm
A shiver ran through the tree

questions.prompt: Compare the statement that nature provides food and shelter with the image of treacherous claws. Must one cancel the other?
facilitatorNotes: The first lesson emphasizes belonging and care; the storm reveals danger within that same world. The text adds complexity rather than proving that nature is entirely kind or hostile. Readers can support an interpretation of changing judgment rather than a single fixed moral.
evidence: every other creature finds food and shelter
under softest touch hides treacherous claws

questions.prompt: What makes the mimosa climb more than a return to the starting point?
facilitatorNotes: She chooses it after fear, hesitates and persists despite painful bark and awkward branches. The fragrance links the two lessons through sensation, while her independent action rebuilds confidence without erasing danger.
evidence: for one minute stood irresolute
the bark hurt my hands
I kept on climbing higher and higher

days.title: The Story of My Life: learning an abstract word (chapter vi)
days.challenge: Follow unsuccessful definitions and explain how an analogy differs from a literal identity.
days.focus: How naming an internal act helps Keller understand an invisible relationship.
days.context: Keller can name objects but is beginning to ask about ideas that cannot simply be touched. Sullivan teaches through a bead-pattern task and an analogy involving rain.
days.contentNote: The chapter generalizes from Keller’s educational experience. Its descriptions of deaf children and conversation are historical observations, not a complete account of sign languages or present-day deaf education.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter VI, complete chapter prose; from “I HAD now the key to all language, and I was eager to learn to use it. Chil…” through “…expression of the speaker's face, and a look is often the very soul of what one says.”

questions.prompt: Why do flowers and sunlight seem plausible answers to Helen’s question, and why are they insufficient?
facilitatorNotes: They are beautiful sensations that give pleasure, so they fit what love seems to do. But treating love as one touchable or felt object cannot express a relation between people; Sullivan rejects identities before offering an analogy.
evidence: Is love the sweetness of flowers?
I thought it strange that my teacher could not show me love.

questions.prompt: How does correcting the bead pattern prepare Helen for understanding love?
facilitatorNotes: The teacher names thinking at the moment Helen attends to her own mental process. That creates an example of a real thing known without handling it, opening a route toward another abstract idea.
evidence: the word was the name of the process that was going on in my head
my first conscious perception of an abstract idea

questions.prompt: Explain both the strength and the limit of the cloud-and-rain comparison.
facilitatorNotes: Unseen or untouchable causes can be recognized by their effects, just as affection can be felt through happiness and connection. Love is not weather; the comparison supplies an approach to meaning. The final discussion shows that one breakthrough still requires years of conversational practice.
evidence: You cannot touch love either
invisible lines stretched between my spirit and the spirits of others
This process was continued for several years

days.title: The supposedly haunted room (Tom Sawyer, chapter xxviii)
days.challenge: Notice social prejudice within a statement meant as praise.
days.focus: Evaluate a discovery and the limits of a generalization.
days.context: Tom and Huck seek a box of stolen treasure. They suspect Joe, now disguised as a Spaniard, is using a room in a temperance tavern.
days.contentNote: The text contains repeated racist slurs, a racialized villain, and alcohol. Discuss Huck’s gratitude alongside the hierarchy his words still accept.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXVIII, complete chapter; opens “That night Tom and Huck were ready for their adventure. They hung about the neig”; closes “hering around. Any time you see something’s up, in the night, just skip right around and maow.””.
