questions.prompt: What extra work does arranging a doll, a bed and word cards do beyond memorizing the word “doll”?
facilitatorNotes: The arrangement turns a sentence’s relation into an action: an object is on another object. The wardrobe game transfers the relation to a new scene, showing meaning rather than simple matching.
evidence: making a sentence out of the words
carrying out the idea of the sentence with the things themselves
I pinned the word girl on my pinafore

questions.prompt: Why can the clay map help while the strings and orange stick confuse?
facilitatorNotes: A raised map makes terrain available to touch; the globe model’s visible or tangible aids can be mistaken for physical features. Keller’s North Pole joke recognizes the problem afterward. Accept discussion of model usefulness and its limits together.
evidence: feel the mountain ridges and valleys
The illustrative strings and the orange stick representing the poles seemed so real

questions.prompt: How does the arithmetic paragraph qualify the celebration of Sullivan’s teaching?
facilitatorNotes: Even patient, concrete instruction does not make every subject appealing. Helen does a few groups and leaves with a clear conscience. The humorous admission keeps the account of joyful education from claiming universal ease or constant enthusiasm.
evidence: Arithmetic seems to have been the only study I did not like.
my conscience was at rest for the day

days.title: The Story of My Life: shells, plants and a growing mind (chapter vii)
days.challenge: Distinguish observation, imaginative personification and an extended analogy about education.
days.focus: Growth in natural objects as a way of explaining intellectual development.
days.context: Keller continues her account of Sullivan’s informal teaching with fossils, a shell, lilies and tadpoles, then reflects on why the lessons worked.
days.contentNote: The animals and plants are often imagined as having human motives. Read these as literary interpretations rather than biological explanations.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter VII, natural-history episodes and closing reflection; from “Once a gentleman, whose name I have forgotten, sent me a collection of foss…” through “…lent, or an aspiration or a joy in me that has not been awakened by her loving touch.”

questions.prompt: How do the fossils and the living shell stretch Keller’s understanding in different directions?
facilitatorNotes: Fossils make vanished life imaginable and somewhat frightening; the shell connects a present structure to both natural processes and mental growth. One opens historical time, the other an analogy for transforming knowledge.
evidence: the keys which unlocked the treasures of the antediluvian world
become pearls of thought

questions.prompt: What do the lily-queen and the ambitious tadpole add that a scientific report would not?
facilitatorNotes: Royal dress and ambition give movement emotional character and invite imaginative attention. The text does not establish that the plant feels pride or the tadpole has completed a travel ambition; readers should separate observed changes from the narrator’s playful account.
evidence: the lily-queen by right divine
He had made his leap, he had seen the great world

questions.prompt: Trace the brook-to-river analogy. What does it suggest a teacher can and cannot do?
facilitatorNotes: Sullivan guides and supplies experiences; the child’s mind grows through its own flow and increasing capacity. The later insistence on liberty and felt success or disappointment means a teacher cannot simply compel joyful learning.
evidence: like a shallow brook
fed by mountain streams and hidden springs
not every teacher can make him learn

days.title: American Indian Stories: arrival and the loss of long hair (from “The School Days of an Indian Girl”)
days.challenge: Reconstruct unfamiliar routines from the child’s viewpoint and interpret physical actions through the cultural meanings she supplies.
days.focus: The difference between being managed and being understood, culminating in resistance to forced hair-cutting.
days.context: The children have left their Dakota families for an eastern missionary school. Promises of apples and a new experience now meet the reality of a journey, a dormitory and institutional rules.
days.contentNote: Contains racial staring, forced assimilation, restraint and a child’s hair being cut against her will. Historical racial language is retained. The passage is emotionally demanding and may benefit from shared discussion.

excerpt.locator: The School Days of an Indian Girl, I “The Land of Red Apples” and II “The Cutting of My Long Hair”; from “THE SCHOOL DAYS OF AN INDIAN GIRL…” through “… mother used to do; for now I was only one of many little animals driven by a herder.”

questions.prompt: How does the remembered telegraph pole function differently from the train passengers’ staring eyes?
facilitatorNotes: The pole offers a familiar connection to home, even though the child had once imagined it was hurt. The staring people turn her into an object of curiosity. The contrast shows how familiarity, not simply technological novelty, shapes her experience.
evidence: I resented being watched.
seeing one familiar object
I used to wonder what the paleface had done to hurt it.

questions.prompt: Why is tossing the girl into the air not experienced as affection, and how does the dining-room confusion deepen the same problem?
facilitatorNotes: The woman does not ask what the child wants or recognise her dignity; routine signals are equally unexplained. The girl must guess rules while being watched. The memoir distinguishes adults’ possible intentions from what their actions do to a child.
evidence: My mother had never made a plaything of her wee daughter.
I was both frightened and insulted
I was afraid to venture anything more.

questions.prompt: What makes cutting the braid a loss beyond a change of hairstyle? How does the closing image sharpen the criticism?
facilitatorNotes: The child links shingled hair to captivity and humiliation, meanings the school ignores. Restraint and the absence of comfort break her sense of agency; the herder image contrasts institutional control with her mother’s reasoned care.
evidence: shingled hair by cowards
No, I will not submit! I will struggle first!
one of many little animals driven by a herder.

days.title: American Indian Stories: misunderstood words and acts of rebellion (from “The School Days of an Indian Girl”)
days.challenge: Track how the same word changes meaning with a question, and how fear produces two different forms of retaliation.
days.focus: Language barriers, coercive discipline and the child’s attempts to reclaim power.
days.context: The young pupils understand little English. These two sections follow a disastrous attempt to prepare for questioning, an angry kitchen task and a frightening religious lesson.
days.contentNote: Contains corporal punishment, threats of supernatural torture and a nightmare. The critique concerns how adults teach and discipline in these scenes; it does not require rejecting or affirming any religion.

excerpt.locator: The School Days of an Indian Girl, III “The Snow Episode” and IV “The Devil”; from “III.…” through “…om, there was a ragged hole in the page where the picture of the devil had once been.”

questions.prompt: Why does Thowin’s repeated “No” produce changing reactions without expressing changing intentions?
facilitatorNotes: She knows only the practised reply, while the adult changes the questions. The same sound is interpreted as defiance and then compliance. The scene exposes the danger of assuming comprehension from an answer.
evidence: the only word at her command
Are you going to obey my word the next time?
Are you going to fall in the snow again?

questions.prompt: How is the turnip episode both obedience to an instruction and resistance to authority?
facilitatorNotes: She keeps mashing after the task is complete, exploiting the literal command to break the jar. Her satisfaction and small regret make the account less simple than an unqualified celebration of revenge.
evidence: the order was, "Mash these turnips," and mash them I would!
I felt triumphant in my revenge
a wee bit sorry to have broken the jar.

questions.prompt: Why does scratching out the pictured devil offer the child a sense of action after the nightmare?
facilitatorNotes: The picture made the threat concrete, so damaging it lets her attack a visible representation of what she could not control in sleep. The adult narrator calls the teaching a legend, placing its fear-making power beside stories from her own childhood.
evidence: little girls who disobeyed school regulations were to be tortured by him
I began by scratching out his wicked eyes
a ragged hole in the page

days.title: Saturday’s Child
days.challenge: Track parallel birth images and recognize personified Poverty, Pain, Death, and Sorrow as participants in an extended contrast.
days.focus: Unequal beginnings expressed by reversing familiar celebratory images of infancy.
days.context: The speaker contrasts the welcome given to fortunate children with the conditions of his own birth. Read the repeated “Some” against each “I” or “me.”
days.contentNote: The poem uses death and sorrow as figures surrounding a difficult birth; it also quotes a parent’s rejection of another mouth to feed.

excerpt.locator: Saturday’s Child; complete individual poem; opening “SOME are teethed on a silver spoon, With the stars strung for a rattle; I cut my teeth”; closing “life, And handed me to Sorrow, The only kind of middle wife My folks could beg or borrow.”.

questions.prompt: How does the silver spoon become different from the speaker’s “implements of battle”?
facilitatorNotes: One image implies inherited comfort and ornament, the other preparation for struggle. Teeth connect both images to infancy, making the contrast about unequal starting conditions rather than later choices alone.
evidence:
I cut my teeth as the black raccoon—
For implements of battle.

questions.prompt: What happens when Poverty and Pain take the roles of people who traditionally welcome and protect a child?
facilitatorNotes: The personification makes deprivation intimate and present from the beginning. These figures function as a grim alternative family; responses should distinguish that crafted symbolism from a factual birth record.
evidence:
Dame Poverty gave me my name,
And Pain godfathered me.

questions.prompt: How does the father’s plain sentence differ from the elaborate imagery around it?
facilitatorNotes: The blunt counting of mouths abruptly reduces a child to an expense. Its ordinary speech gives the symbolic contrasts a concrete emotional sting; it may suggest material desperation as well as rejection.
evidence: And, “One mouth more to feed.”

days.title: A hat and a lost goose: part 1 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the blue carbuncle)
days.challenge: Follow a chain of possession without confusing finder and owner.
days.focus: Distinguish identifying clues from a unique identification.
days.context: Watson visits Holmes just after Christmas and finds him examining a battered hat connected with a street disturbance and a lost goose.
days.contentNote: A street assault, accidental broken window, alcohol, and preparation of a goose for food are mentioned.

excerpt.locator: The Blue Carbuncle, opening through Watson’s request for inferences; opens “I had called upon my friend Sherlock Holmes upon the second morning after Christmas, ”; closes ““Then, pray tell me what it is that you can infer from this hat?””.

questions.prompt: Why does the man’s flight not by itself prove he has committed a deliberate crime?
facilitatorNotes: He has accidentally broken a window while defending himself and sees a uniformed stranger approaching. Fear of being blamed offers an explanation without proving prior criminal intent.
evidence: shocked at having broken the window

questions.prompt: Why do the name on the goose and initials in the hat fail to identify one owner?
facilitatorNotes: They narrow the search but refer to a very common name in a large city. A clue can be accurate while still insufficiently specific.
evidence: some hundreds of Henry Bakers in this city

questions.prompt: What does Holmes mean by telling Watson he can see everything but fails to reason from it?
facilitatorNotes: Watson records wear, stains, initials, and a missing elastic. Holmes distinguishes noticing details from forming explanations, though those explanations will still need evaluation.
evidence: You fail, however, to reason from what you see.

days.title: The deductions and the jewel: part 2 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the blue carbuncle)
days.challenge: Question confident claims rather than treating a famous detective as infallible.
days.focus: Rank inferences by the strength of their support.
days.context: Holmes has a worn hat and a goose found after a street disturbance. He explains what he believes the hat reveals before the finder returns with a discovery.
days.contentNote: The passage contains unsupported claims linking head size with intelligence, sexist assumptions, alcohol, and a criminal accusation.

excerpt.locator: The Blue Carbuncle, Holmes’s hat analysis through the newspaper court report; opens “He picked it up and gazed at it in the peculiar introspective fashion which was chara”; closes “tense emotion during the proceedings, fainted away at the conclusion, and was carried out of court.’”.

questions.prompt: Compare the evidence for recently cut hair with the claim that a large hat proves intelligence. Which is better supported within the passage?
facilitatorNotes: Cut hair fragments directly connect with a haircut. Hat size supplies no demonstrated relationship to intelligence; Holmes’s confidence does not make that claim a reliable inference.
evidence: a large number of hair-ends, clean cut by the scissors

questions.prompt: What assumption allows Holmes to infer a wife’s lack of affection from an unbrushed hat?
facilitatorNotes: He assumes a loving wife is responsible for maintaining her husband’s hat. Other explanations for dust remain possible, making this a gendered assumption rather than a necessary conclusion.
evidence: his wife has ceased to love him

questions.prompt: What distinction should readers make between Horner’s previous conviction and proof of this theft?
facilitatorNotes: A past conviction may influence suspicion, but it does not establish this act. The report includes allegations and missing physical evidence, so the current accusation still requires testing.
evidence: the stone could not be found either upon his person or in his rooms

days.title: A replacement bird: part 3 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the blue carbuncle)
days.challenge: Connect a seemingly trivial inquiry with its human stakes.
days.focus: Analyze a test designed to distinguish competing explanations.
days.context: A stolen jewel has been found inside the goose. Holmes advertises for Henry Baker, planning to learn whether he knows what his bird contained.
days.contentNote: Holmes briefly lists violence, suicide, and acid attack associated with the jewel’s fictional history; alcohol appears.

excerpt.locator: The Blue Carbuncle, tracing plan through the decision to visit Breckinridge; opens ““Hum! So much for the police-court,” said Holmes, thoughtfully, tossing aside the pap”; closes “ed in our hands. Let us follow it out to the bitter end. Faces to the south, then, and quick march!””.

questions.prompt: Why does Holmes offer both a fresh goose and the remains of the original?
facilitatorNotes: Someone interested only in dinner should accept a replacement; someone seeking the hidden gem would need the original remains. Baker’s indifference to the crop supports innocence.
evidence: I will confine my attentions to the excellent bird

questions.prompt: How does the goose club explain Baker’s possession without placing him at the jewel theft?
facilitatorNotes: He paid small weekly contributions and received a Christmas bird from the inn. That supplies a normal transfer in the chain, which investigators can trace backward.
evidence: on consideration of some few pence every week

questions.prompt: Why does Holmes remind Watson of Horner before continuing through the city?
facilitatorNotes: The pursuit now concerns a person facing years in prison, not merely an entertaining puzzle. Holmes also allows that investigation could confirm guilt, showing the outcome is not assumed.
evidence: It is possible that our inquiry may but confirm his guilt

days.title: The wager and the ledger: part 4 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the blue carbuncle)
days.challenge: Distinguish records of a transaction from motives inferred about people.
days.focus: Explain how a conversational tactic changes access to evidence.
days.context: The Alpha Inn bought its geese from Breckinridge in Covent Garden. Holmes and Watson ask him where those birds originated.
days.contentNote: The investigation uses a deceptive wager; Holmes makes a broad judgment based on a man’s appearance and newspaper.

excerpt.locator: The Blue Carbuncle, arrival at Breckinridge’s stall through Holmes’s explanation of the wager; opens “We passed across Holborn, down Endell Street, and so through a zigzag of slums to Cov”; closes “fellow said that there are others besides ourselves who are anxious about the matter, and I should—””.

questions.prompt: What does Breckinridge’s irritation reveal beyond his refusal to answer?
facilitatorNotes: Other people have repeatedly asked about the same geese. The irritation therefore becomes a clue that another interested searcher exists.
evidence: if you were as pestered as I am

questions.prompt: Why does arguing that the bird was country-bred succeed where a direct question failed?
facilitatorNotes: It challenges the seller’s expertise and offers a wager he can win. To prove Holmes wrong, Breckinridge voluntarily produces the information he had withheld.
evidence: D’you think you know more about fowls than I

questions.prompt: How do the two books work together to connect supplier and buyer?
facilitatorNotes: The small book indexes suppliers by category and ledger number; the larger ledger records the dated purchase and sale. Together they trace Mrs. Oakshott’s geese to the Alpha.
evidence: the numbers after their names are where their accounts are in the big ledger

days.title: The other searcher: part 5 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the blue carbuncle)
days.challenge: Compare a plea for sympathy with its omission of another person’s suffering.
days.focus: Reinterpret a witness’s role when new evidence appears.
days.context: Breckinridge’s records have traced the goose to Mrs. Oakshott. As Holmes and Watson leave, another man urgently questions the dealer.
days.contentNote: The scene involves framing an innocent person, emotional distress, and alcohol offered to a faint suspect.

excerpt.locator: The Blue Carbuncle, the quarrel at the stall through Holmes’s rebuke to Ryder; opens “His remarks were suddenly cut short by a loud hubbub which broke out from the stall w”; closes “but you thought little enough of this poor Horner in the dock for a crime of which he knew nothing.””.

questions.prompt: Why does the searcher’s real name matter more than his first offered name?
facilitatorNotes: James Ryder is the hotel attendant whose testimony helped accuse Horner. The identity links the goose search directly to the original theft.
evidence: my real name is James Ryder

questions.prompt: How does Holmes’s description of a blue egg after the bird’s death communicate more than ordinary news about poultry?
facilitatorNotes: It indirectly tells Ryder that the hidden jewel has been recovered. The strange metaphor tests recognition before Holmes openly displays the stone.
evidence: the bonniest, brightest little blue egg

questions.prompt: What does Holmes point out that Ryder leaves out of his plea about his parents?
facilitatorNotes: Ryder asks consideration for his own family but had arranged suffering for an innocent man. Holmes requires him to confront that harm rather than treating fear as sufficient remorse.
evidence: you thought little enough of this poor Horner in the dock

days.title: Two barred tails: part 6 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the blue carbuncle)
days.challenge: Distinguish a predicted outcome from one shown in the narrative.
days.focus: Evaluate an explanation and a discretionary decision.
days.context: Ryder has admitted his involvement in the jewel theft. Holmes demands to know how the stone entered the goose and reached the market.
days.contentNote: A goose is forced to swallow a jewel and later another is killed for food. The ending debates punishment and forgiveness.

excerpt.locator: The Blue Carbuncle, Ryder’s offer to flee through the final dinner invitation; opens ““I will fly, Mr. Holmes. I will leave the country, sir. Then the charge against him w”; closes “ell, doctor, we will begin another investigation, in which, also, a bird will be the chief feature.””.

questions.prompt: Which mistaken assumption ruins Ryder’s plan to recover the stone?
facilitatorNotes: He assumes the barred tail uniquely identifies his chosen goose. His sister explains that two birds have the same marking, so he carries away the wrong one.
evidence: there were two barred-tailed ones

questions.prompt: How does Ryder’s fear reverse his expectation of sudden wealth?
facilitatorNotes: He becomes suspicious of every passerby, loses control of the hiding place, and gains no money. His account emphasizes anxiety and damage to his character rather than enjoyment.
evidence: without ever having touched the wealth for which I sold my character

questions.prompt: What assumptions support Holmes’s decision to release Ryder, and which outcomes remain unshown?
facilitatorNotes: Holmes expects Ryder’s absence to collapse the case against Horner and terror to deter future crime. The story ends before either prediction is independently verified; readers may debate mercy and accountability.
evidence: it is just possible that I am saving a soul

days.title: American Indian Stories: the machine and the uneasy homecoming (from “The School Days of an Indian Girl”)
days.challenge: Connect the school’s mechanical imagery to the adolescent’s later sense of not belonging at home or away.
days.focus: How institutional harm can persist after departure and strain relationships that remain loving.
days.context: After describing misunderstandings at school, the narrator turns to rigid daily routines, a classmate’s death and four summers back in her western home.
days.contentNote: Contains illness, a child’s death, distress and historical racial and disability language. “Consumption” is the historical term used in the source. The mother’s and daughter’s pain should not be reduced to either one’s personal failure.

excerpt.locator: The School Days of an Indian Girl, V “Iron Routine” and VI “Four Strange Summers”; from “V.…” through “…nters, when I should be grown tall, and there would be congenial friends awaiting me.”

questions.prompt: What do the pencil, bell, harness and “civilizing machine” have in common as images of schooling?
facilitatorNotes: They depict automatic control that records compliance without attending to individual pain. The teacher is also described as hard-working and well-meaning, making the indictment more complex than simple personal malice.
evidence: her pencil black-marked our daily records
the civilizing machine
the hard-working, well-meaning, ignorant woman

questions.prompt: How does the phrase “neither a wild Indian nor a tame one” connect the return home with the school routine?
facilitatorNotes: She experiences the categories imposed on her as a trap: education has not granted secure belonging in either setting. Adolescence compounds this dislocation. Readers should question the dehumanising wild/tame vocabulary rather than adopt it as a neutral classification.
evidence: I was neither a wee girl nor a tall one
neither a wild Indian nor a tame one
the effect of my brief course in the East

questions.prompt: Why does the mother’s offer of the Bible deepen distress despite her wish to comfort?
facilitatorNotes: She offers the only printed material available, trying to meet a daughter she sees as literate and changed. The daughter experiences it as useless in this crisis, then recognises that her mother’s grief is for her. The scene supports mutual love and failed communication at once.
evidence: for her sake
the only printed matter we had in our home
she was grieving for me.

days.title: American Indian Stories: a prize that does not satisfy (from “The School Days of an Indian Girl”)
days.challenge: Follow contradictory emotional responses to public recognition and distinguish two separate oratory contests.
days.focus: Achievement as a challenge to prejudice that cannot by itself repair loneliness or family estrangement.
days.context: The narrator pursues college despite her mother’s objections. After social isolation, she enters first a college speaking contest and then an intercollegiate contest.
days.contentNote: Contains racist mockery and a quoted slur directed at an Indigenous woman, which Zitkala-Sa records exactly to show the hostility she faced from a rival college’s students at the oratorical contest.

excerpt.locator: The School Days of an Indian Girl, VII “Incurring My Mother’s Displeasure”; from “VII.…” through “…aw my mother far away on the Western plains, and she was holding a charge against me.”

questions.prompt: What changes the narrator’s judgment of her own classmates during the first contest?
facilitatorNotes: Their flowers and cheering reveal kindness she had not expected after months of distant courtesy. She interprets the bouquet as a rebuke to her own hard feelings, though that does not erase earlier isolation.
evidence: courteous to me at a safe distance
a large bouquet of roses
This friendly token was a rebuke to me

questions.prompt: How does winning a prize answer the hostile banner, and what does it not answer?
facilitatorNotes: It defeats the immediate attempt to portray her as unworthy and forces the banner down. It does not erase the prejudice that produced it, nor her longing for home. Avoid turning the scene into a claim that success automatically cures racism.
evidence: a drawing of a most forlorn Indian girl
one of them was mine!
the white flag dropped out of sight

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter end alone by a fire rather than on the triumphant stage?
facilitatorNotes: The private ending allows the reader to see a hunger hidden by public victory. Her mother’s imagined charge remains unresolved; the emotional sequence qualifies rather than cancels the achievement.
evidence: I laughed no more in triumph when thus alone.
The little taste of victory did not satisfy a hunger in my heart.
she was holding a charge against me.

days.title: American Indian Stories: a teacher’s first day (from “An Indian Teacher among Indians”)
days.challenge: Read gestures and descriptions cautiously, recognising when the narrator marks a judgment as an impression rather than a fact.
days.focus: The gap between a public reputation for achievement and the private cost of pursuing it.
days.context: Illness has interrupted the narrator’s college course. Reluctant to return home, she takes work at an eastern school for Indigenous children and meets her employer.
days.contentNote: Contains illness and historical racial language. The short section calls for slow attention to inferred attitudes and the narrator’s exhaustion rather than rapid plot reading.

excerpt.locator: An Indian Teacher Among Indians, I “My First Day”; from “AN INDIAN TEACHER AMONG INDIANS…” through “…upon me. I threw myself upon the bed, and, closing my eyes, forgot my good intention.”

questions.prompt: What two motives shape her decision to teach, and how do they complicate a simple story of ambition?
facilitatorNotes: She wants to work for her people but also avoids the painful truth she expects in her mother’s rebuke. Purpose and pride coexist; the passage does not require selecting only one as the real motive.
evidence: my pride kept me from returning to my mother
a work for the Indian race
far too true to be comfortable

questions.prompt: Which descriptions of the employer are directly observable, and which are tentative interpretations?
facilitatorNotes: His height, handshake and words are reported actions; a shadow on his face and disappointment in his voice are qualified by “imagined” and “thought.” The reader should recognise the possibility that exhaustion and expectation influence her interpretation.
evidence: I imagined that a visible shadow flitted across his countenance
I thought I heard a subtle note of disappointment
he smiled kindly upon me.

questions.prompt: How does the room’s description prepare for the final image of water-soaked logs?
facilitatorNotes: Ghastly walls, aged curtains and stiff chairs offer little comfort after travel, while the heavy-log simile makes exhaustion physically oppressive. Her inability to act on a good intention follows from depletion, not a lack of ideas or commitment.
evidence: trying hard to imagine years of contentment there
years of weariness lay like water-soaked logs upon me
forgot my good intention.

days.title: Spring in New Hampshire
days.challenge: Follow the suspended “Too ... for me” syntax across several lines and connect daytime work with evening exhaustion.
days.focus: The conflict between the capacity to enjoy beauty and labor that consumes time and energy.
days.context: The speaker can perceive spring intensely while being kept from enjoying it. Read each six-line stanza as one unfolding sentence.

excerpt.locator: SPRING IN NEW HAMPSHIRE (To J. L. J. F. E.); complete individual poem; opening “Too green the springing April grass, Too blue the silver-speckled sky, For me to linger here, alas, While”; closing “me to spend the evening hours, When fields are fresh and streams are leaping, Wearied, exhausted, dully sleeping.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem repeat “Too” for grass, sky, night, flowers, and stars?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition makes beauty feel abundant enough to demand a response. Each sentence delays the work or exhaustion that prevents that response, creating pressure between delight and limitation.
evidence: Too green the springing April grass,

questions.prompt: How does the shift from golden hours to washing and scrubbing affect the first stanza’s tone?
facilitatorNotes: Concrete labor punctures the expansive scene and makes lost time visible. It may sound frustrated rather than contemptuous of cleaning itself; the complaint is about being confined when the world calls.
evidence:
Wasting the golden hours indoors,
Washing windows and scrubbing floors.

questions.prompt: Why is evening freedom not enough to resolve the conflict?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker is too exhausted to use it. The second stanza shows that labor consumes energy as well as hours, so merely ending work does not restore the missed experience.
evidence: Wearied, exhausted, dully sleeping.

days.title: The Story of My Life: gifts, friendship and a first history lesson (chapters viii–ix)
days.challenge: Compare immediate childhood interpretations with later corrections, and trace growing participation in a community.
days.focus: Giving, direct conversation and revised historical admiration as forms of growing beyond the self.
days.context: These consecutive chapters move from Keller’s first Christmas with Sullivan to her 1888 visit to Boston and the Perkins Institution.
days.contentNote: Includes the loss of a pet bird, historical racial terminology and an initially idealized account of the Pilgrims that Keller later qualifies by naming persecution.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapters VIII–IX, complete consecutive chapter prose; from “THE first Christmas after Miss Sullivan came to Tuscumbia was a great event…” through “… to me; indeed, I was thinking of him when I called Boston "The City of Kind Hearts."”

questions.prompt: How do the Christmas games and gift-giving show language changing Helen’s role in the family?
facilitatorNotes: Hints require inference and shared secrets; preparing and handing out gifts makes her an active giver as well as a recipient. The bird’s care adds responsibility, while its disappearance abruptly complicates the joyful chapter.
evidence: prepared surprises for everybody else
more about the use of language than any set of lessons
I did not stop to look at my own gifts

questions.prompt: Why does Keller describe Perkins as her own country after comparing herself to a foreigner?
facilitatorNotes: Other children know the manual alphabet, making direct exchange possible without mediation. Shared communication transforms belonging; her surprise that they are blind also exposes an earlier assumption, not an objective measure of their happiness.
evidence: a foreigner speaking through an interpreter
I was in my own country
pleasure of their companionship

questions.prompt: How does the Plymouth episode show both the value and the danger of a vivid history lesson?
facilitatorNotes: A touchable rock and model make distant events concrete but encourage a simplified heroic picture. The adult adds the persecution she learned about later, preserving admiration for courage while correcting the assumption of universal generosity.
evidence: perhaps that made the coming of the Pilgrims and their toils and great deeds seem more real
I thought they desired the freedom of their fellow men as well as their own.
their acts of persecution

days.title: The Story of My Life: sea and mountain adventures (chapters x–xi)
days.challenge: Compare changing judgments across several episodes and notice how comic reversals alternate with danger.
days.focus: Curiosity, misplaced confidence and learning from an encounter’s consequences.
days.context: Keller visits Cape Cod, then returns to her family’s mountain cottage in Alabama. The two chapters connect outdoor pleasure with moments of surprise and danger.
days.contentNote: Contains near-drowning, hunting references, historical racial terminology and a dangerous escape from a train. These are narrated experiences, not instructions for outdoor or railway activity.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapters X–XI, complete consecutive chapter prose; from “JUST before the Perkins Institution closed for the summer, it was arranged …” through “… we reached home and found the cottage empty; the family were all out hunting for us.”

questions.prompt: How does the horseshoe-crab episode revise Helen’s idea of a successful adventure?
facilitatorNotes: Carrying the heavy creature home first feels like an accomplishment; its escape leads her to consider its own needs. She shifts from possession and disappointment toward relief at its possible freedom, though she never knows its fate.
evidence: This feat pleased me highly
it was not kind or wise to force this poor dumb creature out of his element

questions.prompt: What makes the hunters’ return comic, and how does Keller prepare that reversal?
facilitatorNotes: Their extravagant boasts and energetic departure promise success; exhausted people, horses and dogs return without a kill. The joke about almost seeing a rabbit reduces their claims further, contrasting anticipated glory with ordinary dinner.
evidence: the greatest luck of the season
and not a single kill!
he saw his tracks

questions.prompt: Compare the sea and trestle escapes. How do physical details make sudden danger understandable?
facilitatorNotes: Both remove a sense of firm ground: water surrounds her and the bridge shakes above a gorge. The sea is personified as playing with a toy; the train presses heat, smoke and vibration upon her body. Compare the responses without assuming the danger erases her pleasure in exploration.
evidence: The good, firm earth had slipped from my feet
the hot breath from the engine on my face
the trestle shook and swayed

days.title: The Story of My Life: winter movement and learning to speak (chapters xii–xiii)
days.challenge: Connect images of motion and release while distinguishing an initial achievement from sustained mastery.
days.focus: The excitement of new possibilities and the labour needed to make them dependable.
days.context: Keller describes a northern winter, then her determination to learn spoken language in 1890 with Sarah Fuller and Sullivan’s continuing help.
days.contentNote: Contains historical terms for deaf and nonspeaking people and personal comparisons of silence with confinement. Keller’s preference for speech is her own; it does not establish speech as superior to sign languages. Editorial footnote markers and cross-references are omitted.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapters XII–XIII, complete consecutive chapter prose; from “AFTER my first visit to Boston, I spent almost every winter in the North. O…” through “…orth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands!"”

questions.prompt: How does the winter chapter move from stillness to freedom, and what language carries that movement?
facilitatorNotes: Sleeping roots, frozen ground and a marble frieze suggest arrested life; tobogganing supplies plunging and leaping. The chain-breaking image turns a physical ride into a brief imaginative release, not literal escape from gravity.
evidence: curled up in the dark, lay fast asleep
like figures in a marble frieze
we snapped the chain that binds us to earth

questions.prompt: Why does Keller interrupt the story of eleven speech lessons with “it must not be supposed”?
facilitatorNotes: She corrects a misleading triumph narrative: producing elements or one sentence is not being generally understood. Continuing tactile feedback and repetition matter alongside motivation; Sullivan’s work prevents the account from becoming a story of unaided success.
evidence: most people would not have understood one word in a hundred
My work was practice, practice, practice.

questions.prompt: What does the reunion reveal about communication beyond the simple opposition of speech and silence?
facilitatorNotes: Keller’s spoken words matter deeply, but her mother is speechless and her father communicates pride through silence; Mildred’s touch and movement also carry affection. The manual alphabet remains efficient for receiving messages. Different modes work together rather than one erasing the others.
evidence: my mother pressed me close to her, speechless and trembling with delight
my father expressed his pride and affection in a big silence
more convenient and more rapid than lip-reading

days.title: Simon the Cyrenian Speaks
days.challenge: Interpret a dramatic monologue that retells a familiar story from a new perspective.
days.focus: Choice, compassion, and racial suspicion in a retold Gospel scene.
days.context: In the Gospels, Simon of Cyrene, a man from North Africa, is made to carry Jesus’s cross. Cullen imagines Simon as a Black man telling his own story.
days.contentNote: The poem draws on the Christian crucifixion story; discussion does not require religious belief.

excerpt.locator: Simon the Cyrenian Speaks; complete individual poem; opening “HE never spoke a word to me, And yet He called my name; He”; closing “What all of Rome could not have wrought With bruise of lash or stone.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Simon at first refuse?
facilitatorNotes: He suspects he is chosen for degrading labor because of his race. Given the history of racism, the suspicion is reasonable, not merely stubborn.
evidence:
He only seeks to place it there
Because my skin is black.

questions.prompt: What changes his mind?
facilitatorNotes: He sees meekness, a dream, and a gleam in Christ’s eyes. Pity, not compulsion, moves him.
evidence: But He was dying for a dream,

questions.prompt: How does the last stanza distinguish choosing to help from being forced?
facilitatorNotes: Rome’s violence could compel bodies but not this willing act. Readers can discuss how freely given help preserves dignity.
evidence:
What all of Rome could not have wrought
With bruise of lash or stone.

days.title: My Mother
days.challenge: Compare two linked sonnets and explain how the second answers the first.
days.focus: Grief, numbness, and the continuing life of a rural community.
days.context: Two linked sonnets recall the day the speaker’s mother died in rural Jamaica. The “trades” are the steady trade winds.
days.contentNote: The poem describes a mother’s death and the speaker’s numb grief.

excerpt.locator: MY MOTHER; complete individual poem; opening “I Reg wished me to go with him to the field, I paused because”; closing “the earth where mortals sow and reap— Beneath its breast my mother lies asleep.”.

questions.prompt: What do the mother’s gestures communicate when she does not speak?
facilitatorNotes: She sends him out, pointing to his cap, and her eyes promise another day. The reassurance proves false; her love shows in sending him away.
evidence: Her eyes said: I shall last another day.

questions.prompt: Why might the speaker hear the news “listlessly, without a moan”?
facilitatorNotes: Shock, exhaustion, or anticipated grief are all possible. The quiet response contrasts with the loss of “the only one I loved.”
evidence: I heard him listlessly, without a moan,

questions.prompt: The second sonnet describes a busy morning. How does the final line change the scene?
facilitatorNotes: Children and workers continue their lives above the buried mother. Readers may find consolation in continuity or an ache in the world’s indifference.
evidence: Beneath its breast my mother lies asleep.

days.title: American Indian Stories: returning home as a recruiter (from “An Indian Teacher among Indians”)
days.challenge: Follow changing interpretations of a journey, a stranger and a house, revising each when new information appears.
days.focus: The irony of recruiting children to an institution whose promises the narrator’s own family cannot rely upon.
days.context: Worn down by school work, the narrator is sent west to recruit pupils. She welcomes the chance to see her mother, but the homecoming reveals losses she had not understood.
days.contentNote: Contains discrimination, poverty, historical racial terminology and a crisis of religious trust. The source’s explanatory footnote is retained with the passage.

excerpt.locator: An Indian Teacher Among Indians, II “A Trip Westward”; from “II.…” through “…[Footnote 1: An absolute Power.]”

questions.prompt: Why is “turn you loose to pasture” a particularly troubling description of this assignment?
facilitatorNotes: The employer presents demanding recruitment as restoration and speaks through an animal metaphor. She needs nourishment but is sent across a continent to persuade parents to entrust children to strangers. Her own childhood makes that task especially ironic.
evidence: I am going to turn you loose to pasture!
I needed nourishment
a lean pasturage

questions.prompt: What do the mistaken assumptions about the driver and the house have in common?
facilitatorNotes: Mother and daughter each judge before knowing the relevant facts: the driver is not a chosen companion, and the uncared-for house reflects lack of means rather than indifference. Both scenes model the need to revise impressions, though their emotional stakes differ.
evidence: He is a driver!
Do you have no interest in a more comfortable shelter?
we are left without means to buy even a morsel of food

questions.prompt: How does Dawée’s lost job challenge the promise that education alone will bring security?
facilitatorNotes: He has the education but loses the role to a white replacement and, according to the mother, suffers after seeking justice. The problem lies in power and access, not simply failure to learn. The narrator’s silence and angry appeal show how deeply this contradicts her work’s premise.
evidence: take your brother's pen from him
not been able to make use of the education
I found no words with which to answer satisfactorily.

days.title: American Indian Stories: behind the display of schooling (from “An Indian Teacher among Indians”)
days.challenge: Trace how physical landscapes become metaphors for a system and separate staged evidence from lived experience.
days.focus: The contrast between outsiders’ satisfying impressions and the narrator’s account of what those impressions conceal.
days.context: After hearing about the family’s hardships, the narrator returns east. She reconsiders school employment and the public claims made on behalf of Indigenous education.
days.contentNote: Contains historical racial and disability language, addiction, reported medical neglect and the mother’s anger at dispossession. The critique describes institutional conduct and particular experiences, not every member of a group.

excerpt.locator: An Indian Teacher Among Indians, III “My Mother’s Curse upon White Settlers” and IV “Retrospection”; from “III.…” through “… whether real life or long-lasting death lies beneath this semblance of civilization.”

questions.prompt: How does the growing number of lights across the river turn an ordinary night scene into evidence of threat for the mother?
facilitatorNotes: As the daughter’s eyes adjust, more settler fires appear, making encroachment visible. The mother links them to prior family losses and to hypocrisy. The same light that often suggests welcome instead signals shrinking space and powerlessness here.
evidence: the shrinking limits of the village
I saw more and more twinkling lights
there is the light of another white rascal!

questions.prompt: Explain the extended tree image from uprooting to the hope of lightning. What has education removed, and what capacity remains?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator imagines losing connections to mother, nature, faith and friends, with bark stripped from a vulnerable self. Yet the bare pole reaching upward still hopes to discharge pent-up consciousness: expression remains possible. Accept supported readings of anger, resistance or renewed purpose rather than a single required symbol.
evidence: uprooted from my mother, nature, and God
Now a cold bare pole I seemed to be
flash a zigzag lightning across the heavens

questions.prompt: Why is the students’ attractive sample work insufficient evidence for the visitors’ conclusions?
facilitatorNotes: The work is made for display, while visitors see docility and neat pages without examining health, coercion or long-term life. The ending asks whether visible order conceals harm. This is a critique of the evidence and what it leaves out, not a claim that students’ work lacks skill.
evidence: sample work _made_ for exhibition
the white visitors walked out of the schoolhouse well satisfied
whether real life or long-lasting death lies beneath this semblance of civilization.

days.title: The Great Spirit
days.challenge: Connect sensory imagery, analogy and dialogue in an argument that is personal rather than a conventional formal essay.
days.focus: A vision of kinship that rejects coercive belief while continuing to offer hospitality to someone who disagrees.
days.context: In this essay from American Indian Stories, Zitkala-Sa describes a walk, a return to her mother’s home and a conversation with a visiting preacher. The account states her own spiritual outlook.
days.contentNote: Includes historical racial and religious terms, a threat of hellfire and a remembered attempted arson. The author’s criticism of doctrine is supplied for interpretation, without requiring agreement or treating any community as uniform.

excerpt.locator: American Indian Stories, complete essay “The Great Spirit”; from “THE GREAT SPIRIT…” through “… flowing fringes are the spangles and oscillating brilliants of sun, moon, and stars.”

questions.prompt: How do the grain of sand, prairie flowers and Yellow Breast make spiritual value independent of size?
facilitatorNotes: Small lives are depicted as active, expressive and included within a larger mystery. The speaker is small too, not a ruler standing outside nature. Students may examine one image closely and connect it to the statement about great and small.
evidence: like a grain of throbbing sand
living symbols of omnipotent thought
both great and small are so surely enfolded in His magnitude

questions.prompt: What work does the comparison to piano keys do in the discussion of human differences?
facilitatorNotes: Similar appearance does not eliminate individual voice; shared colour does not make people interchangeable. The music analogy supports a diverse common life, while the warning about echoes resists merely repeating another’s beliefs.
evidence: the ivory keys of one instrument
varies from them in pitch and quality of voice
mere echoes of another's note

questions.prompt: How does feeding the preacher complicate the speaker’s sharp disagreement with him?
facilitatorNotes: She refuses the threat-based framework but does not refuse relationship or food. Hospitality enacts the kinship she has described, even while her language about his creed remains severe. Readers may recognise both generosity and tension rather than calling her wholly tolerant or wholly dismissive.
evidence: I offered midday meal to the converted Indian
Cousin, I have relished it,
both God's creatures

days.title: The Wild Swans at Coole
days.challenge: Connect a precise recurring observation with shifts in tense, bodily feeling, and unanswered questions.
days.focus: The contrast between a changing observer and creatures imagined as enduring in vitality.
days.context: A speaker counts swans at the same place after many years. Notice what is measured exactly and what remains unknowable.

excerpt.locator: THE WILD SWANS AT COOLE; complete individual poem; opening “The trees are in their autumn beauty, The woodland paths are dry, Under the October twilight the water”; closing “lake's edge or pool Delight men's eyes, when I awake some day To find they have flown away?”.

questions.prompt: How do the exact count and nineteenth autumn differ from the swans’ sudden movement into broken rings?
facilitatorNotes: Counting and dates suggest an effort to hold experience steady, while the flight interrupts that control. The contrast can make the scene both familiar and ungraspable.
evidence: Are nine and fifty swans.

questions.prompt: What supports the claim that the observer has changed more than the swans, and what part of that claim is an interpretation?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker reports a sore heart and a formerly lighter tread. He imagines the swans’ hearts as unaged; the poem does not prove that these are the same birds or that animals never change.
evidence: Their hearts have not grown old;

questions.prompt: Why end by imagining the swans delighting other people rather than simply describing their departure?
facilitatorNotes: Beauty may continue beyond this speaker’s possession or presence. Readers may hear generosity, fear of loss, or both; the unanswered question keeps the future open.
evidence:
Delight men's eyes, when I awake some day
To find they have flown away?

days.title: The Weary Blues
days.challenge: Hear how rhythm, repetition, and quoted song lines make a poem sound like the music it describes.
days.focus: The blues as both expression of sorrow and a source of release.
days.context: The title poem of Hughes’s first book describes a night on Lenox Avenue in Harlem. The speaker listens to a pianist singing the blues, a form whose verses often repeat a line before answering it.
days.contentNote: The poem uses the period term “Negro.” A quoted blues verse expresses a wish to have died, and the last line compares sleep to death.

excerpt.locator: THE WEARY BLUES; complete individual poem; opening “Droning a drowsy syncopated tune, Rocking back and forth to a mellow croon, I”; closing “echoed through his head. He slept like a rock or a man that’s dead.”.

questions.prompt: How do the lines about the singer’s playing and his foot make the poem sound like music?
facilitatorNotes: Rhymed couplets, repeated lines such as “He did a lazy sway,” and the drumming “Thump, thump, thump” create a rocking beat. Students can read aloud and mark where the rhythm drags or pushes.
evidence: Thump, thump, thump, went his foot on the floor.

questions.prompt: Compare the two songs the man sings. How do they differ?
facilitatorNotes: The first resolves to put troubles “on the shelf”; the second sinks into dissatisfaction and despair. The blues holds both coping and sorrow, so neither verse alone defines the singer.
evidence:
I’s gwine to quit ma frownin’
And put ma troubles on the shelf.

questions.prompt: What does the ending suggest about what the music has done for the singer?
facilitatorNotes: He sleeps deeply after the song, but the blues still echoes in his head. Readers may stress release, exhaustion, or sorrow that continues; avoid reading the simile as a literal death.
evidence: He slept like a rock or a man that’s dead.

days.title: The Open Window
days.challenge: Track what each character knows and distinguish the narrator’s account from stories told inside it.
days.focus: The manufacture of believable fiction from ordinary details and a listener’s uncertainty.
days.context: Framton Nuttel arrives with a letter of introduction and knows almost nothing about the household. Notice how the niece tests that lack of knowledge before telling her story.
days.contentNote: The story contains an invented account of drowning, a nervous visitor’s fright, and a fabricated threat from dogs; the period phrase “pariah dogs” is retained.

excerpt.locator: THE OPEN WINDOW; complete individual story; opening ““My aunt will be down presently, Mr. Nuttel,” said a very self-possessed young lady of fifteen; “in the”; closing “Romance at short notice was her speciality.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Vera ask about Framton’s acquaintance with the district before mentioning the alleged tragedy?
facilitatorNotes: His answers show that he cannot check her details against prior knowledge. Her apparent small talk gathers the conditions for a convincing invention; readers can point to the four-year gap and the supposedly three-year-old event.
evidence: “Then you know practically nothing about my aunt?”

questions.prompt: Which ordinary details become frightening because of Vera’s first story, and what does that show about evidence?
facilitatorNotes: The white coat, spaniel, open window, and repeated song match her description, but the match does not prove death or ghosts. She builds the false explanation around real, predictable details; students should distinguish accurate observations from the interpretation attached to them.
evidence: A tired brown spaniel kept close at their heels.

questions.prompt: How does the final explanation about dogs change our understanding of Vera’s earlier performance?
facilitatorNotes: It reveals the speed and adaptability of her invention rather than confirming Framton’s fear. The narrator’s final sentence invites admiration for craft and concern about cruelty at the same time; the story does not require approving the prank.
evidence: Romance at short notice was her speciality.

days.title: Dusk
days.challenge: Separate observed facts from Gortsby’s confident inferences and revise conclusions when the final object changes ownership.
days.focus: The limits of skepticism when evidence is selected and interpreted through a desired self-image.
days.context: Gortsby sits in a park at dusk and judges strangers he sees there. Follow the cake of soap closely, noting what it can and cannot establish.

excerpt.locator: DUSK; complete individual story; opening “Norman Gortsby sat on a bench in the Park, with his back to a strip of bush-planted sward,”; closing ““Yes, sir, a cake of soap.””.

questions.prompt: What does the opening description reveal about Gortsby’s habit of turning appearances into stories?
facilitatorNotes: He labels dusk the hour of defeat and imagines strangers’ unhappy homes without direct knowledge. The narrator identifies this as his imagination, preparing us to question later certainty rather than accept him as an objective detective.
evidence: So Gortsby’s imagination pictured things

questions.prompt: Why does finding soap seem decisive to Gortsby, and what missing link does he overlook?
facilitatorNotes: The object matches the young man’s claim, but Gortsby has not established who dropped it. His earlier insistence on material proof becomes overconfidence when a plausible item appears.
evidence: it had evidently fallen out of the youth’s overcoat pocket

questions.prompt: Does the ending prove every part of the young man’s story false, or something more limited?
facilitatorNotes: The older man’s claim strongly undermines the soap’s supposed corroboration and makes a trick likely. It does not independently verify the hotel, letter, or every detail; strong readers distinguish a persuasive narrative implication from exhaustive proof.
evidence: “Yes, sir, a cake of soap.”

days.title: The Lumber Room
days.challenge: Follow a child’s concealed plan while noticing how the narrator’s irony separates official adult wisdom from attentive observation.
days.focus: Imaginative freedom and the contest between rigid authority and a child’s ingenuity.
days.context: A “lumber-room” here means a storage room for unused household objects. Nicholas has been barred from an outing and forbidden to enter the garden.
days.contentNote: The story includes a hunted stag in a tapestry, imagined danger from wolves, and a child delaying help to an adult trapped in an empty tank; these acts invite evaluation rather than imitation.

excerpt.locator: THE LUMBER ROOM; complete individual story; opening “The children were to be driven, as a special treat, to the sands at Jagborough. Nicholas was not”; closing “he considered, that the huntsman would escape with his hounds while the wolves feasted on the stricken stag.”.

questions.prompt: How do the frog and the tight boots establish a recurring problem with the aunt’s authority?
facilitatorNotes: Adults assert knowledge or issue judgments without attending to the child’s evidence. Nicholas is deceptive about the frog, but the boots show a real ignored need; responses should not make either side wholly innocent.
evidence: He told you twice, but you weren’t listening.

questions.prompt: What does Nicholas do with the tapestry that makes the lumber-room more than a collection of expensive objects?
facilitatorNotes: He studies details, tests possible outcomes, and creates a continuing story about hunter, arrows, dogs, and wolves. The room feeds inquiry and imagination rather than simple ownership.
evidence: To Nicholas it was a living, breathing story;

questions.prompt: How does the quiet ending distinguish Nicholas’s silence from the aunt’s and the other children’s?
facilitatorNotes: The others are disappointed or humiliated; Nicholas is absorbed in the unresolved story he encountered. The ending rewards imaginative life, while readers can still question his decision not to help immediately.
evidence: in the absorption of one who has much to think about;

days.title: The Cat and the Moon
days.challenge: Follow changing movements and questions while distinguishing a narrator’s imaginative comparisons from an animal’s proven thoughts.
days.focus: The kinship between earthly and celestial change, seen through a cat’s eyes.
days.context: A cat named Minnaloushe watches the moon. Read the poem as an imaginative encounter rather than as an explanation of astronomy or animal vision.

excerpt.locator: THE CAT AND THE MOON; complete individual poem; opening “The cat went here and there And the moon spun round like a top, And the nearest kin”; closing “Minnaloushe creeps through the grass Alone, important and wise, And lifts to the changing moon His changing eyes.”.

questions.prompt: How does the moon’s spinning like a top prepare for the later invitation to dance?
facilitatorNotes: The opening already gives the sky playful movement. The dance develops that motion into an imagined meeting between cat and moon, bridging ordinary animal activity and a grand celestial object.
evidence: And the moon spun round like a top,

questions.prompt: Why might the suggestion that the moon could learn a new dance turn reverse the usual hierarchy between sky and earth?
facilitatorNotes: The small cat becomes a possible teacher rather than merely a creature influenced from above. The conditional “Maybe” keeps the reversal playful rather than asserting a fact.
evidence: Maybe the moon may learn,

questions.prompt: What is the effect of ending with changing eyes looking at a changing moon?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated adjective makes their kinship visible and returns us to observation after speculative questions. Readers can see mutual rhythm without claiming the cat consciously understands lunar phases.
evidence:
And lifts to the changing moon
His changing eyes.

days.title: The Collar-Bone of a Hare
days.challenge: Interpret an odd, precise image as a way of viewing the world.
days.focus: Escape, perspective, and mockery of convention.
days.context: The speaker imagines sailing to a magical land of dancing and pipes, then looking back at ordinary life through a small bone found on the shore.

excerpt.locator: THE COLLAR-BONE OF A HARE; complete individual poem; opening “Would I could cast a sail on the water Where many a king has”; closing “At all who marry in churches, Through the white thin bone of a hare.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker imagine learning in the first stanza’s land?
facilitatorNotes: Lightness and freedom from lasting commitment. Readers may find the wish attractive, childish, or sad.
evidence:
And learn that the best thing is
To change my loves while dancing

questions.prompt: Why look at the world through the bone of a hare?
facilitatorNotes: A tiny, worn, pierced bone is a strange lens: it distances and shrinks the world. The precise image makes the mockery playful.
evidence: Through the white thin bone of a hare.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker mock, and whose bitterness is it?
facilitatorNotes: He laughs at marrying in churches, but calling that world “bitter” may reveal his own disappointment. The fantasy can be read as escape from hurt.
evidence: At the old bitter world where they marry in churches,

days.title: A Dream of Her Grandfather
days.challenge: Read a brief vision story slowly enough to connect its frame, symbol, and message.
days.focus: How a dream links generations working for a people’s welfare.
days.context: Zitkala-Sa was a Yankton Dakota writer who worked in Washington, D.C., for Native American rights. In this short third-person story, the granddaughter’s situation closely resembles the author’s own.

excerpt.locator: American Indian Stories, complete story “A Dream of Her Grandfather”; from “Her grandfather was a Dakota "medicine man." Among the Indians of his day h…” through “…She caught the glad tidings and was thrilled with new hope for her people.”

questions.prompt: What connects the grandfather’s journey and the granddaughter’s work in Washington?
facilitatorNotes: Both go to the capital on behalf of their people, the grandfather on pony-back as a delegate and the granddaughter with “the white man’s tongue.” The story presents her work as continuing his.
evidence: followed in the footsteps of her grandfather to the very seat of government to carry on his humanitarian work

questions.prompt: Why is she disappointed when she first opens the chest, and how does the gift revise her expectation?
facilitatorNotes: She expected beaded regalia, objects she once coveted as a child, but receives a living vision of a camp. Recall the rebuke that such things “were never made for relics”: the gift is a people, not artifacts.
evidence: Why does my grandfather send such a light gift in a heavy, large box?

questions.prompt: What does the crier proclaim, and what does the story leave unexplained?
facilitatorNotes: He announces a new day and help nearby. The story never says what the help is or when it will come; readers may treat it as prophecy, encouragement, or longing. The vision is fragile, “so illusive a breath might have blown it away.”
evidence: Be glad! Rejoice! Look up, and see the new day dawning! Help is near!

days.title: The Schartz-Metterklume Method
days.challenge: Identify how mistaken identity survives through social assumptions and distinguish satire’s target from conduct worth endorsing.
days.focus: The gap between educational slogans and the consequences of applying them without ethical limits.
days.context: Lady Carlotta misses her train after intervening on behalf of an overloaded horse. A stranger assumes she is an expected governess, and she decides to play along.
days.contentNote: An invented anecdote jokes about domestic violence, and the mock lesson threatens corporal punishment and makes children enact an abduction. These attitudes and actions are part of the satire, not approved teaching or justified abuse.

excerpt.locator: THE SCHARTZ-METTERKLUME METHOD; complete individual story; opening “Lady Carlotta stepped out on to the platform of the small wayside station and took a turn or”; closing ““Oh dear, no,” said Lady Carlotta; “not at all tiresome—for me.””.

questions.prompt: How does the first encounter show Mrs. Quabarl helping create the deception rather than merely receiving it?
facilitatorNotes: She announces an identity instead of checking it and proceeds with orders. Lady Carlotta exploits that certainty; the narrator’s “dangerous meekness” signals that agreement is a performance.
evidence: “You must be Miss Hope, the governess I’ve come to meet,”

questions.prompt: What changes when the parents’ wish to make history feel real becomes the staged seizure of the lodge-keeper’s daughters?
facilitatorNotes: An appealing teaching slogan becomes coercive when children are treated as props and participation is not voluntary. Readers can recognize the joke about fashionable methods while naming the harm and refusing the governess’s defense of it.
evidence: make children understand history by acting it themselves

questions.prompt: How does the final qualification “for me” prevent the episode from being a harmless adventure for everyone?
facilitatorNotes: Carlotta has enjoyed control and freedom while others bear fear and embarrassment. The closing line can sound triumphant and selfish together; it asks us to notice whose experience defines “tiresome.”
evidence: “not at all tiresome—for me.”

days.title: A Holiday Task
days.challenge: Follow a comic mystery while checking how social discomfort affects a character’s decisions and how the ending changes the apparent explanation.
days.focus: The difference between solving an identity puzzle and taking responsibility for its consequences.
days.context: Jerton is uncomfortable drawing attention to himself in a crowded hotel. A nearby woman claims she cannot remember who she is and recruits his help.
days.contentNote: The narrator uses an antisemitic ethnic description of a bystander; it is retained as historical prejudice, not a valid character judgment. The story also treats memory loss comically and includes theft-like borrowing and gambling.

excerpt.locator: A HOLIDAY TASK; complete individual story; opening “Kenelm Jerton entered the dining-hall of the Golden Galleon Hotel in the full crush of the luncheon hour.”; closing “Jerton heard no more. He fled down to the Turkish bath, and stayed there for hours.”.

questions.prompt: How does Jerton’s fear of being watched help explain his willingness to become involved?
facilitatorNotes: He seeks ordinary conversation to look unconcerned, then hesitates to challenge or interrupt strangers. His social anxiety helps carry him into increasingly awkward obligations; avoid treating this as a general account of people with anxiety.
evidence: with the uncomfortable and wholly groundless idea that nearly every one in the room was staring at him.

questions.prompt: What is faulty about the woman’s expensive tests for who she is not?
facilitatorNotes: They spend money and rely on current choices as if those prove identity. Her knowledge of many people’s habits is striking beside her claimed ignorance of her own name; the later confirmation of recurring memory loss complicates a simple fraud interpretation.
evidence: I’m trying to find out by various little tests who I am _not_

questions.prompt: Why does learning that she is a golf champion fail to give Jerton a satisfying resolution?
facilitatorNotes: The word Lady is explained and her condition is partly corroborated, but he remains beside tampered luggage with its angry owner approaching. Solving the label does not undo the practical consequences of helping.
evidence: she’s the Lady Champion at golf in my part of the world.

days.title: The Scholars
days.challenge: Identify satire by contrasting respectable appearances with the passionate circumstances of making the texts they study.
days.focus: The distance between living poetic experience and professional literary commentary.
days.context: The speaker caricatures scholars editing poems written in youthful passion. Catullus is named as one of the poets they study; the final question imagines the poet walking into their world.

excerpt.locator: THE SCHOLARS; complete individual poem; opening “Bald heads forgetful of their sins, Old, learned, respectable bald heads Edit and annotate the lines That young”; closing “friend; If they have sinned nobody knows. Lord, what would they say Should their Catullus walk that way?”.

questions.prompt: Why repeat “bald heads” instead of giving the scholars individual names or thoughts?
facilitatorNotes: The bodily shorthand makes them a comic collective and emphasizes age against the young writers. It is the speaker’s caricature, not a reliable rule about older people or scholarship.
evidence: Old, learned, respectable bald heads

questions.prompt: How do coughing in ink and wearing out carpets make scholarly work seem different from the poets tossing in bed?
facilitatorNotes: The scholars’ actions appear routine and physically fussy, while the young writers’ restless bodies signal emotional urgency. Readers can also question whether the satire undervalues the real care of editing.
evidence: They'll cough in the ink to the world's end;

questions.prompt: What does the imagined arrival of Catullus test about the scholars’ relationship with poetry?
facilitatorNotes: It asks whether they could recognize or tolerate the living person behind their respectable object of study. The question remains unanswered, allowing amusement or a sharper charge of hypocrisy.
evidence: Should their Catullus walk that way?

days.title: Subway Wind
days.challenge: Follow a long chain of images from the underground city to islands and identify where physical description becomes imaginative escape.
days.focus: Captivity and freedom expressed through wind, crowded bodies, and remembered open spaces.
days.context: The poem begins in packed subway cars and lets the wind lead the imagination elsewhere. Trace the repeated connections between successive places.

excerpt.locator: SUBWAY WIND; complete individual poem; opening “Far down, down through the city’s great, gaunt gut The gray train rushing bears the weary wind; In”; closing “Where fields lie idle in the dew drenched night, And the Trades float above them fresh and free.”.

questions.prompt: What does calling the city’s interior a “great, gaunt gut” make the subway journey feel like?
facilitatorNotes: The alliteration and bodily image make the passage constricted and consuming. Readers may hear a huge organism carrying people inside it; explain the effect rather than assuming a literal creature.
evidence: the city’s great, gaunt gut

questions.prompt: Why is the children’s swallowed laughter an important interruption of the opening machinery?
facilitatorNotes: It introduces vulnerable human voices that cannot compete with the roar. Their desire for air parallels the captive wind’s desire for open space.
evidence: Their laugh is swallowed in the deafening roar

questions.prompt: How does the final “fresh and free” answer the wind we met in the packed cars?
facilitatorNotes: The open trade winds reverse weary, captive, heavy air into release. This may be the speaker’s imagined alternative rather than a journey actually completed by the subway wind.
evidence: And the Trades float above them fresh and free.

days.title: Blue-Star Woman: a riddle of identity (part 1 of 3)
days.challenge: Explain a conflict between two kinds of evidence: written records and cultural memory.
days.focus: Irony in a story about proving who one is to a government office.
days.context: In this 1921 story set on a Sioux reservation, the government is dividing tribal land into individual allotments. To receive a share, a person must prove tribal membership to officials.
days.contentNote: The story depicts poverty and hunger, and it uses period terms such as “civilized peoples” ironically.

excerpt.locator: American Indian Stories, “The Widespread Enigma Concerning Blue-Star Woman,” opening through Blue-Star Woman’s words about walking in the dark; from “It was summer on the western plains. Fields of golden sunflowers facing eas…” through “…It's like walking in the dark. In this darkness, I am growing fearful of everything."”

questions.prompt: Why is “Who am I?” a riddle for Blue-Star Woman when she knows her own name?
facilitatorNotes: The law requires documentary proof of membership and parentage; her own answer, “I am a being,” does not count. Identity defined by official records conflicts with identity known to oneself and one’s community.
evidence: In the eyes of the white man's law, it was required of her to give proof of her membership in the Sioux tribe.

questions.prompt: Which Dakota teachings and circumstances make the official’s question about her parents hard to answer?
facilitatorNotes: She was orphaned young; the names of the dead should not be spoken carelessly; a “roving people” kept no written records; and oral reports conflict. The barrier is cultural as well as practical.
evidence: the names of the dead should not be idly spoken

questions.prompt: How does the narrator use irony when describing Blue-Star Woman’s “progress” in the white man’s civilization?
facilitatorNotes: Listing a coffee habit and a log hut as achievements gently mocks the measures of “civilization.” The remark that generosity is “said to be a fault” of Indian people is also ironic. Readers may hear humor, bitterness, or both.
evidence: The coffee habit was one of the signs of her progress in the white man's civilization

days.title: Blue-Star Woman: the nephews’ bargain (part 2 of 3)
days.challenge: Distinguish what characters say about themselves from what the narrator and their actions reveal.
days.focus: A swindle made possible by hunger and bureaucracy.
days.context: Blue-Star Woman, an elderly Sioux woman, has spent years failing to prove to officials that she is entitled to a share of tribal land. She is eating a rare breakfast of fried bread and coffee.
days.contentNote: The story depicts fraud against a poor elder and refers to blood shed in taking Native land.

excerpt.locator: American Indian Stories, “The Widespread Enigma Concerning Blue-Star Woman,” arrival of the two men through Blue-Star Woman’s return into her hut; from “Oblivious to the world, she had not heard the footfall of two Indian men wh…” through “…. Gathering upon her arm the mats and cooking utensils, she hobbled into her log hut.”

questions.prompt: How do the two men present themselves, and what details reveal their real purpose?
facilitatorNotes: They claim kinship, education, and concern, but they eat all her bread and talk of profit. The narrator calls their work a “grafting business” and compares them to wolves.
evidence: Masking their real errand with long-drawn faces, they feigned a concern for her welfare only.

questions.prompt: What argument persuades Blue-Star Woman to promise half her land?
facilitatorNotes: The men exploit hunger: half a crust is better than none. Their back-fire analogy admits they work with “crooks.” Readers may judge her choice foolish or rational under desperate conditions; she herself feels guilt afterward.
evidence: Wouldn't you rather have a half of a crust of bread than none at all?

questions.prompt: The narrator calls the nephews the “by-product” of a bureaucracy. Whom does this claim blame besides the two men?
facilitatorNotes: A system that treats Native people as “wards” and demands proofs creates a market for tricksters. Responsibility is shared, though readers may still hold the individuals accountable. Compare the White-Horse-Riders, who helped the poor without pay.
evidence: They and their occupation were the by-product of an unwieldly bureaucracy over the nation's wards.

days.title: Blue-Star Woman: Chief High Flier’s letter (part 3 of 3)
days.challenge: Evaluate how a story’s ending answers or undercuts the hope offered in a vision.
days.focus: Consent, voice, and power in a dispute over land.
days.context: Two men have promised to win Blue-Star Woman a land allotment in exchange for half of it. The scene moves to the reservation where that land will be taken.
days.contentNote: An elderly chief is falsely accused, arrested, and jailed; the story mentions the killing of Sitting Bull by Indian police and describes hunger.

excerpt.locator: American Indian Stories, “The Widespread Enigma Concerning Blue-Star Woman,” from the superintendent’s meeting to the end of the story; from “Under the brooding wilderness silence, on the Sioux Indian Reservation, the…” through “…delible thumb mark, his signature it was, upon the deed, and drove home with his son.”

questions.prompt: Chief High Flier’s letter is written in a child’s hand. What arguments does it make about the land?
facilitatorNotes: The tribe was not asked; its own children lack land and food; treaties were supposed to protect them. The closing suggestion that Washington share its own land is pointed irony. Its plain English is persuasive rather than weak.
evidence: We were not asked to give land, but our land is taken from us to give to another Indian.

questions.prompt: Why does the chief burn the letter, and how is his act used against him?
facilitatorNotes: He fears it will only reach bureaucrats, so he sends it “on the wings of fire.” Officials claim he tried to burn the agency. The story calls him “the voiceless man of America”; readers can discuss how an act of prayer becomes a charge.
evidence: He sent his message on the wings of fire and he believed she would get it.

questions.prompt: How does the ending repeat the nephews’ bargain, and what does that repetition suggest?
facilitatorNotes: The same men profit again, this time from the chief’s own land. The Statue of Liberty vision offers hope, but the thumbprint on a deed is the final act. Readers may argue that the story ends in hope, bitterness, or both.
evidence: I pledged to pay them half of your land if they got you out of jail.

days.title: The Stalled Ox
days.challenge: Track shifts in power through dialogue and compare an artist’s repeated formulas with the disruptive scene that changes his career.
days.focus: Unexpected artistic opportunity emerging from conflict between practical demands and observation.
days.context: A painter known for peaceful dairy-cow scenes is asked to remove an unfamiliar ox from a neighbor’s garden. The request tests what his expertise actually includes.
