days.contentNote: The narration uses a stereotyped comparison involving Kurdish and Japanese people. It is retained for historical fidelity and should be questioned, not treated as a reliable description of either group.

excerpt.locator: THE STALLED OX; complete individual story; opening “Theophil Eshley was an artist by profession, a cattle painter by force of environment. It is not to”; closing “of _Madame Adnré Blusset_, but nothing in the nature of a real reconciliation has taken place between them.”.

questions.prompt: What do the near-identical titles of Eshley’s successful paintings suggest about the art world’s encouragement?
facilitatorNotes: It rewards a repeatable safe subject and discourages departures, as the rejected alternatives show. The comic variations in title expose how little the pictures change beneath new labels.
evidence: “A Mid-day Sanctuary,” a study of a walnut tree, with two dun cows under it.

questions.prompt: Why is Adela’s sarcastic suggestion to sketch the ox a turning point?
facilitatorNotes: Eshley takes it literally and returns to the skill he possesses instead of continuing the failed cattle drive. The action also reverses power: the person commanded to solve a nuisance now treats it as valuable subject matter.
evidence: “It was your suggestion,” said Eshley,

questions.prompt: Does the successful painting repair the neighborly relationship? Explain what the last gifts do and do not accomplish.
facilitatorNotes: Professional success does not compensate Adela’s lost control and damaged room. The replacement book and plants acknowledge material losses, but the final line explicitly withholds real reconciliation.
evidence: nothing in the nature of a real reconciliation has taken place between them.

days.title: The Dawn
days.challenge: Follow one long, winding sentence and its allusions to a single claim.
days.focus: A paradoxical wish for ignorance from a learned speaker.
days.context: The speaker wishes to be as ignorant as the dawn, which has looked down on all of human history without caring. He alludes to a legendary Irish queen who marked out a town’s boundary with a brooch pin and to astronomers of ancient Babylon.

excerpt.locator: THE DAWN; complete individual poem; opening “I would be ignorant as the dawn That has looked down On that old”; closing “would be—for no knowledge is worth a straw— Ignorant and wanton as the dawn.”.

questions.prompt: Why would anyone wish to be “ignorant”? What has the dawn seen?
facilitatorNotes: The dawn has watched great human efforts to measure and calculate without needing that knowledge. Its indifference looks like freedom.
evidence: I would be ignorant as the dawn

questions.prompt: How does the poem picture the Babylonian astronomers?
facilitatorNotes: “Withered,” “pedantic” men doing sums contrast with “careless planets.” Human calculation looks small beside free motion.
evidence: And took their tablets and did sums;

questions.prompt: Is the claim that knowledge is worth nothing meant literally?
facilitatorNotes: It is an exaggerated mood rather than a doctrine; “wanton” means free and playful. Readers may note the irony of a learned poet making the claim.
evidence: for no knowledge is worth a straw

days.title: The Story-Teller
days.challenge: Compare two embedded stories through their listeners’ questions, and distinguish narrative satisfaction from approval of a character’s fate.
days.focus: The conflict between predictable moral instruction and stories that respond inventively to an audience.
days.context: Aunt and children share a railway carriage with a stranger. Each adult tells a story, and the children’s reactions become part of the evidence about how stories work.
days.contentNote: The stranger’s invented fairy tale ends with a wolf devouring a child; the account is frightening but not anatomically graphic. Discussion can question the entertainment value of cruelty rather than endorse it.

excerpt.locator: THE STORY-TELLER; complete individual story; opening “It was a hot afternoon, and the railway carriage was correspondingly sultry, and the next stop was at”; closing “next six months or so those children will assail her in public with demands for an improper story!””.

questions.prompt: What weakness does the question about rescuing a girl who was not good expose in the aunt’s first story?
facilitatorNotes: It challenges the supposed causal link between virtue and rescue: people might help someone in danger regardless. The child tests the story’s reasoning, not just its entertainment, showing why a ready-made moral can fail.
evidence: “Wouldn’t they have saved her if she hadn’t been good?”

questions.prompt: How do the medals become more than a surprising decoration in the bachelor’s tale?
facilitatorNotes: Their repeated clinking is planted before it betrays the hiding place. The object associated with reward becomes a cause of danger, making the reversal structurally prepared rather than an unrelated shock.
evidence: the medal for obedience clinked against the medals for good conduct and punctuality.

questions.prompt: Are the bachelor’s success and the aunt’s objection incompatible?
facilitatorNotes: He demonstrably holds attention, while her concern about what the story teaches can still be discussed. Students may judge the tale witty, cruel, liberating, or mixed; they should separate keeping children quiet from resolving educational or ethical questions.
evidence: “I kept them quiet for ten minutes, which was more than you were able to do.”

days.title: Fur
days.challenge: Track a cooperative plan that secretly changes direction, using differences between what readers and Suzanne know.
days.focus: Gift-giving, self-interest, and the fragile reciprocity of a friendship.
days.context: Two friends plan how to guide a wealthy relative toward buying a desired birthday present. Watch for the moment when their interests stop being aligned.
days.contentNote: The story treats animal-fur clothing as a luxury status object and includes a passing bereavement anecdote.

excerpt.locator: FUR; complete individual story; opening ““You look worried, dear,” said Eleanor.”; closing “friendships of the two young women; as far as Eleanor is concerned the cloud has a silver-fox lining.”.

questions.prompt: How does Suzanne recast wanting a more expensive present as a form of good sense rather than greed?
facilitatorNotes: She calls a small demand wasteful because the donor can afford more. The logic centers on extracting the opportunity’s maximum value, exposing self-justification beneath her denial of greed.
evidence: I don’t want to be greedy, of course, but I don’t like being wasteful.

questions.prompt: Which refused favor changes Eleanor’s role in the plan, and why does that matter to the story’s view of friendship?
facilitatorNotes: Suzanne will not join the bridge game to free Eleanor for a conversation, despite accepting Eleanor’s help. The narrator identifies the unequal sacrifice; Eleanor’s retaliation is intelligible without automatically being justified.
evidence: the sacrifices of friendship were beautiful in her eyes as long as she was not asked to make them.

questions.prompt: How does the final silver-fox lining turn a familiar optimistic phrase into a pointed ending?
facilitatorNotes: The cloud is the damaged friendship, but the valuable lining belongs to Eleanor. The phrase converts emotional loss into material profit and lets readers infer her successful manipulation of the gift.
evidence: the cloud has a silver-fox lining.

days.title: The Jester
days.challenge: Interpret paradox and reversal in a short dramatic monologue.
days.focus: Performance, masks, and the gap between an audience’s response and a performer’s experience.
days.context: The speaker presents himself as a jester holding the two theatrical masks of tragedy and comedy. In Hughes’s time, Black performers were often expected to play comic stereotypes for white audiences.

excerpt.locator: THE JESTER; complete individual poem; opening “In one hand I hold tragedy And in the other Comedy,— Masks for the”; closing “booted fool of silly men. Once I was wise. Shall I be wise again?”.

questions.prompt: Why might the speaker call tragedy and comedy “Masks for the soul” rather than his true feelings?
facilitatorNotes: Masks conceal and perform; the audience laughs or weeps as the mask directs. The speaker’s inner feeling may differ from either mask.
evidence: Masks for the soul.

questions.prompt: How do the reversed lines about tears and laughter challenge the audience?
facilitatorNotes: The chiasmus makes what entertains the audience the source of the speaker’s pain. “Cry at my grinning mouth” demands that listeners see behind the grin.
evidence:
Tears are my laughter.
Laughter is my pain.

questions.prompt: What does the final question add after “Once I was wise”?
facilitatorNotes: It suggests a lost dignity replaced by an imposed role as the “fool of silly men.” The poem ends with a possibility, not an answer; readers may hear hope of renewal or bitterness.
evidence:
Once I was wise.
Shall I be wise again?

days.title: Wisdom Cometh with the Years
days.challenge: Question a familiar proverb by following the poem’s apparent self-criticism into its final qualification.
days.focus: Youthful generosity and feeling weighed against the possible costs of maturity.
days.context: The speaker repeatedly calls himself young, then asks not to lose the capacity for tears and dreams. The title’s promise of wisdom is not accepted without a cost.

excerpt.locator: Wisdom Cometh With the Years; complete individual poem; opening “NOW I am young and credulous, My heart is quick to bleed At courage in the tremulous Slow”; closing “tears, And dream that false is true; Though wisdom cometh with the years, The barren days come, too.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the first stanza give courage to a slowly sprouting seed?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker sees fragile growth as brave and responds emotionally to it. This makes sensitivity an attentive strength, even while he calls himself credulous.
evidence:
At courage in the tremulous
Slow sprouting of a seed.

questions.prompt: Does the willingness to give away every stitch make the speaker admirable, foolish, or both?
facilitatorNotes: The lines allow admiration for generosity and concern about its impracticality. The poem’s own language mixes sensitivity with self-questioning, so students should examine the tension rather than assign a flat label.
evidence:
I own no stitch I would not give
To him that asked me to.

questions.prompt: How does the final line change what we expect from “wisdom cometh with the years”?
facilitatorNotes: Wisdom may bring discernment but also emotional barrenness. The speaker asks to retain lavish feeling, complicating a simple progress story from foolish youth to superior age.
evidence: The barren days come, too.

days.title: The Byzantine Omelette
days.challenge: Keep track of two different unions and distinguish a character’s declared principles from her choices when those principles become inconvenient.
days.focus: Satire of privileged reform, dependency, and a solution that reverses the original problem.
days.context: Sophie publicly supports social reform while enjoying wealth and the prestige of a noble guest. A dispute among household workers interrupts the dinner she has planned.
days.contentNote: The story caricatures political and class positions, and includes a comic threat of injury in an overheated bath. It is a fictional satire, not a factual account of unions or political beliefs.

excerpt.locator: THE BYZANTINE OMELETTE; complete individual story; opening “Sophie Chattel-Monkheim was a Socialist by conviction and a Chattel-Monkheim by marriage. The particular member of that wealthy”; closing “exciting, such as a drawing-room meeting or a Fabian conference; it is doubtful, indeed, whether she wants to.”.

questions.prompt: How does Sophie’s enthusiasm for a duke test her stated opposition to social distinctions before the strike begins?
facilitatorNotes: She dislikes rank in principle but values its prestige in her own house. The narrator explicitly pairs those positions, so the contradiction is established before inconvenience can serve as an excuse.
evidence: As a good Socialist, Sophie disapproved of social distinctions,

questions.prompt: Why does Richardson’s personal political opinion fail to predict whether she will keep working?
facilitatorNotes: Her union obligation and need to earn a living govern her action despite her stated dislike of the strike. The difference complicates a simple division into people whose beliefs automatically match their conduct.
evidence: I’ve my living to make, same as other people, and I’ve got to belong to the union.

questions.prompt: How does dismissing Gaspare solve one problem while creating its mirror image?
facilitatorNotes: The household staff want a former strikebreaker dismissed; the kitchen union then defends its member against summary dismissal. The ending exposes clashing loyalties and Sophie’s instrumental approach, not a complete general argument that labor organization is impossible.
evidence: They demand his instant reinstatement and an apology to the union.

days.title: The Boar-Pig
days.challenge: Track what the child secretly controls and how formal politeness and language lessons become bargaining tools.
days.focus: The use of respectable excuses to disguise both social ambition and coercion.
days.context: Two uninvited women try to enter a garden party by a back route. Matilda sees their plan. French phrases include “Comprends pas” (do not understand), “Suis anglaise” (I am English), and “nous parlons français” (we speak French).
days.contentNote: Matilda recounts forcibly feeding another child and later uses a pig to frighten visitors. These comic actions are coercive and should not be treated as acceptable behavior.

excerpt.locator: THE BOAR-PIG; complete individual story; opening ““There is a back way on to the lawn,” said Mrs. Philidore Stossen to her daughter, “through a”; closing “examine the books of the fund you will find the acknowledgment: “Collected by Miss Matilda Cuvering, 2s. 6d.””.

questions.prompt: Why is the mother prepared to take a troublesome route to a party that has not invited her?
facilitatorNotes: She fears the social explanation for absence more than the awkwardness or dishonesty of entering uninvited. The distinction between a garden party and the season’s important party reveals the value she places on rank.
evidence: it would be far more troublesome to invent explanations as to why we weren’t there

questions.prompt: How do Matilda’s French-only rule and her conscience change when money is mentioned?
facilitatorNotes: She initially presents them as obligations beyond her control, then makes a precise financial exception. The pattern exposes a bargaining strategy; the women’s own wish to evade ordinary entry rules complicates their indignation.
evidence: I could not do violence to my conscience for anything less than ten shillings

questions.prompt: Why is the charity-book entry a sharper ending than simply confirming or denying that Matilda stole all the money?
facilitatorNotes: It proves that some money reached the fund while leaving a large difference between the ten shillings collected and the smaller recorded donation. The narrator corrects the mother’s absolute accusation in a way that also reveals partial dishonesty.
evidence: “Collected by Miss Matilda Cuvering, 2s. 6d.”

days.title: An Irish Airman Foresees His Death
days.challenge: Separate the dramatic speaker’s stated motives from expected public explanations of wartime action.
days.focus: A carefully balanced voice that questions duty, allegiance, pleasure, and the value of a life.
days.context: The poem is a dramatic speech by an airman who expects to die. Analyze the speaker’s reasoning without assuming that it is advice to the reader.
days.contentNote: The speaker anticipates death in war and describes past and future life as a waste; discussion should distinguish this dramatic stance from an instruction to devalue life.

excerpt.locator: AN IRISH AIRMAN FORESEES HIS DEATH; complete individual poem; opening “I know that I shall meet my fate Somewhere among the clouds above; Those that I fight I”; closing “seemed waste of breath, A waste of breath the years behind In balance with this life, this death.”.

questions.prompt: What do the paired statements about not hating enemies and not loving those guarded remove from a conventional explanation of fighting?
facilitatorNotes: They reject simple hatred and patriotic affection as sufficient motives for this speaker. The balanced clauses do not mean he feels nothing: later lines identify local attachment and delight.
evidence:
Those that I fight I do not hate
Those that I guard I do not love;

questions.prompt: Why name Kiltartan’s poor when considering what the war’s outcome might change?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker measures public events by a specific community’s welfare rather than abstract national gain. His assertion that no result helps them is his perspective, not a fact the poem independently demonstrates.
evidence: My countrymen Kiltartan's poor,

questions.prompt: How does the final balancing language relate to the earlier “lonely impulse of delight”?
facilitatorNotes: The impulse sounds immediate, while balance suggests deliberate retrospective judgment. Students can debate whether the calm structure justifies the choice or reveals its narrowness; the poem leaves that evaluation to the reader.
evidence: In balance with this life, this death.

days.title: On Being Asked for a War Poem
days.challenge: Examine a brief refusal that is itself a poem, attending to modesty, irony, and the audience the speaker chooses.
days.focus: The limits a poet places on public authority while retaining a smaller human purpose.
days.context: The title supplies the request being answered. Read the six lines once as a sincere refusal and once as a pointed public response.
days.contentNote: The title and argument concern war, but the poem contains no battle depiction.

excerpt.locator: ON BEING ASKED FOR A WAR POEM; complete individual poem; opening “I think it better that in times like these A poet keep his mouth shut, for in truth”; closing “please A young girl in the indolence of her youth, Or an old man upon a winter's night.”.

questions.prompt: What kind of authority does the speaker deny to poets when he says they cannot set a statesman right?
facilitatorNotes: He denies special political expertise simply from being a poet. Readers may hear sincere humility or an ironic distancing from demanded public speech; the text does not require deciding that poets can never discuss politics.
evidence: We have no gift to set a statesman right;

questions.prompt: What work remains for poetry in the examples of a young girl and an old man?
facilitatorNotes: It may offer pleasure, company, or reflection across ages and seasons. These modest examples are not nothing, even though they are contrasted with advising statesmen.
evidence: Or an old man upon a winter's night.

questions.prompt: How does writing a poem about keeping quiet complicate the refusal?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker uses the requested form to explain a boundary, so silence becomes a public position. A good response can find a paradox without declaring the poem logically worthless or hypocritical.
evidence: A poet keep his mouth shut, for in truth

days.title: Dawn in New York
days.challenge: Contrast an exalted opening with what the speaker actually observes.
days.focus: Natural light against electric light in a city sonnet.
days.context: A sonnet set in Manhattan at daybreak, when a few streetcars, elevated trains, and subway cars carry people home from the night.
days.contentNote: The poem mentions people returning from nights of drinking.

excerpt.locator: DAWN IN NEW YORK; complete individual poem; opening “The Dawn! The Dawn! The crimson-tinted, comes Out of the low still skies, over”; closing “wane. The Dawn comes to New York. And I go darkly-rebel to my work.”.

questions.prompt: How does the excited greeting of the dawn differ from what the speaker sees in the cars?
facilitatorNotes: Crimson dawn thrills the speaker, but the passengers are worn-out revelers. The contrast sets nature’s renewal against the city’s exhausted night.
evidence: Their eyes wine-weakened and their clothes awry,

questions.prompt: Why call the passengers grotesques “beneath the strong electric lights”?
facilitatorNotes: Artificial light distorts and exposes them. Readers can debate whether the speaker judges nightlife or pities those caught in it.
evidence: Grotesques beneath the strong electric lights.

questions.prompt: What does the last line add?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker joins the workday resentfully; “darkly” can suggest mood and identity. Readers may connect it to “The Tired Worker” if they have read it.
evidence: And I go darkly-rebel to my work.

days.title: The Tired Worker
days.challenge: Follow a sonnet’s turn from evening calm to morning dread.
days.focus: Who owns a worker’s time, and how the city shapes his feelings.
days.context: A sonnet spoken by a laborer at the end of a working day in the city.

excerpt.locator: THE TIRED WORKER; complete individual poem; opening “O whisper, O my soul! The afternoon Is waning into evening, whisper soft! Peace,”; closing “my brain, my life! Have pity! No! Once again the harsh, the ugly city.”.

questions.prompt: Whom does the speaker address in the first lines, and why?
facilitatorNotes: He speaks to his own soul, heart, and body, as if they were separate listeners. Self-address shows him trying to calm a divided, rebellious self.
evidence: O whisper, O my soul!

questions.prompt: What does the line about day and night suggest about work?
facilitatorNotes: The day belongs to employers; only the night is his own. The poem treats time as something owned.
evidence: The wretched day was theirs, the night is mine;

questions.prompt: How does the dawn image turn against the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: Dawn usually signals hope, but here it means returning to work. The sonnet’s final couplet ends in the “harsh” city rather than rest.
evidence: O dawn! O dreaded dawn! O let me rest

days.title: The Quince Tree
days.challenge: Follow a fabricated secret and notice the exact point at which a character’s public rule changes under personal pressure.
days.focus: Storytelling used to expose conditional respectability and secure practical aid.
days.context: Vera wants an older tenant to keep her cottage and its quince tree. Her aunt thinks the tenant should move; watch how Vera redirects the argument.

excerpt.locator: THE QUINCE TREE; complete individual story; opening ““I’ve just been to see old Betsy Mullen,” announced Vera to her aunt, Mrs. Bebberly Cumble; “she seems”; closing “Betsy’s arrears of rent were to come from; and she would have hated leaving that jolly quince tree.””.

questions.prompt: What does Vera value in the cottage that the aunt’s calculation of rent and furniture leaves out?
facilitatorNotes: The garden and unique quince tree carry attachment and pleasure beyond monetary efficiency. The joke about not making jam also resists reducing the tree to productive use; readers can still recognize the aunt’s concern about unpaid rent.
evidence: to have a quince tree and not to make quince jam shows such strength of character.

questions.prompt: At what point does “a theft is a theft” cease to guide the aunt’s proposed action?
facilitatorNotes: Once Vera names the admired future son-in-law, the aunt postpones speaking until after the wedding. The contrast exposes a principle applied differently when her own family prospects are involved.
evidence: “I shall speak to Cuthbert about it—after the wedding,”

questions.prompt: How does the last explanation redefine the word mystery?
facilitatorNotes: It shifts from supposedly stolen jewels to the practical question of paying rent. Vera’s fiction is morally questionable but materially effective; students can debate the means without denying the concrete help it produces.
evidence: the mystery was where old Betsy’s arrears of rent were to come from;

days.title: “Down Pens”
days.challenge: Follow a debate built from interruptions and test whether a proposed reform escapes the behavior it criticizes.
days.focus: Ritual gratitude, honest feeling, and the comic labor of social correspondence.
days.context: After many holiday thank-you letters, a couple tries to compose one more. A “counterfoil” is the detachable part of a form kept or returned as a record.

excerpt.locator: “DOWN PENS”; complete individual story; opening ““Have you written to thank the Froplinsons for what they sent us?” asked Egbert.”; closing ““Meanwhile,” said Janetta, “what am I to say to the Froplinsons?””.

questions.prompt: How does confusing William the Conqueror with Wordsworth establish the problem before the couple discusses sincerity?
facilitatorNotes: The gift has made so little impression that its recipient barely identifies it. The mistake turns an obligation to express delight into a performance unsupported by attention or genuine enjoyment.
evidence: “Well, it was William Wordsworth, then,”

questions.prompt: Why does Janetta object to calling Wordsworth their favorite poet even though polite exaggeration seems normal in their letters?
facilitatorNotes: The lie could generate more unwanted Wordsworth gifts and repeat the writing problem. Her objection is practical rather than a sudden commitment to complete truth, which keeps the satire focused on the system’s incentives.
evidence: a Wordsworth booklet next Christmas, and another calendar the Christmas after

questions.prompt: What is comic about Egbert’s plan to stop unnecessary writing, and how does the final question test its usefulness?
facilitatorNotes: He prepares a stack of letters to newspaper editors to campaign against excess correspondence, while the immediate letter remains unwritten. The idea can have merit and still fail to solve the present task.
evidence: “Meanwhile,” said Janetta, “what am I to say to the Froplinsons?”

days.title: A Song of Praise
days.challenge: Follow a poem that answers an unseen rival and reverses a standard of beauty.
days.focus: Praise as argument against prevailing ideals of beauty.
days.context: The speaker answers a listener who praises a fair-haired love by praising his own dark-skinned beloved.
days.contentNote: The poem reverses period beauty standards, and one stanza calls an African dance “barbaric,” a word readers can examine.

excerpt.locator: A Song of Praise; complete individual poem; opening “YOU have not heard my love’s dark throat, Slow-fluting like a reed, Release the”; closing “her and despair; Then seal your lips until the sun Discovers one as fair.”.

questions.prompt: How does the second stanza describe the beloved’s walk, and what does “arrogance” suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Her walk recalls a dance carrying “the soul of Africa”; arrogance becomes pride and confidence. Students may ask whether “barbaric” is reclaimed here or repeats a stereotype.
evidence: Is winged with arrogance.

questions.prompt: How does the third stanza balance the second?
facilitatorNotes: The bold dance is matched by extreme lightness: she does not even bend grass. Strength and grace coexist.
evidence: She does not dent the smoothest moss

questions.prompt: Whom does the final stanza address, and what reversal does it make?
facilitatorNotes: The rival who prized pale beauty is now “to-be-pitied.” Readers may ask whether praising one beauty requires belittling another.
evidence: You-proud-and-to-be-pitied one,

days.title: For Paul Laurence Dunbar
days.challenge: Unpack a compressed four-line epitaph phrase by phrase.
days.focus: Humor as a mask for pain, honored in a tribute from one poet to another.
days.context: One of a series of short epitaphs in Color. Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906) was a Black poet popular for comic dialect verse who also wrote of hidden sorrow, most famously in “We Wear the Mask.”

excerpt.locator: For Paul Laurence Dunbar; complete individual poem; opening “BORN of the sorrowful of heart, Mirth was a crown upon his head; Pride”; closing “Pride kept his twisted lips apart In jest, to hide a heart that bled.”.

questions.prompt: What paradox appears in the first two lines?
facilitatorNotes: Dunbar is born of sorrow yet crowned with mirth. The crown makes humor an honor and a burden.
evidence: Mirth was a crown upon his head;

questions.prompt: What does “Pride kept his twisted lips apart” suggest about why he joked?
facilitatorNotes: Humor shields wounded pride; “twisted” suggests a forced smile or grimace. Readers might connect it to audiences who wanted only comic verse from him.
evidence: Pride kept his twisted lips apart

questions.prompt: Why might Cullen choose an epitaph, a few lines for a tomb, to honor another poet?
facilitatorNotes: The form’s compression mirrors the hidden depth it describes, and it fixes Dunbar’s private pain as his memorial. Students may judge whether a tribute that reveals pain honors or exposes him.
evidence: to hide a heart that bled.

days.title: Lenox Avenue: Midnight
days.challenge: Read for musical layers and ambiguous tone rather than trying to turn every image into a literal event.
days.focus: An urban soundscape that holds affection, pain, rhythm, and an unsettling cosmic audience.
days.context: The poem places a speaking voice on Lenox Avenue at midnight. Say the short lines aloud and listen for changes in pace.

excerpt.locator: LENOX AVENUE: MIDNIGHT; complete individual poem; opening “The rhythm of life Is a jazz rhythm, Honey. The gods are laughing at us.”; closing “Lenox Avenue, Honey. Midnight, And the gods are laughing at us.”.

questions.prompt: How do street cars and rain make the claim that life has a jazz rhythm more concrete?
facilitatorNotes: Their rumble and swish provide different textures of sound beneath the emotional voice. The poem lets a city’s ordinary noises act like musical accompaniment rather than treating music as separate from life.
evidence:
To the rumble of street cars,
To the swish of rain.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of placing “Honey” beside both the opening claim and the closing location?
facilitatorNotes: The intimate address suggests a companion and softens or complicates the pain around it. Readers may hear tenderness, weary familiarity, or a singer addressing an audience, but should not invent a definite speaker biography.
evidence:
Lenox Avenue,
Honey.

questions.prompt: Are the laughing gods comforting, cruel, or distant? Compare at least two readings before choosing.
facilitatorNotes: Their laughter can make suffering seem mocked, or make life a performance viewed from beyond it. The poem supplies no explicit explanation; strong responses acknowledge uncertainty and connect the laughter to weary pain and the repeated frame.
evidence: And the gods are laughing at us.

days.title: The Story of My Life: the Frost King accusation (chapter xiv)
days.challenge: Separate similarity of texts, memory of exposure and evidence of deliberate deception.
days.focus: How an accusation changes a child’s relationship with writing and trusted adults.
days.context: Keller recalls writing a story at eleven that closely resembled Margaret Canby’s earlier tale. This first portion follows the accusation and the search for how she encountered the original.
days.contentNote: Includes a distressed child wishing she might die during an intimidating inquiry. The passage distinguishes remembered distress from evidence about plagiarism and intent. Editorial footnote markers are omitted.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XIV, composition, accusation and investigation of the story’s source; from “THE winter of 1892 was darkened by one cloud in my childhood's bright sky. …” through “…back to me so naturally that I never suspected that it was the child of another mind.”

questions.prompt: Why does the ease of composing “The Frost King” mean something different to the child and to the adult narrator?
facilitatorNotes: The child takes fluent images as her own invention and feels joy. The adult now treats effortless phrasing as a warning that remembered words may have returned. Her later caution does not show that she knowingly copied at the time.
evidence: I thought then that I was "making up a story,"
they are not the offspring of my own mind

questions.prompt: What can the similarity of the two tales establish, and what further claim does the inquiry try to establish?
facilitatorNotes: Similarity supports a relationship between texts and prior exposure; the inquiry presses whether she remembers the source and deliberately deceived Anagnos. Keller accepts the textual dependence while denying conscious recollection. Keep those propositions separate.
evidence: so much alike in thought and language
force me to acknowledge that I remembered

questions.prompt: How strong is the later explanation involving Mrs. Hopkins, and where does uncertainty remain?
facilitatorNotes: Hopkins remembers reading from the collection, though neither reader remembers this specific tale and the copy is gone. It is a plausible reconstruction supported by textual similarity; Keller states greater confidence in exposure than the surviving recollections alone can prove.
evidence: although she could not remember reading "The Frost Fairies" any more than I
the language was ineffaceably stamped upon my brain

days.title: The Story of My Life: imitation, memory and authorship (chapter xiv)
days.challenge: Weigh a writer’s general argument about learning against evidence and qualifications in her personal account.
days.focus: The difference between learning through imitation and claiming someone else’s work.
days.context: After the discovery that her childhood story repeated Canby’s tale, Keller reflects on other borrowed phrases, the fear of writing and conflicting recollections of the inquiry.
days.contentNote: Continues the account of a painful childhood accusation. The discussion explains influence and memory without presenting unattributed copying as acceptable.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XIV, lasting effects and retrospective discussion; from “In my trouble I received many messages of love and sympathy. All the friend…” through “…ey appear to me, without a thought of defending myself or of laying blame on any one.”

questions.prompt: How does Canby’s encouraging prediction sit beside Keller’s description of later writing?
facilitatorNotes: Canby expects future independent achievement; Keller still fears accidental borrowing even in private letters. The contrast shows that kindness helps but does not simply undo the inquiry’s effect. Sullivan’s encouragement keeps writing possible.
evidence: I have never played with words again for the mere pleasure of the game
persistent encouragement of Miss Sullivan

questions.prompt: Compare the patchwork and puzzle images. What different difficulty does each explain?
facilitatorNotes: Patchwork describes the mixture of her own uneven ideas and polished borrowed thoughts; the puzzle describes fitting words to an intended design. One concerns the origins of material, the other expression. Neither analogy proves that all copying becomes original merely by rearrangement.
evidence: crude notions of my own, inlaid with the brighter thoughts
the words will not fit the spaces

questions.prompt: How does Keller preserve Anagnos’s conflicting account while maintaining her own interpretation?
facilitatorNotes: She reports his claim to have voted for her and the divided court, but distinguishes that reported vote from the hostility she experienced and later loss of friendship. The ending calls these facts as they appear to her, acknowledging a situated account.
evidence: he cast his vote with those who were favourable to me
all the facts as they appear to me

days.title: If We Must Die
days.challenge: Analyze an argument made through a sonnet’s contrasts and turn.
days.focus: Dignity and resistance in the face of mob violence.
days.context: McKay published this sonnet in 1919, a year when white mobs attacked Black communities in many American cities. The poem names no particular group; the speaker addresses “kinsmen” facing an attack.
days.contentNote: The poem concerns facing violent death and calls for fighting back in self-defense.

excerpt.locator: IF WE MUST DIE; complete individual poem; opening “If we must die, let it not be like hogs Hunted and penned in”; closing “we’ll face the murderous, cowardly pack, Pressed to the wall, dying, but fighting back!”.

questions.prompt: What contrast does the opening set up between two ways of dying?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker refuses a dehumanized death, hunted like animals, and calls for a noble one. The question is how to die, not whether.
evidence: If we must die, let it not be like hogs

questions.prompt: How does the poem picture the attackers, and why use animal images?
facilitatorNotes: Those who would treat the speakers as hogs become barking dogs and a “cowardly pack.” The images reverse who is truly inhuman; readers can discuss their force and their risks.
evidence: While round us bark the mad and hungry dogs,

questions.prompt: Is the final line a statement of despair or of dignity?
facilitatorNotes: Both readings have support: the speakers are outnumbered and dying, yet they fight back and expect to force honor from their enemies.
evidence: Pressed to the wall, dying, but fighting back!

days.title: The Story of My Life: confidence and the World’s Fair (chapter xv)
days.challenge: Identify how tangible experiences expand understanding while noticing the limitations of an exhibition’s viewpoint.
days.focus: Rebuilding confidence through writing and encounters with a wider world.
days.context: After the Frost King accusation, Keller begins a childhood autobiography and visits Niagara and the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair.
days.contentNote: Includes romanticized references to Columbus, Pizarro and the exhibition of non-European cultures. These descriptions reflect the fair’s unequal historical viewpoint; peoples and religions are more than exhibits. Touching moving machinery in the account is not safety advice.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XV, complete chapter prose; from “THE summer and winter following the "Frost King" incident I spent with my f…” through “…tales and toys to the appreciation of the real and the earnest in the workaday world.”

questions.prompt: How do “The Frost King was forgotten” and the next paragraphs complicate each other?
facilitatorNotes: The return home restores happiness, yet writing reawakens intense fear of borrowed ideas. The initial claim describes a period of relief, not permanent erasure; the autobiography becomes deliberate practice in recovering confidence.
evidence: The Frost King" was forgotten
An impish fear clutched my hand
I wrote timidly, fearfully, but resolutely

questions.prompt: What assumption does Keller challenge when people ask what Niagara can mean to her?
facilitatorNotes: The questions assume beauty depends on seeing or hearing in a familiar way. Her experience includes vibration and bodily response, and she compares the difficulty of defining it with anyone’s difficulty defining love or goodness.
evidence: felt the air vibrate and the earth tremble
any more than I can fathom or define love or religion or goodness

questions.prompt: Why does the hourglass receive more attention than the ship, and what does this reveal about the fair’s power and limits?
facilitatorNotes: A small touchable object prompts an imagined human experience of waiting, showing how exhibits can make history vivid. Yet the heroic Columbus story and concentrated representations of whole cultures are selective; vividness does not guarantee a complete historical account.
evidence: This small instrument impressed me most
land of the Pyramids concentrated in a model Cairo
a sort of tangible kaleidoscope

days.title: Yet Do I Marvel
days.challenge: Follow a fourteen-line argument that affirms belief while accumulating questions it cannot settle.
days.focus: The final turn from universal suffering to the specific wonder and burden of being a Black poet.
days.context: The poem describes Tantalus as tormented by unreachable fruit and Sisyphus as endlessly struggling. These named figures join the mole and mortal human body in the speaker’s questions.
days.contentNote: The poem discusses death, mythic suffering, religious doubt, and racial barriers without graphic narration.

excerpt.locator: Yet Do I Marvel; complete individual poem; opening “I DOUBT not God is good, well-meaning, kind, And did He stoop to quibble could tell why The”; closing “hand. Yet do I marvel at this curious thing: To make a poet black, and bid him sing!”.

questions.prompt: How does the confident opening “I DOUBT not” interact with the questions and examples that follow?
facilitatorNotes: The opening asserts trust, yet the examples expose unresolved suffering. A response may emphasize continuing faith, strained faith, or both; it should not ignore either the affirmation or the accumulating difficulty.
evidence: I DOUBT not God is good, well-meaning, kind,

questions.prompt: Why might the small blind mole belong in the same argument as the famous sufferers Tantalus and Sisyphus?
facilitatorNotes: It brings inexplicable limitation into ordinary nature before the grander mythic examples. The speaker ranges across kinds and scales of suffering rather than confining the issue to one story.
evidence: The little buried mole continues blind,

questions.prompt: What does the final command to sing add to the fact of being made a poet?
facilitatorNotes: The poet has both an impulse or gift and an obligation to express it under racial constraints. The line can convey wonder, irony, defiance, or a mixture; require evidence from the preceding struggle, not a single mandated emotional label.
evidence: To make a poet black, and bid him sing!

days.title: The Story of My Life: languages and school expectations (chapters xvi–xvii)
days.challenge: Explain different rates of progress without reducing them to a learner’s effort or a subject’s inherent difficulty.
days.focus: How teaching methods, access and expectations shape an educational experience.
days.context: Keller moves from self-directed reading to scheduled lessons, then attends the Wright-Humason School in New York for two years.
days.contentNote: Includes the death of a supportive friend and historical language about deaf education. Statements about her difficulties and ambitions are personal, not descriptions of every deafblind learner.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapters XVI–XVII, complete consecutive chapter prose; from “BEFORE October, 1893, I had studied various subjects by myself in a more or…” through “…e discouraged. His going away left a vacancy in our lives that has never been filled.”

questions.prompt: How does Keller’s response to Latin grammar change, and what does her joke about Tabby explain?
facilitatorNotes: At first classification seems needless when she already recognizes meaning; the elaborate cat taxonomy caricatures that feeling. Closer study later reveals linguistic beauty, so she does not simply reject analysis.
evidence: order, vertebrate; division, quadruped
as I got deeper into the subject, I became more interested

questions.prompt: Why does German progress faster than French at the New York school?
facilitatorNotes: The German teacher uses the manual alphabet and can converse frequently with Keller; the French teacher relies on speech that Keller cannot easily read from her lips. This evidence points to access and interaction, not a proven difference in the languages’ intrinsic difficulty.
evidence: we talked together in German whenever we had a chance
I could not read her lips easily

questions.prompt: How can Keller call these years happy while admitting disappointment and depression?
facilitatorNotes: Speech goals remain unmet and arithmetic frustrates her, but geography, park walks and relationships supply pleasure. The final loss of Spaulding adds grief without retrospectively cancelling those experiences. Encourage an account with several strands rather than a single success/failure label.
evidence: we did not quite reach our goal
The two years in New York were happy ones
a vacancy in our lives that has never been filled

days.title: The Story of My Life: preparing for college (chapter xviii)
days.challenge: Distinguish intellectual study, access to materials and examination procedures within one educational account.
days.focus: What participation requires beyond admission to a classroom.
days.context: Keller enters the Cambridge School in 1896 to prepare for Radcliffe. Sullivan interprets lessons, and Keller later takes the preliminary entrance examinations.
days.contentNote: The text uses “normal pupils” for seeing and hearing students, a historical contrast that does not make disabled pupils abnormal in worth or belonging.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XVIII, complete chapter prose; from “IN October, 1896, I entered the Cambridge School for Young Ladies, to be pr…” through “…greatly, and I sped on to the end of the ordeal with a light heart and a steady hand.”

questions.prompt: Why is permission for Sullivan to attend class necessary but insufficient for equal access?
facilitatorNotes: She can interpret speech, but books take time to emboss, notes cannot be made while Keller receives language, and reading needs extend beyond class hours. Identify distinct practical barriers rather than treating interpretation as a complete solution.
evidence: very difficult to have textbooks embossed in time
I could not make notes in class
read and reread notes and books I did not have in raised print

questions.prompt: How do the responses to Burke and Macaulay show Keller becoming a critical reader?
facilitatorNotes: She responds intensely to Burke’s argument but questions Macaulay’s confident style and possible sacrifice of accuracy for effect. Admiration does not always equal agreement; her affection for Johnson also admits selective blindness to faults.
evidence: his positiveness wearied me at times
his frequent sacrifices of truth to effect kept me in a questioning attitude

questions.prompt: What does Keller’s comparison of preliminary and final examinations suggest about interpreting scores?
facilitatorNotes: In the preliminaries she can hear her typed answers read back and revise; later she must rely on memory unless time remains. She also knows some preliminary subjects better. The account provides several reasons for different performance, not a simple decline in ability.
evidence: no one reads the papers to me after they are written
two reasons
subjects with some of which I was in a measure familiar

days.title: The Story of My Life: mathematics, teaching and unfamiliar notation (chapter xix)
days.challenge: Sort obstacles caused by subject knowledge, teaching arrangements, materials and test format.
days.focus: Why an examination may demand more than the skill it appears to measure.
days.context: Disagreements over Keller’s workload lead to private tutoring. Her final Radcliffe examinations introduce unfamiliar mathematical braille shortly before testing.
days.contentNote: Keller uses harsh self-descriptions such as “stupidity”; these reflect her frustration, not an objective assessment or a label to apply to learners.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XIX, complete chapter prose; from “WHEN I began my second year at the Gilman school, I was full of hope and de…” through “…aced obstacles in my way, I have the consolation of knowing that I overcame them all.”

questions.prompt: How do the arrival of embossed books and Keith’s teaching change what had looked like a lack of mathematical aptitude?
facilitatorNotes: Materials remove some access barriers, and patient explanations make relations and reasoning clearer. Keller still finds mathematics difficult; the change supports a mixed account of subject challenge and instructional conditions rather than either blaming her alone or claiming all difficulty vanishes.
evidence: The embossed books and other apparatus arrived
My tutor had plenty of time to explain
even mathematics Mr. Keith made interesting

questions.prompt: Why does knowledge of literary braille not solve the problem with the examination papers?
facilitatorNotes: Different braille systems use different mathematical symbols; her practiced English notation differs from the American version supplied. Recognizing language letters is not the same as fluently interpreting brackets, braces and radicals under time pressure.
evidence: the various signs and symbols in geometry and algebra in the three systems are very different
I could not tell the combinations of bracket, brace and radical

questions.prompt: What does “I do not blame any one” leave open for criticism?
facilitatorNotes: Keller denies intentional obstruction but identifies effects: unfamiliar notation, little preparation in writing answers and inability to review typewritten work slow her. Readers can criticize a process without claiming malice, and her eventual success does not make the obstacles necessary.
evidence: had not trained me to write examination papers
they unintentionally placed obstacles in my way

days.title: The Story of My Life: what college learning is for (chapter xx)
days.challenge: Trace a sustained argument through deliberately crowded metaphors and a self-correcting ending.
days.focus: The difference between accumulating information and making knowledge meaningful.
days.context: Now at Radcliffe, Keller weighs the college she imagined against demanding courses and examinations. This concluding section follows her description of classes and access arrangements.
days.contentNote: Uses comic, exaggerated images of distress and references to historical massacres among exam facts. The final deafness metaphor belongs to the author’s rhetoric, not a judgment about deaf people.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XX, closing reflection beginning “But college is not the universal Athens”; from “But college is not the universal Athens I thought it was. There one does no…” through “…e pulsations a heavenward striving, one must indeed be deaf to the harmonies of life.”

questions.prompt: What kind of literary teaching does Keller criticize, and what exception keeps her argument from rejecting scholarship altogether?
facilitatorNotes: She objects to endless commentary that overwhelms contact with a work, not to thorough knowledge itself. Kittredge’s interpretation restores Shakespeare as a living poet; the flower analogy contrasts dissection alone with appreciation.
evidence: I do not mean to object to a thorough knowledge
I object only to the interminable comments
He brings back Shakespeare, the poet.

questions.prompt: How does the imagined question about Huss dramatize a problem that a general complaint about tests would miss?
facilitatorNotes: The frantic search retrieves irrelevant knowledge but not the needed fact until time is gone. The rag-bag scene distinguishes having encountered information from retrieving it usefully under pressure, and its comedy exposes rather than literally records one specific examination.
evidence: all the things you know which are not on the examination paper
the proctor informs you that the time is up

questions.prompt: Why acknowledge mixed metaphors before ending with a leisurely walk and “knowledge is happiness”?
facilitatorNotes: Keller recognizes that her crowded images reproduce mental confusion; the calmer final image proposes patient, receptive learning as a remedy. She revises her romantic expectations without abandoning education’s value. Readers may consider whether the conclusion resolves the conflict or states an aspiration.
evidence: the mixed metaphors mocking and strutting about before me
our minds hospitably open to impressions of every sort
knowledge is happiness

days.title: The Story of My Life: learning to love books (chapter xxi)
days.challenge: Follow an author’s account of her own reading and test her generalizations against her examples.
days.focus: How a reader who learned language through touch describes the pleasures and limits of early reading.
days.context: Keller, deaf and blind from early childhood, learned language through finger-spelling with her teacher Anne Sullivan. Writing as a Radcliffe College student, she now turns from events to the books that shaped her.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XXI, opening through the paragraph on The Jungle Book; from “I HAVE thus far sketched the events of my life, but I have not shown how mu…” through “…ragedies. And if they point a moral, it is so subtle that we are not conscious of it.”

questions.prompt: Keller says she read early books “whether I understood one word in ten.” What did that uncomprehending reading give her anyway?
facilitatorNotes: Words and whole sentences she did not understand were stored and later “flash out” in her speech and writing. She credits memory and exposure while admitting she took “no conscious account” of meaning. Readers may question whether this counts as reading.
evidence: these words and sentences would flash out quite naturally

questions.prompt: Why does she describe the Fauntleroy afternoon in such sensory detail?
facilitatorNotes: She says the vivid details contrast with her vague memories of earlier reading: this was the first book she understood. The same scene shows dependence, too, when Sullivan’s tired fingers stop and Keller feels her “deprivations.”
evidence: I have given these details at the risk of being tedious

questions.prompt: What is Keller’s objection to animal fables, and how does she distinguish The Jungle Book?
facilitatorNotes: She dislikes caricatures of people dressed as animals and La Fontaine’s morality of self-love; she enjoys stories where animals remain real animals. Students may point out that Kipling’s animals also speak. Keller hedges her view with “I may be wrong.”
evidence: I do not object so much to the cynical and satirical fables as to those in which momentous truths are taught by monkeys and foxes.

days.title: The Story of My Life: Greece, Homer and the Bible (chapter xxi)
days.challenge: Evaluate a writer’s claims about reading when she also qualifies them.
days.focus: Imagery that a blind writer builds from language and touch, and an honest account of childhood bias.
days.context: Keller has described her earliest books and her dislike of fables. She now explains how ancient Greece and the Bible entered her reading life.
days.contentNote: Keller discusses religious texts and admits a childhood prejudice that Hebrews and Egyptians were “barbarians,” which she presents as a mistake. Her religious views are her own.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XXI, from the paragraph on antiquity through the paragraph on things unseen; from “My mind opened naturally and joyously to a conception of antiquity. Greece,…” through “…eep, comforting sense that "things seen are temporal, and things unseen are eternal."”

questions.prompt: Keller says great poetry “needs no other interpreter than a responsive heart.” What experience supports this, and what does she concede?
facilitatorNotes: The Iliad makes her forget her physical limitations. She concedes that professors find “greater riches” than she does. Students may notice that she criticizes analysis while offering a careful analysis herself.
evidence: Great poetry, whether written in Greek or in English, needs no other interpreter than a responsive heart.

questions.prompt: How does the comparison of Virgil and Homer work?
facilitatorNotes: Virgil is cool, still, and sculpted; Homer is warm, alive, and moving. Keller, who cannot see, builds visual images from language and from touch, such as marble. Readers can judge whether the images persuade.
evidence: Virgil is serene and lovely like a marble Apollo in the moonlight

questions.prompt: Why did Keller once find Bible stories dull, and what does she notice about her own reasoning?
facilitatorNotes: She had met enthusiastic Greeks but no Hebrews or Egyptians, so familiarity made one set of stories attractive and the other “queer.” Her admission exposes how bias can masquerade as taste.
evidence: Curiously enough, it never occurred to me to call Greek patronymics "queer."

days.title: The Story of My Life: Shakespeare, history and a literary Utopia (chapter xxi)
days.challenge: Identify a thesis that arrives at the end of a long personal survey.
days.focus: Sympathy, interpretation, and why books feel like a place of equality to Keller.
days.context: Keller has explained her love of Greek literature and her changing view of the Bible. She turns to Shakespeare, history, and modern writers.
days.contentNote: Keller recalls horror at violent scenes in Macbeth and King Lear and uses Shylock with Satan and Judas in ways that echo period religious stereotypes; discuss them as historical attitudes.

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter XXI, from the paragraph on Shakespeare to the end of the chapter; from “I do not remember a time since I have been capable of loving books that I h…” through “…iculously little importance compared with their "large loves and heavenly charities."”

questions.prompt: Why did Keller feel sorry for Shylock and Satan as a child?
facilitatorNotes: She thought they could not be good without help or a fair chance. Readers can discuss whether the sympathy is wise or naive, and how it might connect to her own dependence on others’ help.
evidence: they could not be good even if they wished to, because no one seemed willing to help them or to give them a fair chance

questions.prompt: Why did she make a “secret compact” to stop studying critics’ interpretations, and why does she break it?
facilitatorNotes: Commentary discouraged and annoyed her; studying with Professor Kittredge later lets her see “veil after veil lift.” The admission qualifies her earlier claim that a responsive heart is enough.
evidence: so I made a secret compact with myself not to try any more

questions.prompt: What does Keller mean by calling literature a place where she is “not disfranchised”?
facilitatorNotes: To be disfranchised is to be shut out from rights and participation. Books talk to her “without embarrassment or awkwardness,” unlike some people. The political word turns a personal pleasure into a claim about equal access.
evidence: In a word, literature is my Utopia. Here I am not disfranchised.

days.title: The Fisherman
days.challenge: Revise an initial assumption about a vividly described person when the poem reveals that he is imagined.
days.focus: The ideal reader as a response to disappointment with a real audience.
days.context: The poem begins with a fisherman who seems visible, then examines the poet’s desired audience. Pay attention to the later admission about the man’s existence.
days.contentNote: The speaker uses contemptuous descriptions of an audience and mentions drunken cheering; these are part of the dramatic argument.

excerpt.locator: THE FISHERMAN; complete individual poem; opening “Although I can see him still, The freckled man who goes To a grey place on a hill”; closing “I am old I shall have written him one Poem maybe as cold And passionate as the dawn.'”.

questions.prompt: Which details initially make the fisherman seem like a particular observed person, and how does the later revelation alter them?
facilitatorNotes: Freckles, clothing, dawn fishing, and the wrist movement build specificity. Learning that he is a dream makes that vividness an act of artistic construction rather than proof of an actual model.
evidence:
A man who does not exist,
A man who is but a dream;

questions.prompt: How does the list of disliked public figures explain the need for an imagined listener without proving that the poet’s judgment is fair?
facilitatorNotes: The list shows frustration with applause, jokes, and unpunished knavery. It establishes the speaker’s standards and anger, but readers can question his contempt or idealization rather than adopt it wholesale.
evidence:
The beating down of the wise
And great Art beaten down.

questions.prompt: How can a poem be both cold and passionate like dawn?
facilitatorNotes: Cold can suggest clear restraint or the physical air, while passionate suggests intensity and fresh energy. The ending imagines disciplined feeling, not necessarily an emotionless work; different interpretations should preserve both adjectives.
evidence:
Poem maybe as cold
And passionate as the dawn.'

days.title: America
days.challenge: Hold opposing evaluations together and follow a sonnet’s movement from bodily images to a distant future.
days.focus: Love, resistance, and historical impermanence within one address to a personified nation.
days.context: The speaker addresses America as “she” and refuses a simple choice between admiration and criticism. Track the connecting words “Although,” “Yet,” and “Darkly.”
days.contentNote: The poem includes metaphorical bodily attack and the word “hell” to describe a hostile society.

excerpt.locator: AMERICA; complete individual poem; opening “Although she feeds me bread of bitterness, And sinks into my throat her tiger’s tooth, Stealing my breath”; closing “and granite wonders there, Beneath the touch of Time’s unerring hand, Like priceless treasures sinking in the sand.”.

questions.prompt: How can America’s vigor strengthen a speaker who also describes her as hateful?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker draws energy from the same power that resists him, creating a paradox rather than canceling the injury. Responses should keep both the tiger’s tooth and the strengthening tides in view.
evidence: Giving me strength erect against her hate.

questions.prompt: What does the comparison with a rebel standing before a king reveal about the speaker’s stance?
facilitatorNotes: It combines unequal power with dignity and refusal to be cowed. He rejects terror but also says he bears no malice or jeering; this is controlled confrontation, not simple surrender or uncontrolled anger.
evidence: Yet as a rebel fronts a king in state,

questions.prompt: How does the final image of treasures sinking in sand change the scale of America’s apparent power?
facilitatorNotes: Time makes even granite wonders vulnerable. Calling them priceless allows admiration to coexist with the forecast of decline; the ending need not be reduced to either a curse or a celebration.
evidence: Like priceless treasures sinking in the sand.

days.title: America’s Indian Problem
days.challenge: Distinguish an author’s argument from the documentary evidence she quotes.
days.focus: A reform argument built from history and an official investigation.
days.context: Zitkala-Sa campaigned for Native American citizenship and for reform of the federal Indian Bureau. This essay closes American Indian Stories (1921) and quotes at length from a 1915 report by the Bureau of Municipal Research.
days.contentNote: The essay describes dispossession, fraud, malnutrition, and the killing or confinement of Native people who resisted, and it uses period terms such as “aborigine,” “red man,” and “paleface.”

excerpt.locator: American Indian Stories, complete essay “America’s Indian Problem,” including its quoted report extracts; from “The hospitality of the American aborigine, it is told, saved the early sett…” through “…stly dealing with a large population which had no political rights."--Edict Magazine.”

questions.prompt: How do the opening stories of Newport’s cross and DeSoto’s pearls support Zitkala-Sa’s claim about how land was taken?
facilitatorNotes: Native hospitality is answered by deception and plunder. The anecdotes are vivid and quoted from earlier histories, which makes them memorable but selective; students can discuss how much such examples prove.
evidence: It was in this fashion that the old world snatched away the fee in the land of the new.

questions.prompt: What does Zitkala-Sa want changed, according to her own paragraphs before the quoted report?
facilitatorNotes: She seeks citizenship instead of wardship, fair settlement of treaties, and a constructive program instead of “piecemeal legislation.” She addresses American women as allies.
evidence: Wardship is no substitute for American citizenship, therefore we seek his enfranchisement.

questions.prompt: Why does she rely on an investigators’ report for the rest of the essay, and what does it say about the Indian Office’s records?
facilitatorNotes: An official investigation supplies evidence beyond personal testimony. It says the government does not know the condition of the funds it holds in trust. Readers should distinguish her argument from the report’s language and notice its 1915 date.
evidence: it does not know and the officers do not know what is the present condition of the Indian funds in their keeping.

days.title: A marriage in the society papers: part 1 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the noble bachelor)
days.challenge: Read social reporting for its implicit judgments as well as its facts.
days.focus: Compare measures of importance based on rank, money, and intellectual interest.
days.context: Watson recalls a marriage scandal whose public reports omitted important facts. A letter from Lord St. Simon brings the case to Baker Street.
days.contentNote: The newspapers use class and national stereotypes and frame marriage partly as an exchange of wealth and status.

excerpt.locator: The Noble Bachelor, opening through the notices before the disappearance; opens “The Lord St. Simon marriage, and its curious termination, have long ceased to be a su”; closes “, near Petersfield. Those are all the notices which appeared before the disappearance of the bride.””.

questions.prompt: How does Lord St. Simon’s request to postpone other business contrast with Holmes’s stated priorities?
facilitatorNotes: The lord assumes his rank and personal urgency entitle him to precedence. Holmes values the interest of a case more than the client’s social position, though his own scale is also selective.
evidence: the status of my client is a matter of less moment to me than the interest of his case

questions.prompt: What exchange does the society notice imply beneath the language of a fashionable marriage?
facilitatorNotes: The American heiress brings money while the noble family brings social standing. Its reference to the depleted estate challenges the suggestion that only the bride gains.
evidence: the Californian heiress is not the only gainer

questions.prompt: Why does the opening warning about public knowledge matter when Watson begins reading newspaper notices?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says the public possesses only part of the story. Readers should treat the notices as evidence of what was reported, not as a complete explanation.
evidence: the full facts have never been revealed to the general public

days.title: The report and the visitor: part 2 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the noble bachelor)
days.challenge: Examine how a witness presents his own social importance.
days.focus: Separate a newspaper’s reported observations from a theory of wrongdoing.
days.context: The notices describe the planned wedding of an English nobleman and an American heiress. Watson now reads the report of her disappearance.
days.contentNote: A bride is feared missing; the report speculates about foul play and a jealous former companion. Class prejudice shapes descriptions.

excerpt.locator: The Noble Bachelor, Holmes’s surprised question through his request for the bride’s character; opens ““Before the what?” asked Holmes, with a start.”; closes ““Now, what is your own impression as to the young lady’s—your wife’s character?””.

questions.prompt: What makes the footman’s evidence less certain than a simple identification of the departing bride?
facilitatorNotes: He believes the person seen in outdoor clothes cannot have been his mistress. The account distinguishes an observed figure from his interpretation of who it could be.
evidence: refused to credit that it was his mistress

questions.prompt: Why does Holmes want Watson to remain during the interview?
facilitatorNotes: He explicitly wants another listener to check his memory. That recognizes a practical limit in recalling testimony rather than treating his own recollection as infallible.
evidence: if only as a check to my own memory

questions.prompt: How does St. Simon’s account of meeting Hatty reveal the center of his attention?
facilitatorNotes: He describes being amused by her company and assumes she could see his pleasure. His wording tells more about his own response than about what she thought; readers should not take it as direct access to her feelings.
evidence: I was amused by her society, and she could see that I was amused.

days.title: A bouquet and an unexamined assumption: part 3 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the noble bachelor)
days.challenge: Challenge an explanation whose assumptions favor its speaker.
days.focus: Notice details a witness dismisses and distinguish possibility from probability.
days.context: St. Simon supplies the private details missing from the newspaper. Holmes asks about the bride’s behavior before and after the ceremony.
days.contentNote: The dialogue contains sexist generalizations, class prejudice, and speculation about a woman’s mental state.

excerpt.locator: The Noble Bachelor, the bride’s character through Lestrade’s arrival; opens “The nobleman swung his glasses a little faster and stared down into the fire. “You se”; closes “noon, Lestrade! You will find an extra tumbler upon the sideboard, and there are cigars in the box.””.

questions.prompt: Why is the dropped bouquet worth recording even though St. Simon calls the incident trivial?
facilitatorNotes: A stranger returns it just before the bride’s mood changes. The timing makes it potentially significant, while the account has not yet established a cause.
evidence: She dropped her bouquet as we went towards the vestry.

questions.prompt: What distinction does Holmes insist on when discussing whether Flora caused the disappearance?
facilitatorNotes: He allows a possible explanation without calling it likely. St. Simon’s account of Flora’s anger supplies a motive to consider, but not proof of what happened.
evidence: I did not say a probable one.

questions.prompt: What assumption underlies St. Simon’s theory that his bride suffered a nervous disturbance?
facilitatorNotes: He assumes no one could reasonably give up the status marriage to him offers. That self-serving premise narrows his imagination instead of testing other possible commitments or information.
evidence: I can hardly explain it in any other fashion.

days.title: Two sides of a note: part 4 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the noble bachelor)
days.challenge: Distinguish finding a clue from understanding its significance.
days.focus: Evaluate rival interpretations of the same physical evidence.
days.context: Lestrade has searched the Serpentine lake while Holmes has formed a different explanation. He brings objects recovered from the water.
days.contentNote: The investigators discuss possible death; Holmes ridicules Lestrade rather than explaining his reasoning patiently. Tobacco and alcohol appear.

excerpt.locator: The Noble Bachelor, Lestrade’s wet arrival through Holmes’s departure; opens “The official detective was attired in a pea-jacket and cravat, which gave him a decid”; closes “ut-door work,” he remarked, “so I think, Watson, that I must leave you to your papers for a little.””.

questions.prompt: What unsupported step links the recovered wedding clothes to Lestrade’s search for a body?
facilitatorNotes: He assumes clothes in the water mean their wearer must be nearby. Discarded clothes could have arrived separately, so their location does not alone establish a death.
evidence: if the clothes were there the body would not be far off

questions.prompt: How does the reverse side of the note change the kind of investigation available?
facilitatorNotes: The message invites interpretation of initials and intentions; the hotel bill offers a transaction that may be checked against records. Holmes recognizes useful information Lestrade has already seen but dismissed.
evidence: the fragment of a hotel bill

questions.prompt: How does Holmes’s decision to go out qualify his mocking treatment of Lestrade?
facilitatorNotes: He concedes that practical investigation has value and leaves to test or complete his theory. The scene does not support a simple claim that sitting and thinking can replace all fieldwork.
evidence: There is something in what the fellow says about out-door work

days.title: The bride tells her story: part 5 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the noble bachelor)
days.challenge: Evaluate a character’s explanation without assuming it excuses every choice.
days.focus: Use a first-person account to reinterpret earlier clues.
days.context: Holmes has arranged a supper and summoned St. Simon. Two new guests arrive, allowing the missing woman to give her own account.
days.contentNote: The account describes a presumed death and invokes a stereotyped frontier story of attack and captivity involving Apache people; no Indigenous perspective is supplied. It also discusses a secret earlier marriage.

excerpt.locator: The Noble Bachelor, the unexpected supper through Mrs. Moulton’s apology; opens “It was after five o’clock when Sherlock Holmes left me, but I had no time to be lonel”; closes “, and I am very sorry if I have given you pain, and I hope that you do not think very meanly of me.””.

questions.prompt: How does Hatty’s account transform the dropped bouquet from an accident into a purposeful act?
facilitatorNotes: She drops it toward Frank so he can pass her a note when returning it. The incident now connects a recognized person with a secret message.
evidence: he slipped the note into my hand when he returned me the flowers

questions.prompt: How do the two newspaper reports have opposite effects on the couple’s lives?
facilitatorNotes: The earlier report wrongly persuades Hatty that Frank has died; the wedding notice later helps Frank locate her. Published information can mislead or help depending on its accuracy and what readers infer.
evidence: there was my Frank’s name among the killed

questions.prompt: What responsibility does Hatty accept even while explaining her confusion and fear?
facilitatorNotes: She admits she should have spoken to St. Simon and recognizes that concealment would put her in the wrong. Readers can understand her shock while judging the harm caused by leaving others uninformed.
evidence: I know I ought to have spoken to Lord St. Simon

days.title: Explanation and compassion: part 6 of 6 (Sherlock Holmes, the noble bachelor)
days.challenge: Consider whether understanding an outcome changes how a disappointed person should be judged.
days.focus: Distinguish a coherent reconstruction from the evidence used to test it.
days.context: Hatty has explained that her first husband, believed dead, returned on the wedding day. Holmes must now explain how he found them and manage St. Simon’s response.
days.contentNote: The ending discusses lost marital status and wealth; Holmes’s imagined political union reflects his period’s national assumptions.

excerpt.locator: The Noble Bachelor, St. Simon’s response through the closing violin request; opens “Lord St. Simon had by no means relaxed his rigid attitude, but had listened with a fr”; closes “in, for the only problem we have still to solve is how to while away these bleak autumnal evenings.””.

questions.prompt: How does Holmes move from the hotel bill to a verifiable address?
facilitatorNotes: High prices narrow the likely hotels; matching ledger entries identify Moulton; a forwarding address leads to Gordon Square. These checks provide a traceable route rather than simply a lucky guess.
evidence: His letters were to be forwarded to 226 Gordon Square

questions.prompt: Why does Holmes call the sequence natural even though the result looked inexplicable to Lestrade?
facilitatorNotes: The missing private history makes each action intelligible. The outward clues were puzzling because the investigators initially lacked the relationship that connected them.
evidence: Nothing could be more natural than the sequence of events

questions.prompt: How does Holmes’s final response complicate Watson’s criticism of St. Simon’s manners?
facilitatorNotes: He asks Watson to imagine sudden personal and financial loss. This permits compassion for disappointment without requiring approval of the lord’s earlier arrogance or hostility.
evidence: we may judge Lord St. Simon very mercifully

days.title: Fruit of the Flower
days.challenge: Follow changes from surface portraits of parents to hints of hidden feeling, then interpret the final family metaphor.
days.focus: The speaker’s challenge to a family’s surprise at the passions their child inherits.
days.context: The poem begins with orderly portraits of a father and mother, then questions whether those portraits tell the whole story.
days.contentNote: The poem uses religious contrasts and the period image of a “naked tribal dance.” Discuss these as the speaker’s figurative language, not as a general account of a culture.

excerpt.locator: Fruit of the Flower; complete individual poem; opening “MY father is a quiet man With sober, steady ways; For simile, a folded fan; His nights are”; closing “a bud, Extract of that same root; Why marvel at the hectic blood That flushes this wild fruit?”.

questions.prompt: How do the folded fan and calm pool make the parents seem reserved, and what hints later reopen those images?
facilitatorNotes: Both initial images suggest contained feeling. The father’s eyes and the mother’s bodily response to a patch of ground imply concealed history or passion; readers need not invent a specific secret to notice the contradiction.
evidence: For simile, a folded fan;

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker ask “Why should” twice rather than simply accuse the parents of hypocrisy?
facilitatorNotes: The questions present the son’s passions as understandable continuations of theirs. They invite reconsideration and expose surprise, while leaving affection, irritation, or both available in the tone.
evidence: Why should she think it devil’s art

questions.prompt: What does the final root-bud-fruit sequence argue about the relationship between parents and child?
facilitatorNotes: The child’s vivid feeling grows from the same living source, so difference in expression does not mean complete disconnection. The metaphor can support continuity without claiming that every personality trait is biologically fixed.
evidence:
Who plants a seed begets a bud,
Extract of that same root;

days.title: The Living Beauty
days.challenge: Untangle a long sentence and examine the qualifications “say” and “maybe dream” before accepting the speaker’s claim of contentment.
days.focus: Art, aging, desire, and the difference between enduring objects and an individual’s experience of them.
days.context: The speaker contrasts cast or carved beauty with living beauty. Notice that his opening statement about contentment is tentative.

excerpt.locator: THE LIVING BEAUTY; complete individual poem; opening “I'll say and maybe dream I have drawn content— Seeing that time has frozen up the blood, The”; closing “we are old, The living beauty is for younger men, We cannot pay its tribute of wild tears.”.
