questions.prompt: Why does “I’ll say and maybe dream” make the claim of contentment uncertain from the start?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker may be trying to persuade himself rather than reporting settled peace. That qualification matters when interpreting the later acceptance of age; the poem can contain resignation and desire at once.
evidence: I'll say and maybe dream I have drawn content—

questions.prompt: How does the burned wick and spent oil image make aging more concrete than simply announcing “we are old”?
facilitatorNotes: It presents youth as a flame sustained by a finite supply. Students can discuss depleted energy or passion, while recognizing that the metaphor is the speaker’s experience rather than a universal account of aging.
evidence: The wick of youth being burned and the oil spent—

questions.prompt: Why might bronze or marble beauty be unsatisfying despite its apparent permanence?
facilitatorNotes: It is indifferent to solitude, and when viewers are gone their experience of it is gone too. The ending suggests that living beauty demands emotional tribute unavailable to this speaker; readings can question that conclusion while explaining it.
evidence: Being more indifferent to our solitude

days.title: Flame-Heart
days.challenge: Track what the speaker cannot date against what remains vividly present, and compare the altered refrain across three stanzas.
days.focus: The selectivity of memory and the survival of childhood feeling through one repeated flower image.
days.context: Ten years separate the speaker from the remembered childhood scenes. A poinsettia’s recurring color becomes a link across that gap.
days.contentNote: The poem includes figurative references to blood-red flowers and “wine-thrilled” feeling; these are retained.

excerpt.locator: FLAME-HEART; complete individual poem; opening “So much have I forgotten in ten years, So much in ten brief years! I have forgot What”; closing “in the flame-heart’s shade. We were so happy, happy, I remember, Beneath the poinsettia’s red in warm December.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem list forgotten seasons and months so precisely if the speaker cannot remember them?
facilitatorNotes: The list demonstrates the kind of intimate knowledge that has faded and the effort to recover it. Memory is incomplete but not empty; the detailed names remain even when their timing is lost.
evidence:
I have forgot the special, startling season
Of the pimento’s flowering and fruiting;

questions.prompt: How does the recurring poinsettia line serve a different purpose from the questions about dates?
facilitatorNotes: It provides a stable sensory anchor amid uncertainty. The repeated red and warm December preserve feeling and place even when a complete calendar cannot be reconstructed.
evidence: The poinsettia’s red, blood-red in warm December.

questions.prompt: What changes in the last stanza when the speaker says the days have been “embalmed” and then recalls happiness?
facilitatorNotes: The word preserves moments almost like something lost or dead, while happiness makes them emotionally alive. The final refrain loses the emphatic blood-red phrase; responses may explore gentleness or emotional resolution without calling the memories fully recovered.
evidence: Oh some I know! I have embalmed the days,

days.title: For a Poet
days.challenge: Reread the repeated lines and examine images that can suggest both precious preservation and burial.
days.focus: The uncertain relationship between sheltering dreams and sealing them away.
days.context: This complete short poem appears in Color’s Epitaphs section. Listen to how repeated wrapping and storing can sound protective or final.
days.contentNote: The poem’s setting and images invite reflection on death and artistic loss.

excerpt.locator: For a Poet; complete individual poem; opening “I HAVE wrapped my dreams in a silken cloth, And laid them away in a box of gold;”; closing “I have wrapped my dreams in a silken cloth, And laid them away in a box of gold.”.

questions.prompt: What do silk and gold say about the value placed on the dreams, and why is value not the same as freedom?
facilitatorNotes: The materials honor the dreams as precious, yet the box confines them. A response can see loving preservation, withdrawal, or burial, but should account for both luxurious care and enclosure.
evidence: And laid them away in a box of gold;

questions.prompt: How do the moth’s “lips” disturb the safety suggested by wrapping?
facilitatorNotes: A moth can consume cloth, so the delicate personification places decay beside protection. Its lips may also sound like a kiss; that ambiguity deepens rather than removes the threat.
evidence: Where long will cling the lips of the moth,

questions.prompt: What is the effect of claiming not to be angry while describing the earth’s breath as keen and cold?
facilitatorNotes: The denial may signal forgiveness, resignation, or an effort to master hurt. Readers should hear the cold world beside the repeated safe enclosure rather than assume the speaker has never suffered.
evidence: I hide no hate; I am not even wroth

days.title: The Hawk
days.challenge: Track three quoted speeches and the final phrase “hawk of the mind” to reconsider the earlier literal scene.
days.focus: The conflict between demands for useful service and an imagination that claims freedom.
days.context: The first voice wants a hunting bird brought under control; the next refuses. The final voice introduces the idea that the hawk may represent a mental power.

excerpt.locator: THE HAWK; complete individual poem; opening “'Call down the hawk from the air; Let him be hooded or caged Till the yellow eye has”; closing “that I, who had sat Dumbfounded before a knave, Should give to my friend A pretence of wit.'”.

questions.prompt: How do the empty larder, angry cook, and wild scullion make the demand to cage the hawk sound practical rather than purely cruel?
facilitatorNotes: The household needs food and order, so the demand has a material motive. The poem can still question that motive’s claim over the hawk; acknowledge the conflict rather than treating one side as having no reason.
evidence: For larder and spit are bare,

questions.prompt: What has the hawk learned that makes a hood or wrist unacceptable?
facilitatorNotes: Pride in free movement over wood, mist, and cloud has changed its willingness to serve. The refusal joins bodily freedom with self-knowledge rather than simply a dislike of one keeper.
evidence: Now I have learnt to be proud

questions.prompt: How does “hawk of the mind” alter the meaning of the speaker’s inability to find wit before a knave?
facilitatorNotes: It suggests an imagination or intellect absent from immediate social usefulness. The final complaint can be read as the cost of mental freedom or frustration with an elusive gift; the unanswered question leaves the relationship unsettled.
evidence: Yellow-eyed hawk of the mind,

days.title: Men Improve with the Years
days.challenge: Test a title against the poem that follows it.
days.focus: Aging, longing, and doubt beneath a show of wisdom.
days.context: An aging speaker compares himself to a weather-worn marble triton, a sea-god statue in a fountain, as he gazes at a young woman’s beauty.

excerpt.locator: MEN IMPROVE WITH THE YEARS; complete individual poem; opening “I am worn out with dreams; A weather-worn, marble triton Among the streams; And”; closing “youth; But I grow old among dreams, A weather-worn, marble triton Among the streams.”.

questions.prompt: What does the image of the marble triton suggest about the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: Stone, weathered, decorative, and fixed in place. The image returns at the end, framing him as stuck.
evidence:
A weather-worn, marble triton
Among the streams;

questions.prompt: How does “And yet and yet” test the title’s claim?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker doubts his own contentment with wisdom; the title becomes ironic.
evidence:
And yet and yet
Is this my dream, or the truth?

questions.prompt: What does the speaker regret?
facilitatorNotes: He wishes they had met when he had “burning youth.” Fire contrasts with stone; he views beauty “as though I had found in book / A pictured beauty,” at a distance.
evidence:
O would that we had met
When I had my burning youth;

days.title: Poetry
days.challenge: Identify the addressed “thee” through the title and examine how a poem can express fear of poetry itself.
days.focus: The tension between devotion to art and protection of ordinary human loves.
days.context: This is a poem addressed to Poetry. Its frightening images concern the power of art, not a narrated physical assault.
days.contentNote: The poem uses symbolic death, sacrifice, and an altar to express artistic anxiety.

excerpt.locator: POETRY; complete individual poem; opening “Sometimes I tremble like a storm-swept flower, And seek to hide my tortured soul from thee. Bowing my”; closing “thy magic cup! I fear, I fear my truly human heart Will perish on the altar-stone of art!”.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker’s comparison with a storm-swept flower establish the power difference between speaker and Poetry?
facilitatorNotes: The flower is exposed and easily battered, while Poetry has thunder, light, and breath. The comparison makes the artist vulnerable to the art rather than simply its master.
evidence: Sometimes I tremble like a storm-swept flower,

questions.prompt: What does the speaker fear losing in the “magic cup,” and why is magic not purely attractive here?
facilitatorNotes: Earthly loves, pleasure, and passion might be swallowed by artistic absorption. The attractive power also threatens disappearance; students can discuss a conflict between art and life without assuming the author rejected art.
evidence: The loves which are to me of vital worth,

questions.prompt: What paradox is created by expressing fear of art in a carefully made poem?
facilitatorNotes: The poem demonstrates art’s power even as it questions its demands. The final fear can be sincere, dramatized, or both; use the crafted address and images to avoid treating it as a simple instruction to stop writing.
evidence: Will perish on the altar-stone of art!

days.title: To My Friends
days.challenge: Work through long sentences and reversals between poverty and wealth to identify the speaker’s final plain claim.
days.focus: The value of a small circle of friends and the reciprocity of faithfulness.
days.context: The speaker addresses a few friends in grand language, then calls that language “fine heroics” and restates the point simply.

excerpt.locator: To My Friends; complete individual poem; opening “YOU feeble few that hold me somewhat more Than all I am; base clay and spittle joined To”; closing “In brief, these fine heroics come to this, My friends: if you are true, I needs must be.”.

questions.prompt: How can the friends be a “feeble few” and a “golden host” at once?
facilitatorNotes: Their number is small, but their emotional worth is large. The contrast turns conventional military abundance into intimate richness; it can sound affectionate and self-mocking rather than merely insulting.
evidence:
O golden host I count upon the ends
Of one bare hand, with fingers still to spare,—

questions.prompt: What does the poor heart manage to hold “in opulence,” and how does that revise the opening self-description?
facilitatorNotes: It holds friendship richly despite the speaker’s harsh description of his own making. The poem’s value system makes steadfast relationships a form of wealth that survives self-doubt.
evidence:
Is rich enough for this: to harbor there
In opulence its frugal meed of friends.

questions.prompt: Why finish by translating the “fine heroics” into a direct conditional statement?
facilitatorNotes: The shift strips away ornament to emphasize mutual obligation. Some readers may hear dependence in “if,” others reciprocal trust; either should explain how the friends’ truthfulness calls forth the speaker’s.
evidence: My friends: if you are true, I needs must be.

days.title: To You Who Read My Book
days.challenge: Track a sequence of changing metaphors over many short stanzas and explain how direct requests shape a future reader’s role.
days.focus: Poetry offered as a record of a living voice in resistance to time and mortality.
days.context: This opening poem addresses the reader of the collection itself. Mark where the speaker moves from time’s power to the gift of the book and then to instructions for remembering.
days.contentNote: The poem contains intense figurative images of death, including hawks at a throat and an axe cutting a tree; no literal violent event is narrated.

excerpt.locator: To You Who Read My Book; complete individual poem; opening “SOON every sprinter, However fleet, Comes to a winter Of sure defeat: Though he may race Like the”; closing “the blows fall free On a gnarled trunk now, Once he was a tree With a blossomy bough.””.

questions.prompt: How does Time become more than a background in the opening race and singing contest?
facilitatorNotes: Time is an active rival that outruns and outsings every person. The repeated contests deny the speaker an easy victory, making the later gift of poetry a response to a real limit rather than a boast of immortality.
evidence:
Time will outsing
Us every one.

questions.prompt: What changes when the speaker offers the first grapes of his vine and his “own heart’s wine”?
facilitatorNotes: The poem turns from inevitable loss to present generosity and work. Reading becomes an act of receiving something grown and made from a life; the metaphor also links the book to its author without making it identical to a factual biography.
evidence:
I proffer your thirst
My own heart’s wine.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker ask future readers to recall a singing bird and a blossoming tree instead of only a damaged body?
facilitatorNotes: The book preserves signs of vitality that death cannot be allowed to define retroactively. The closing commands ask the reader to reconstruct former life from the poems; the images acknowledge damage while resisting a memory consisting only of it.
evidence:
Once he was a tree
With a blossomy bough.”
